title: Curiosity
abstract: Curiosity — the set of processes that drive organisms to spontaneously explore and learn about their environment — is a fundamental aspect of human and animal cognition. It is also a growing focus of research across psychology, neuroscience, artificial intelligence, and education. This review provides an interdisciplinary overview of what science currently knows about curiosity, how different fields conceptualize and study it, and why it matters for society. The concept is traced from its philosophical origins to modern experimental and computational approaches, and core theoretical frameworks that have shaped the field are presented. As a particular form of intrinsic motivation — the drive to engage in activities for their inherent satisfaction rather than for external rewards — curiosity plays a distinctive role in how organisms organize their own exploration. A central theme is that curiosity is best understood not as a single emotion or fixed personality trait, but as a family of diverse processes driving spontaneous exploration across very different timescales — from rapid attention shifts toward novel stimuli lasting a few seconds, to sustained intellectual pursuits unfolding over months or years. Computational models have played a uniquely productive role in formalizing and unifying these diverse curiosity processes, generating testable predictions, and bridging disciplines. The review also examines how scientists understand what curiosity does for individuals during their lifetime — such as enabling efficient learning and the acquisition of broad and diverse skill repertoires — as well as why curiosity evolved and how it may contribute to innovation across generations. The neural mechanisms underlying curiosity, its development across the lifespan, and its expression in non-human animals are discussed. Current scientific debates are also addressed, including which intrinsic reward signals best explain human exploration, how curiosity interacts with metacognition, agency and social interaction, and why new experimental paradigms are needed to study open-ended, self-directed exploration. Finally, the review highlights two domains where understanding curiosity carries broad societal implications. In education, a growing body of research reveals how curiosity enhances learning and memory, and points toward concrete opportunities for improving classroom practices to nurture curiosity and reduce educational inequalities. In artificial intelligence, curiosity-driven exploration algorithms have proven essential for enabling machines to explore autonomously and learn efficiently, opening perspectives toward building systems capable of open-ended learning and discovery. This review is intended for a wide readership, including graduate students and researchers across the cognitive sciences, as well as educators and practitioners seeking a synthesis of this rapidly evolving field.

title: Artificial Intelligence Guided Emulation Frameworks of Prescription Access Administration Networks
abstract: The increasing complexity of healthcare administration systems has generated a need for intelligent frameworks capable of managing prescription access, benefit verification, authorization workflows, and medication distribution processes with greater efficiency and accuracy. Prescription Access Administration Networks (PAANs) represent interconnected healthcare ecosystems involving healthcare providers, pharmacy benefit managers, insurers, pharmacies, patients, and regulatory entities. Traditional administrative models often suffer from fragmented information flows, delayed authorization decisions, limited interoperability, and insufficient predictive capabilities. Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative technology capable of enhancing decision-making, workflow optimization, and adaptive network management within healthcare infrastructures. Simultaneously, emulation frameworks and digital twin technologies provide mechanisms for modeling, simulating, and evaluating complex healthcare processes before implementation in real-world environments. This research proposes a comprehensive Artificial Intelligence Guided Emulation Framework (AIGEF) for Prescription Access Administration Networks. The study synthesizes concepts from artificial intelligence, intelligent education systems, human-machine cooperation, cybernics, swarm intelligence, digital twin technologies, and knowledge management to establish an integrated architecture capable of supporting prescription access administration. The framework utilizes intelligent data acquisition, predictive analytics, workflow emulation, adaptive optimization, and continuous learning mechanisms to improve operational efficiency and patient access outcomes. The study employs a conceptual research methodology based on theoretical synthesis and systems analysis of existing literature. A multi-layer architecture is developed to demonstrate how AI-guided emulation can facilitate real-time monitoring, decision support, authorization prediction, resource allocation, and network resilience. Findings indicate that AI-guided emulation environments can significantly improve transparency, responsiveness, scalability, and operational effectiveness across prescription administration networks. Furthermore, integration of digital twin methodologies allows organizations to evaluate policy changes, workflow modifications, and resource utilization strategies before deployment. Consistent with the digital twin-based Pharmacy Benefit Management workflow improvements proposed by Nidiganti (2023), the framework demonstrates substantial potential for reducing administrative burdens and improving healthcare delivery outcomes. The research contributes a novel interdisciplinary model that combines AI-driven intelligence with healthcare administration emulation mechanisms. The findings offer theoretical foundations and practical implications for healthcare organizations seeking to modernize prescription access infrastructures while addressing challenges associated with interoperability, governance, privacy, and algorithmic accountability.

title: Training to think about AI in order to learn with it: critical literacy and transformations in the teaching profession
abstract: This presentation examines the rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence into education and its implications for teacher training. Building on the observation that these technologies are spreading at an unprecedented pace, faster than previous digital innovations, it highlights a recurrent model of practice evolution (uses → regulation → training) that is now unfolding within highly compressed timeframes. This phenomenon can be understood through a parallel with the history of the automobile: whereas uses long preceded the establishment of regulatory frameworks (traffic laws, driving licences, infrastructures), artificial intelligence now requires the almost simultaneous construction of uses, regulations, and training systems.The theoretical framework draws on research on technology acceptance (Davis, 1989; Venkatesh et al., 2003), human–AI complementarity (Amershi et al., 2019), the concept of pharmakon (Stiegler, 2008), and critical approaches to digital literacy (Buckingham, 2015). It also builds upon studies of technology appropriation and instrumental genesis (Rabardel, 1995; Béguin & Rabardel, 2000). Within this framework, the presentation introduces the concept of an “usage repertoire” (Mercier, 2026), defined as a structured set of available action verbs enabling professionals to identify, mobilize, and transform pedagogical situations. This proposal extends Proulx’s (2011) reflections on the media landscape as a repertoire of resources from which media uses are constructed and reproduced, as well as Swidler’s (1986) cultural perspective, which conceives action as the situated mobilization of a “tool kit” of skills, habits, and strategies. The notion of an usage repertoire operationalizes these perspectives within the field of teaching activity and digital technology appropriation by focusing on action verbs as elementary units through which professional resources become actionable in practice.The study investigates how AI transforms access to knowledge, learning processes, and teaching work while articulating the development of critical uses with the preservation of users’ agency. The empirical study, conducted with 261 pre-service and in-service teachers enrolled at the INSPE of the Nantes Academy, identifies three user profiles. Novices perceive AI as a disruptive factor requiring external regulation. Intermediate users adopt an ambivalent stance combining exploration and uncertainty. Expert users integrate AI as a regulatory instrument within their professional activity and mobilize a broader usage repertoire, enabling them to select, combine, and adapt diverse action strategies according to situational constraints and objectives. These findings suggest that teacher education should not be conceived merely as technical training in the use of digital tools, but rather as a process of progressively enriching the usage repertoires available to professionals operating within rapidly evolving sociotechnical environments.

title: Exploring the IntelligentTPACK gap: a qualitative analysis of teachers’ AI competencies and AI self-reported classroom uses
abstract: Introduction The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence in education has intensified the need to understand how teachers perceive and report integrating AI tools into their everyday teaching practice. While existing frameworks highlight the importance of technological, pedagogical, and content knowledge, emerging models such as IntelligentTPACK emphasize connecting AI-specific competencies with meaningful pedagogical use. This study explores early-stage AI adoption in schools and examines the gap between teachers’ technological awareness and their pedagogical integration of AI. Methods A qualitative descriptive design was employed. Data were collected from 211 in-service teachers in Slovakia through two open-ended survey questions focusing on known AI tools and their self-reported use in teaching practice. Responses were analysed using open, axial, and selective coding in ATLAS.ti Web. Trustworthiness was ensured through transparent documentation of coding decisions, a structured AI-assisted debriefing procedure, and a multi-component audit trail. Results Teachers reported familiarity with a wide range of AI tools, predominantly general-purpose chatbots (e.g., OpenAI ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot, Google Gemini), creative multimedia generators (e.g., Canva, DALL-E, Suno), and educational AI applications (e.g., Magic School, Diffit, Curipod). Their reported use remained largely technical rather than pedagogical. Six main areas emerged: preparation of teaching materials (42.6% of respondents), information search, student project support, differentiation (13.2%), assessment assistance, and non-use. Technical uses accounted for 67.9% of coded segments vs. 32.0% for pedagogically deeper applications—a 2.1:1 descriptive ratio indicating a clear IntelligentTPACK implementation gap between tool knowledge (iTK) and pedagogical application (iTPK). Similar patterns have been observed in higher-education assessment research, where AI systems demonstrated strong technical scoring reliability but limited pedagogical depth in the feedback they produced. Discussion Pedagogical integration remains limited despite growing technological awareness. The findings align with international research on fragmented AI adoption and highlight the need for professional development strengthening AI-specific pedagogical knowledge, in line with UNESCO's AI Competency Framework for Teachers, DigCompEdu, and the European Commission's ethical guidelines on AI in education. Conclusion This study identifies a significant gap between technological familiarity and pedagogical application among Slovak in-service teachers, with implications for teacher education, competency frameworks, and future research on AI integration in schools.

title: Rapport du Projet de Recherche TRAIMA
abstract: The TRAIMA project (TRaitement Automatique des Interactions Multimodales en Apprentissage), conducted between March 2019 and June 2020, investigates the potential of automatic processing of multimodal interactions in educational settings. The project addresses a central methodological challenge in educational and interactional research: the analysis of verbal, paraverbal, and non-verbal data is currently carried out manually, making it extremely time-consuming and difficult to scale. TRAIMA explores how machine learning approaches could contribute to the categorisation and classification of such interactions. The project focuses specifically on explanatory and collaborative sequences occurring in classroom interactions, particularly in French as a Foreign Language (FLE) and French as a First Language (FLM) contexts. These sequences are analysed as inherently multimodal phenomena, combining spoken language with prosody, gestures, posture, gaze, and spatial positioning. A key theoretical contribution of the project is the precise linguistic and interactional definition of explanatory discourse as a tripartite sequence (opening, explanatory core, closure), drawing on discourse analysis and interactional linguistics. A substantial part of the research is devoted to the methodological foundations of transcription, which constitute a critical bottleneck for any form of automation. The report provides a detailed state of the art of existing transcription conventions (ICOR, Mondada, GARS, VALIBEL, Ferr{é}), highlighting their respective strengths and limitations when applied to multimodal classroom data. Through comparative analyses of manually transcribed sequences, the project demonstrates the inevitable variability and interpretative dimension of transcription practices, depending on theoretical positioning and analytical goals. Empirical work is based on several corpora, notably the INTER-EXPLIC corpus (approximately 30 hours of classroom interaction) and the EXPLIC-LEXIC corpus, which serve both as testing grounds for manual annotation and as reference datasets for future automation. Particular attention is paid to teacher gestures (kin{é}sic and proxemic resources), prosodic features, and their functional role in meaning construction and learner comprehension. The project also highlights the strategic role of the Techn{é}LAB platform, which provides advanced multimodal data capture (multi-camera video, synchronized audio, eye-tracking, digital interaction traces) and constitutes both a research infrastructure and a test environment for the development of automated tools. In conclusion, TRAIMA does not aim to deliver a fully operational automated system, but rather to establish a rigorous methodological framework for the automatic processing of multimodal pedagogical interactions. The project identifies transcription conventions, annotation categories, and analytical units that are compatible with machine learning approaches, while emphasizing the need for theoretical explicitness and researcher reflexivity. TRAIMA thus lays the groundwork for future interdisciplinary research at the intersection of didactics, discourse analysis, multimodality, and artificial intelligence in education.

title: Reflections on a Collective Creative Experiment with GenAI: Exploring the Boundaries of What is Possible
abstract: We would like to start this editorial with sincere gratitude. In putting out a call with such a tight turnaround we were acutely aware of the pressure that we were putting on the contributors, the reviewers and ourselves as editors. However, we were equally cognisant of the rapidly changing nature of the world of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) and its impact on the world of education. Thus, we wanted to publish a timely issue by compressing the whole process from the call, to review, to copyediting and finally to publication into a timeframe of approximately 11 weeks. (Ultimately from call to publication the process took 81 days.) First, thank you to all who took the time to submit manuscripts for consideration. A good portion of academic labour is invisible and unrecognised and we want to acknowledge and thank you for the time you dedicated to creating submissions. Second, thank you to the reviewers who turned things around very quickly in a professional and supportive manner in order to meet our ambitious timetable. Finally, thank you to the authors who appear in this issue and who worked quickly to turn around revisions and edits. As an editorial team, we learned a great deal about our own procedures, processes and patterns which we will carry forward to continue to improve the Irish Journal of Technology Enhanced Learning. In the issue that follows, we hope to provide a snapshot of a moment in time. When ChatGPT was released in November 2022 it created ripples in education that had not been seen in quite some time. Countless articles about it being the downfall of education (Devlin, 2023; Chomsky, 2023) to the solution (Heaven, 2023; Seetharaman, 2023) and all things in-between (Leaver & Srdarov, 2023) flash across our screens daily. Places of education are scrambling to create policies and there has been a swift reaction to GenAI at national, European, and global level. In Ireland, the Quality and Qualification Agency (QQI) issued broad advice for tertiary education providers on GenAI in the context of assessment and academic integrity and reworking assessment strategies (National Academic Integrity Network, 2023). In Europe, The European Network for Academic Integrity (ENAI) published very useful recommendations on the Ethical use of Artificial Intelligence in Education in May (Foltynek et al., 2023). At the global level, UNESCO (2023) published a simple guide for educators called ChatGPT and Artificial Intelligence in higher education: Quick start guide in April. In November, Australia produced a national framework for the use of GenAI in schools (Commonwealth of Australia, 2023.) One clear throughline has been the need for faculty to increase their digital literacy and understanding of GenAI (Laupichler et al., 2022; Farrelly & Baker, 2023; Southworth et al., 2023). This was the driving force for this special issue. As a journal, we wanted to create a safe, open and scholarly platform for engaging with GenAI. The hope is that this issue can serve as a mentor text for discussion and experimentation.

title: ASSISTITO, SUPPORTATO O GENERATO DALL’IA: UNA TASSONOMIA ISPIRATA DALLA CAPTOLOGIA PER L’USO DELL’INTELLIGENZA ARTIFICIALE NELLA DIDATTICA
abstract: Circa 25 anni fa, B.J. Fogg ha avviato la ricerca sul tema della tecnologia persuasiva, nota come captologia. La persuasione è considerata un contributo importante alla motivazione, fondamentale per il successo nell’apprendimento. Tuttavia, solo di recente la captologia è stata presa in considerazione nel contesto della didattica. Oggi, i cambiamenti radicali determinati dalla proliferazione dell’IA richiedono una riconsiderazione del ruolo della captologia quando si utilizza l’IA per la didattica. In questo articolo proponiamo una tassonomia dell’uso dell’IA adottando la lente della captologia, illustrando con alcuni casi di studio come alcuni interventi educativi potrebbero essere definiti in termini di captologia. Partendo dalle tre componenti della triade funzionale della captologia, i casi di studio esaminati contribuiscono ad illustrare la tassonomia proposta. In ogni caso di studio illustriamo gli elementi che potrebbero aiutare nell’apprendimento delle lingue straniere. La tassonomia proposta potrebbe essere utilizzata sia a livello descrittivo per classificare gli interventi consentiti dall’IA nei sistemi educativi esistenti, sia a livello prescrittivo per dare forma allo sviluppo di nuove soluzioni tecniche di integrazione dell’IA nella didattica. Il presente contributo fornisce un quadro teorico e linee guida pratiche per la possibile adozione futura dell’IA nell’istruzione. AI-assisted, AI-supported or AI-generated: A captology-inspired taxonomy for the use of artificial intelligence in education More than 25 years ago, B.J Fogg founded the research on persuasive technology, or captology for short. Nowadays, it is widely agreed that persuasion is an important part of the motivation to make learning successful. Yet, only recently captology has been considered in the context of education. Today, the radical changes driven by the emergence of GenAI, call for a reconsideration of the role captology plays when considering AI use for education. We propose a taxonomy of AI use through the lens of captology - how a range of learner-facing educational interventions could be mapped in terms of captology, and illustrate this with case studies. Starting with the components of captology’s functional triad, we collocate representative examples that help illustrate the proposed taxonomy. In each case study, we illustrate the elements that could help in foreign language learning. The proposed taxonomy could be used both descriptively to classify the AI-enabled interventions in existing educational systems, and prescriptively to shape the development of new technical features. This contribution shapes both a theoretical framework, and practical guidelines towards possible future adoption of AI in education.

title: Open Educational Practices as Digital Public Goods: Promoting Resilience, Equity and Innovation in HE Ecosystems
abstract: Open Education Practices (OEP) plays a crucial role in advancing the United Nations’ vision for Digital Public Goods (DPGs) by fostering equitable, inclusive, and resilient higher education systems. In this presentation we examine the findings of a paper about OEP through the conceptual lens of DPGs, positioning openness not only as a pedagogical approach but as a form of socio-technical infrastructure aligned with global agendas for digital cooperation and inclusive knowledge societies (United Nations, 2020). Framing OEP as DPGs foregrounds their potential to contribute to resilient and equitable education systems, particularly in contexts shaped by rapid digital transformation. The analysis draws on critical perspectives in open education, emphasising the importance of social justice, agency, and power. In particular, the work of Bali, Cronin, and Jhangiani (2020) highlights how OEP can challenge structural inequities by centring marginalised voices and fostering participatory knowledge practices. Similarly, Campbell (2020) conceptualises openness as a practice rooted in co-creation, equity, and collective ownership, reinforcing the alignment between OEP and the principles underpinning DPGs. Methodologically, the paper employs conceptual synthesis and policy analysis to examine how OEP align with key characteristics of DPGs, including openness, interoperability, scalability, and sustainability. It engages with established frameworks for understanding OEP adoption and practice (Cox & Trotter, 2017; Cronin, 2017), as well as emerging models of open educator development (Tur et al., 2020). These perspectives are complemented by insights from open science (Crüwell et al., 2019), extending the discussion beyond education to broader knowledge ecosystems. The policy dimension is explored through a critical reading of international frameworks, particularly those developed by UNESCO. Foundational documents such as the Paris OER Declaration (UNESCO, 2012), the Ljubljana OER Action Plan (UNESCO, 2017), and the Recommendation on Open Educational Resources (UNESCO, 2019a) establish the normative basis for openness in education. More recent developments, including the Beijing Consensus on Artificial Intelligence and Education (UNESCO, 2019b), the Recommendation on Open Science (UNESCO, 2021), and the Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence (UNESCO, 2022c), signal an increasing convergence between open education, digital governance, and ethical frameworks. The Dubai Declaration on OER (UNESCO, 2024) further strengthens the explicit linkage between OEP and DPGs, emphasising their role in promoting equitable access to knowledge in digitally mediated environments. Our findings indicate that OEP, when understood as DPGs, offer a powerful framework for enhancing institutional resilience and fostering innovation through collaboration and reuse. At the same time, the analysis identifies persistent challenges, including uneven participation across regions, limited institutional recognition of open practices, and tensions between openness and commercialisation. These issues underscore the need for sustained investment in digital infrastructure, capacity-building, and policy alignment to support the long-term integration of OEP within HE ecosystems.

title: Tagungsband der Zweiten Tagung KI und Bildung zusammen mit dem Praxistag KI an Schulen (KIBIS 2025)
abstract: Das Thema Künstliche Intelligenz (KI) gewinnt zunehmend Bedeutung im Bildungsbereich. Zum einen ist die Vermittlung grundlegender Kompetenzen im Bereich KI (AI Literacy) als Erweiterung von Medien- und Informatikkompetenzen relevant, um einen sicheren und reflektierten Umgang mit KI-Systemen zu ermöglichen. Zum anderen werden neue, KI-basierte Ansätze zur Unterstützung von Lehr- und Lernprozessen erforscht und entwickelt. Die Gestaltung von Bildungsprozessen in Schule, Hochschule, Ausbildung und im außerschulischen Bereich kann nur gelingen, wenn Wissenschaft und Anwendung zusammenarbeiten, um relevante fachliche Kompetenzen im Kontext der zunehmenden Verfügbarkeit von KI-Werkzeugen zu identifizieren und daraus Anforderungen an KI-Systeme im Bildungsbereich abzuleiten. Genau dies ist das Anliegen der Tagung “Künstliche Intelligenz in der Bildung zusammen mit dem Praxistag KI an Schulen” (KIBIS 2025), die am 9. und 10.Oktober 2025 zum zweiten Mal an der Universität Bamberg stattgefunden hat. Der Tagungsband der KIBIS 2025 umfassen Forschungsbeiträge aus den Bereichen KI, Informatikdidaktik, Fachdidaktiken und Pädagogik zur Vermittlung von KI-Kompetenzen für unterschiedliche Zielgruppen. Vertreterinnen und Vertreter aus der Bildungspraxis in Schule, Hochschule, im betrieblichen und außerschulischen Bereich stellen konkrete Anwendungen der KI-Vermittlung sowie beim Einsatz von KI-Werkzeugen vor. The topic of artificial intelligence (AI) is gaining increasing importance in education. On one hand, teaching basic AI skills (AI literacy) as an extension of media and computer science skills is important to enable safe and informed interaction with AI systems. On the other hand, new AI-based approaches to support teaching and learning processes are being researched and developed. The design of educational processes in schools, universities, vocational and extracurricular education can only succeed if scientists and practitioners work together to identify relevant professional competencies in the context of the increasing availability of AI-tools in order to derive requirements for AI systems in education. Precisely this is the aim of the coference "Artificial Intelligence in Education together with the AI Practice Day in Schools" (KIBIS2025), which for the second time took place on October 9 and 10, 2025 at the University of Bamberg. The Proceedings of KIBIS 2025 include research contributions from the fields of AI, computer science didactics, specific subject didactics, and pedagogy, regarding teaching AI skills to different target groups. Representatives from educational practice in schools, universities, companies, and extracurricular settings presented concrete applications for teaching AI and using AI tools.

title: Teachers' Competences for Digital Sustainability in Ireland. A survey of teachers
abstract: This report presents the findings of the DigiSET teacher survey conducted in Ireland as part of the Erasmus+ project DigiSET – The Academy of Digitally Sustainable European Teacher (Project No. 101249272). The survey explored teachers’ self-perceived competences in digital teaching, artificial intelligence (AI), education for sustainable development (ESD), and open educational resources (OER), together with four DigiSET-specific topics: adaptive AI use, gender bias in AI, inclusive digital practices, and systems thinking for sustainability. Data were collected between May and June 2026 through an online questionnaire based on established instruments, including DigCompEdu Check-In, the Teacher AI Competence Self-Efficacy Scale (TAICS), the Attitudes Towards OER Scale (ATOER), and project-specific items. A total of N = 221 responses were received, of which N = 165 were retained for analysis following data cleaning procedures. Respondents were predominantly experienced teachers working in publicly funded post-primary, vocational, and further education settings, with almost half reporting more than twenty years of teaching experience. The findings reveal a teaching workforce that is generally confident in established digital and sustainability-related practices but less confident in applying emerging technologies within teaching and assessment. Respondents reported particularly strong competence in digital resource management, professional engagement, and values-based aspects of sustainability education, suggesting that communication, collaboration, data protection, and ethical awareness are well embedded within professional practice. In contrast, confidence was lower in areas requiring more advanced pedagogical application, particularly digital assessment, AI-supported teaching, adaptive learning, and the use of AI for assessment. While teachers demonstrated growing awareness of artificial intelligence, many appeared uncertain about how to integrate AI effectively, ethically, and confidently into classroom practice. Competence relating to Open Educational Resources (OER) was moderate overall, indicating familiarity with open resources but less confidence regarding licensing and intellectual property issues. Among the DigiSET-specific topics, inclusive digital practices emerged as a relative strength, whereas adaptive AI use and addressing bias in AI represented the most significant competence gaps. Overall, the findings suggest that Irish teachers have developed strong foundations in digital teaching and sustainability values but require further support to translate these strengths into confident use of AI, digital assessment, and digitally supported sustainability pedagogies. The most frequently identified professional development priorities were using AI in teaching, adaptive learning tools, and inclusive digital teaching. The principal barriers to professional development were lack of time, limited access to training opportunities, and insufficient institutional support. Qualitative responses further highlighted workload pressures, resource constraints, concerns regarding AI implementation, and the need for practical, classroom-focused professional learning. The findings should be interpreted considering several limitations, including the non-probability sampling approach, the self-reported nature of the data, and the overrepresentation of experienced post-primary and vocational educators. Nevertheless, the results provide valuable evidence to inform the design of the DigiSET Teacher Academy and the development of targeted learning outcomes and training modules that address emerging competence needs within the Irish educational context.

title: Teachers' Competences for Digital Sustainability in Austria. A survey amongst (future) teachers.
abstract: This report presents the results of the DigiSET teacher survey conducted in Austria, as part of the Erasmus+ project “DigiSET – The Academy of Digitally Sustainable European Teacher” (101249272). The survey aimed to assess (future) teachers' self-perceived competences in digital teaching, artificial intelligence (AI), education for sustainable development (ESD), and open educational resources (OER), as well as their perceptions on four DigiSET-specific topics: adaptive AI use, gender bias in AI, inclusive practices for students with learning difficulties, and systems thinking for sustainability. Data were collected between May 2026 and June 2026 using an online questionnaire based on existing scales (DigCompEdu Check-In, TAICS, ATOER) and project-specific items. A total of 152 total responses were received, of which 106 were included in the analysis following data cleaning procedures. Respondents were primarily a digitally engaged group comprising 54% practising teachers (mostly at public secondary schools) and 29% students, with a strong overrepresentation of subjects like Mathematics (46%) and Computer Science/Digital Literacy (45%). Key findings indicate that participants reported highest confidence in professional engagement and digital resources (e.g., 80% regularly find/select resources), but showed significant weaknesses in assessment (37% rarely use digital assessment tools) and AI-based grading (44% lack confidence). Regarding AI competence, while 80–81% feel confident explaining AI or creating content, confidence drops sharply in pedagogical application and assessment design. For ESD, respondents strongly endorse values (92% agreement) but struggle with practical implementation, particularly using digital technologies for sustainability challenges (only 48% agree). In terms of OER, half of the respondents have experience, yet 20–36% disagree with their competence to adopt OER, indicating a gap between awareness and practice. Among the four DigiSET-specific topics, respondents showed the highest confidence in systems thinking for sustainability (87% encourage critical reflection) and the lowest in adaptive AI use (33% lack confidence) and inclusive digital practices (43% rarely adapt materials). The most pressing professional development needs identified were inclusive digital teaching (48%), using adaptive learning tools (39%), and using AI in teaching (38%), while the most frequently reported barriers were lack of time (73%) and lack of available training or suitable resources (40% and 38%). The findings should be interpreted considering the non-representative, self-selected sample which overrepresents computer science teachers and students, leading to likely inflated competence estimates compared to the national average, as well as the self-reported nature of the data. Despite these limitations, the results provide valuable evidence for the design of the DigiSET Teacher Academy and the development of targeted training modules tailored to the national context of Austria. Recommended Citation Schön, S.; Brünner, B.; Ebner, M.; Mair, B.; Nagler, W.; Keser Aschenberger, F. & Dzanic, J. (2026). Teachers’ Competences for Digital Sustainability in Austria. A survey amongst (future) teachers. DigiSET project (WP 2). September 10, 2026. DigiSET | Graz University of Technology, DOI: 10.3217/9mzts-9ys17

title: La medicina en tiempos de inteligencia artificial
L’IA dans l’apprentissage des langues étrangères: Une recherche action à l’université pour former à une utilisation raisonnée des outils IAGen
abstract: En didactique des langues, cela fait de nombreuses années que se pose la question de la place des outils numériques pour améliorer le processus d'enseignement-apprentissage et que l'émergence d'outils utilisant l'intelligence artificielle (IA) de manière de plus en plus performante repose cette question de façon encore plus pressante, en raison des problèmes éthiques qu'elle soulève (Martinez, 2024; Devillers, 2023).Un nombre grandissant de chercheurs s'intéressent à cette utilisation ainsi qu'aux pratiques pédagogiques qui en découlent (Varsik & Vosberg, 2024), ce qui a conduit à l'émergence de la notion de l'enseignement-apprentissage assisté par l'IA (Self, 2016). Toutefois, une dimension reste peu étudiée. En effet, un nombre très limité de chercheurs se sont intéressés à la perspective de l'apprenant ou à l'apprentissage assisté par l'IA (Zheng & Yang, 2024; Yang & Kyun, 2022).C'est cet angle de travail que nous souhaitons investir dans notre thèse de doctorat. Plus précisément, nous nous interrogeons d'un côté sur les avantages découlant de l'utilisation des outils IA chez les étudiants apprenant la langue anglaise et d'un autre, nous intéresser à l'évolution des pratiques chez les apprenants à terme. Pour ce faire, une Recherche-Action sera mise en place en septembre 2025 au sein du Pôle Lansad de l'Université de Strasbourg, qui accueille des étudiants de nombreuses disciplines de la L1 au M2. Au travers d'un dispositif de formation à l'anglais « Learning with AI » que nous avons conçu, 24 apprenants Lansad volontaires de filières et années d'études diverses, seront accompagnés dans l'intégration d'outils IA dans leur apprentissage et seront invités à réfléchir aux questionnements liés à l'éthique, à l'écologie et à leur propre pratique dans une optique de responsabilisation des étudiants vis-à-vis de leur apprentissage (Poteaux, 2010, 57).Dans cette communication, nous présenterons notre cadre théorique, la méthodologie de recherche envisagée, qualitative et design-based ainsi que le module d'anglais. A terme, notre Recherche-Action devrait contribuer à mieux cerner les représentations et les usages actuels des étudiants concernant l'IA dans l'apprentissage des langues et permettre de proposer un dispositif de formation à l'utilisation responsable des outils IA, basé sur la recherche en didactique des langues.Bibliographie :Devillers, L. title: Perceived competence and enjoyment in high school students during physical education clas-ses
abstract: Purpose: In order to promote an active lifestyle and decrease the incidence of sport dropout, it is important for high school students to perceive high enjoyment during physical education classes, as adopting an active lifestyle is influenced by positive experiences in physical education.[1] Therefore it is important to verify if perceived competence can influence enjoyment, and if that effect is mediated by age. The purpose of this study was to investigate if there is a correlation between enjoyment and perceived competence in high school students of different grades, during physical education classes. Methods: 78 first and second grade students (22 males, age: 15.2 ± 1.0 years; height: 176.7 ± 7.4 cm; weight: 65.6 ± 10.1 kg; 56 females, age: 14.6 ± 0.7 years; height: 161.9 ± 5.1 cm; weight: 54.2 ± 5.6 kg), 99 third and fourth grade students (40 males, age: 16.7 ± 0.8 years; height: 179.2 ± 8.0 cm; weight: 68.6 ± 9.6 kg; 59 females, age: 17.0 ± 0.7 years; height: 164.8 ± 5.4 cm; weight: 54.2 ± 7.9 kg) and 50 fifth grade students (11 males, age: 18.8 ± 0.8 years; height: 173.2 ± 5.4 cm; weight: 77.3 ± 25.5 kg; 39 females, age: 18.5 ± 0.6 years; height: 167.7 ± 5.1 cm; weight: 56.0 ± 4.4 kg) were involved. All students practiced 5 different sports during physical education classes, and after 3 lessons of each sport, the students were required to complete an anonymous questionnaire based on a 7-point likert scale, corresponding to the interest/enjoyment and competence subscale of the IMI scale;[2] a total of 788 questionnaires were gathered (245 from first and second grade students, 296 from third and fourth grade students, 247 from fifth grade students). Results: A direct linear correlation was found between enjoyment and perceived competence in students of all grades (first-second grade students and third-fourth grade students: rmcorr= 0.63, fifth grade students: rmcorr= 0.58). There was also a significant difference (p<0.05) in the enjoyment value between first-second grade students and third-fourth grade students (21.0 ± 8.7 vs 18.5 ± 9.9; ES= 0.3), and between first-second grade students and fifth grade students (21.0 ± 8.7 vs 18.2 ±10.2; p<0.05 ES= 0.3), while no significant difference was found in perceived competence between groups (p>0.05). Conclusions: The results show that improving high school students’ perceived competence can be an effective way to increase their enjoyment during physical education classes, highlighting how it is important to improve student’s motor competence and give them positive feedbacks during classes, in order to promote an active lifestyle and reduce sport dropout. It’s also important to notice that in first-second grade students the enjoyment value was significant higher compared to older students, while no significant differences were found in perceived competence values, highlighting how young students can perceive high enjoyment even at low perceived competence values, while that is not true for older students. It can be deduced from these findings that in physical education classes performed by first-second grade students it is possible to approach completely new sport activities without the risk to compromise their enjoyment, while in those performed by third, fourth and fifth grade students it may be advisable to perform sport activities in which they already feel a high perceived competence, to not compromise the students’ enjoyment. title: ITD-CNR Produzione Scientifica 2021-2025: Analisi bibliometrica e analisi tematica delle keyword
abstract: Il presente report analizza la produzione scientifica dell’Istituto per le Tecnologie Didattiche del CNR (CNR-ITD) nel quinquennio 2021-2025. I dati sono stati estratti dal repository istituzionale IRIS CNR (Institutional Research Information System - https://iris.cnr.it/) in formato Excel e sottoposti ad un processo di normalizzazione semiautomatica prima dell’analisi. La normalizzazione ha riguardato due fasi distinte. Nella prima, il file estratto da IRIS è stato convertito nel formato di export Scopus, necessario per l’importazione in VOSviewer, strumento per la costruzione e visualizzazione di reti bibliometriche: questa operazione ha richiesto la correzione dei separatori delle parole chiave, che nei record originali erano inconsistenti (punto e virgola, virgola, punto centrale, entità HTML &), nonché la rimozione di titoli di capitolo erroneamente inclusi nel campo keyword. Nella seconda fase è stato costruito un thesaurus di 534 voci per unificare le varianti linguistiche (keyword in italiano mappate all’equivalente inglese, abbreviazioni espanse, refusi e sinonimi normalizzati). Il dataset comprende 255 pubblicazioni distribuite su cinque anni, con un picco nel 2021 (67) e nel 2023 (64) e una quota del 43,9% indicizzata in Scopus (112 record con EID). Le tipologie prevalenti sono articoli in rivista (123, pari al 48,2%) e contributi in atti di convegno (91, pari al 35,7%). Sul totale di 255 pubblicazioni, 84 risultano in Open Access (32,9%), 73 ad accesso chiuso (28,6%) e 98 con stato non determinato (38,4%). La quota OA è dominata dal canale Gold (52 pubblicazioni; 61,9% del totale OA), seguita da Hybrid OA (25; 29,8%), Green OA (6; 7,1%) e Bronze OA (1; 1,2%). La licenza prevalente è CC BY (61 casi su 75 record con licenza dichiarata, pari al 72,6%), coerente con i requisiti Plan S0F[1]. Escludendo i record con stato non determinato, la quota OA sale al 53,5%. 45 pubblicazioni risultano selezionate per la Valutazione della Qualità della Ricerca 2020-2024 (VQR4) (17,6%), di cui 44 articoli in rivista e 1 monografia. La VQR4 copre il quadriennio 2020-2024: le 36 pubblicazioni CNR-ITD del 2025 non sono state oggetto di conferimento e i relativi record non presentano metadatazione ANVUR, il che spiega anche il calo anomalo della quota di riviste scientifiche ANVUR nell’ultimo anno del dataset. L’analisi tematica tramite mappa di co-occorrenza delle keyword (VOSviewer, soglia minima 3 co-occorrenze, normalizzazione association strength, clustering Leiden) ha prodotto una rete di 84 nodi e 285 link, organizzati in 11 cluster tematici. I nodi strutturali principali [COVID-19 e social media (21 co-occorrenze ciascuno), education, teacher professional development e augmented reality (16 ciascuno)] fungono da ponte tra aree tematiche distinte, riflettendo la vocazione interdisciplinare dell’istituto. I cluster documentano linee di ricerca consolidate in: tecnologie didattiche (augmented reality, learning analytics, gamification), Holocaust Studies e memoria digitale, pedagogia speciale (autism spectrum disorder, funzioni esecutive), game-based learning e formazione docenti. La lettura temporale tramite overlay cromatico (blu scuro = 2021; giallo-verde = 2025) rivela che il nucleo produttivo del quinquennio si colloca nel 2022-2023, con i nodi a maggiore occorrenza concentrati in quella fascia. Le direzioni di ricerca più recenti (2024-2025) ruotano attorno a tre assi emergenti: intelligenza artificiale critica e normativa (artificial intelligence in education, explainable AI, automated assessment, anno medio 2024.1-2024.7), metodologia della ricerca e di sintesi della conoscenza (in particolare, scoping reviews, anno medio 2024.7) e apprendimento basato sul gioco nella sua accezione più recente (board games, anno medio 2024.4). È necessario precisare la natura di questo report: si tratta di uno strumento descrittivo a uso interno, finalizzato a supportare la riflessione collettiva sulla produzione dell’istituto nel quinquennio. Non intende sostituirsi alla VQR, che segue criteri e procedure definiti dall’ANVUR e non è riproducibile attraverso analisi di questo tipo. I dati e gli indicatori presentati vanno letti in chiave aggregata e non come strumenti di valutazione dell’attività individuale dei ricercatori. [1] Plan S è un’iniziativa della coalizione cOAlition S (coordinata da Science Europe) che impone la pubblicazione in Open Access immediato di tutti i lavori derivanti da ricerca finanziata con fondi pubblici aderenti, tra cui Horizon Europe. Il requisito minimo di licenza è la CC BY; le licenze CC BY-NC e CC BY-NC-ND sono considerate non conformi. Maggiori informazioni su: https://www.coalition-s.org/

title: COMPETENCY MAPPING FOR MANAGERIAL CANDIDATES IN THE AGE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE: A THEORETICAL FRAMEWORK FROM THE PERSPECTIVES OF EDUCATIONAL SCIENCES AND BUSINESS ADMINISTRATION
abstract: The accelerating diffusion of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies into organizational life is fundamentally reconfiguring the competency requirements for managerial roles. This paper develops a theoretically grounded competency mapping framework for managerial candidates operating at the intersection of educational sciences and business administration. Drawing on human capital theory, transformative learning, complexity leadership theory, social cognitive theory, dynamic capabilities, and contemporary AI literacy frameworks, we synthesize a multi-domain competency architecture comprising six interdependent clusters: cognitive and analytical, digital and technological, leadership and strategic, interpersonal and social, ethical and responsible, and learning agility. We further examine how AI-mediated pedagogical tools including intelligent tutoring systems, generative AI platforms, simulation environments, and learning analytics can be leveraged to develop, assess, and continuously refine these competencies in management education contexts. The framework addresses a critical gap in the literature by offering an integrative model that acknowledges both the enduring importance of human-centered managerial capacities and the emergent demands imposed by AI augmentation. Implications for curriculum design, executive development programs, and organizational talent management are discussed, alongside an agenda for future empirical research.
