title: Socio-affective technologies [SI 1156 T]
Editorial: Ethics in the Metaverse
abstract: Today, with emerging technologies such as VR, AR and MxR, the Metaverse is no longer science fiction. Virtual platforms are presently available and emerging as ways to connect and to digitally and engage in virtual spaces. They are of growing importance as to how we socialise and do business. The Metaverse is becoming a potential product and facility for working, learning, gaming, and more. It may include virtual worlds and other virtual spaces including augmented reality. It may include elements of a real world with digitally augmented content that are live, changing, perceptible and interactive to human users (Smith, 2016). Mixed reality as a metaverse is potentially where affordances of the digital and analogue worlds could work together to create new interactive learning, social and economic opportunities, but also challenges.In this special issue, different concepts of the metaverse and associated ethical issues are explored. Ethical challenges arise as the physical world itself and becomes an interface making reality even more machine-readable, searchable, and personalisable. By wearing a mixed reality device, users may by default be generating profound 3D models of everything they view in their actual physical locations and capturing a range of real-world content which may include both the individual and other people. For example, many mobile devices have inbuilt lidar technology and can create a 3D point cloud of any environment or object (Demir, 2021). Depth sensors are being built into different devices, but mechanisms for protecting one's body image and possessions have not been well established, neither have procedures for mitigating risks of bias against individuals or groups or tracking personal preferences as a result of data obtained by field in view.This information can be used to enhance user experiences, but also capture technologies combined with machine learning can open multiple paths for advertising and manipulation (Bard, 2020). For example, using big data about where millions of people are looking and their facial expressions, eye movements, and body movements, in response to that, can be of ethical concern, because then models can be built of user reactions, both at the mass and the individual level -which then can be used for targeted advertising and political manipulation. How do we reduce the potential of mixed reality experiences to reduce our own privacy, security, autonomy and personal freedoms? How can ethical design approaches for an open metaverse counteract such concerns?The selected contributions explore and address several of these topics:Smith, Molka-Danielsen, Webb-Benjamin, and Rasool introduce an ethical design framework, Shared Consent Framework (SCF), for the design and use of Metaverse technologies with human well-being in focus. The paper begins with an extended definition of the Metaverse and reviews consent challenges that arise and explores the knowledge gap of consent needed to ensure a fair and just use of data within the Metaverse. Specific examples of challenges of consent are examined, such as unauthorised surveillance and the need for ethical and moral standards in large platforms. A novel five stage SCF is presented in response to understanding the limitations of existing consent frameworks. Protocols and approaches to create implementations of the SCF are presented.Rasool discusses the risk associated with the rise and use of technologies such AI, Metaverse and Blockchain technologies, that occur as they become smarter. Potential risks presented are that with further reliance on such technologies, human beings may abdicate their thinking capabilities, including those related to creative problem solving, to machine intelligence. For prevention of cognitive decline in human beings as machines get smarter, the authors call for new approaches within Industry 5.0, Fifth Industrial Revolution (5IR) that "focus on a harmonisation of human and machine intelligence." This paper proposes that the practice of coaching in the future must embody 5IR mindsets, techniques and technologies. Emerging regulations are reviewed, such as the EU AI Act and a novel approach is introduced for 'Coaching 5.0' as the discipline of coaching that is fit for practice in 5IR environments.Raja and Al-Baghli examines the intersection between ethics and the responsible use of VR. The authors' definition of VR is inclusive of technology that companies and creators call the "metaverse," or an artificial virtual world in which people occupy a simulated reality and conduct their business there (Metz, 2021). Explored are the ethical issues that arise in the use of VR, such as consent, privacy and harm. The paper examines current literature, government documents, and conducts an analysis of 300 Amazon reviews of three top-rated VR products-to identify the ethical concerns of various audiences. Three frameworks are reviewed that could guide users towards more responsible VR use: 1) Institutional Review Board (IRB) frameworks, 2) a care ethics framework, and 3) cocreated, living ethical codes. This research draws from these three frameworks to offer a new ethical synthesis framework or ESF framework that could guide responsible use.Peña-Acuña and Rubio-Alcalá identify the growing prevalence of immersive technologies (IM) in educational settings, and the challenges of lack of familiarity and knowledge necessary for the effective development and application of these technologies (Jamaludin, McKay and Ledger, 2020;Costan, et al., 2021;González and Valencia, 2022). A snowball documentary methodology is used to explore the ethical implications of integrating advanced IM into education. Ethical concerns and advantages of applying IM of the Metaverse are identified, highlighting differences and commonalities between AR, VR and MxR technologies. Ethical dimensions of access and inequalities, protection, privacy and data protection, and development and design are examined. A key finding is that while the Metaverse focuses on identity protection, in education, IM exhibit more developed ethical concerns. This research underscores the richness and nuances the challenges of using diverse IM in education as compared to the Metaverase.Seen together, the contributions explore ethical issues related to AI and IM (e.g., VR, AR and MxR) through a multitude of methodologies (e.g., literary reviews, white paper analyses, empirical studies) and perspectives (e.g., legal, user-centered, educational). They develop frameworks and propose responsible approaches to handle risks and secure privacy and consent in the Metaverse. There is clarity in the contributions with respect to understanding that our current systems, processes, and approaches are not prepared enough to respond to IM challenges. Only through works such as covered within this special issue can we start to build towards more ethical and responsible uses of such technologies.As educators, there is a clear challenge with respect to developing peoples' understanding of how such technologies can be both enablers and inhibitors of progress. Existing ethical issues within webbased contexts are complex for users to navigate, what we see through our paper contributions is that many of these challenges remain and are enhanced when mapped into the Metaverse. Metaverse applications keep progressing, ethical issues continue to remain and user education of the impact of these issues on personal privacy, security and wellbeing whilst improving -as our traditional educational structures and our media structures provide more content and develop understanding -struggles to keep pace with the rate of change.For further research, there are several pressing ethical issues which these contributions merely touch upon, but which should be addressed, particularly linked to more positive use of the technologies. For example (but not limited to), the Metaverse could empower persons identifying with marginalized groups and/or vulnerable life situations in ways that we have not explored, e.g., through co-creation methodologies and the development of platforms to strengthen community support and engagement. We strongly encourage such inquiries.

title: Editorial: Assessment and monitoring of human movement, volume II
abstract: The quantitative study of human movement has evolved from classical observational mechanics into a sophisticated, sensor-driven scientific discipline (Edriss et al., 2024;Innocenti, 2018). While early biomechanical principles were framed through anatomical observations, the transition toward technical and objective measurements became essential in the nineteenth century. This shift was marked by the chronophotography of Marey and Muybridge (Marey, 1885(Marey, -1888;;Muybridge, 1887) and early kinetic devices, able to measure joint amplitude and force variations (Amar, 1916), eventually culminating in the introduction of piezoelectric force platforms (Baker, 2007;Bestwick-Stevenson et al., 2022) and others kinematic device as conductive mat (Bosco et al., 1983) and linear encoder (Bosco 1995).In recent decades, the rapid convergence of micro-electro-mechanical systems (MEMS), the Internet of Things (IoT), wireless telemetry, and smart textiles has revolutionized movement assessment (Edriss et al., 2024). The development of specialized instrumentation, such as inertial measurement units (IMUs), global navigation satellite systems (GNSS), ultra-wideband (UWB) tracking, portable gas analyzers, and surface electromyography, offers profound technological and practical advantages across clinical, athletic and educational spectrums (Bourndon et al., 2017;Camomilla et al., 2018). Fundamentally, these specialized instruments replace subjective visual appraisal with granular, highly reproducible kinematic and kinetic metrics. This precision eliminates evaluator bias and enables accurate longitudinal tracking of physical development, technical mastery, and motor recovery (Ancillao, 2018). Furthermore, by concurrently capturing external mechanical demands (e.g., velocity, accelerations, and linear load) and internal physiological responses (e.g., heart rate variability and respiratory parameters), practitioners and sport coaches can optimize training periodization, identify premature fatigue, and guide safe return-to-play protocols (Halson, 2004;Impellizzeri et al., 2019;Taberner et al., 2019). Additionally, modern sensor technologies deliver immediate biofeedback during movement execution, enabling coaches and clinicians to make precise real-time adjustments (Edriss et al., 2024;Zanela et al., 2022;Ziegler., 2026). Finally, the high ecological validity of wearable systems allows for non-invasive data collection in naturalistic environments, supporting early detection of gait anomalies, objective monitoring of disease progression and evidence-based physical education interventions (Doherty et al., 2016;Edriss et al., 2024) Today, integrating multi-sensor fusion with artificial intelligence and machine learning algorithms is propelling human movement monitoring into a predictive, highly personalized era, fundamentally reshaping performance optimization, injury prevention and clinical health management.This Research Topic compiles 14 articles, comprising original research, systematic reviews and mini-reviews, that showcase the latest methodological, technological, and practical advancements in movement assessment. Collectively, these contributions span four interconnected thematic axes that reflect the modern landscape of sports biomechanics, clinical rehabilitation and training load monitoring.High-precision biomechanical profiling has proven essential for decoding movement mechanics and refining discipline-specific performance. In speed skating, applying Classification and Regression Tree (CART) machine learning to 3D kinematics and kinetic force plate data enabled researchers to identify critical inter-limb asymmetry thresholds directly linked to split skating times (Jin et al., 2026). In track and field, kinematic analyses comparing elite Chinese and international female throwers highlighted the crucial role of release velocity, double-support mechanics, and trunkpelvis coupling in hammer throw performance (W. Liu et al., 2025). Similarly, threedimensional motion capture combined with ground reaction force analysis defined the spatial-temporal and force-impulse demands of the skeleton start, establishing empirical guidelines for specialized push simulations and sprint acceleration (Hao and Kong, 2025). In trampolining, electromyography and plantar pressure assessments during the net contact phase revealed sex-specific lower-limb dynamics and balance strategies among elite athletes, emphasizing the necessity of targeted unilateral training (K. Liu et al., 2025). Finally, anthropometric and maturation predictive equations were developed for young kayakers, providing an objective, scientific framework to scale paddle dimensions across developmental age categories (Fernandes et al.. 2025).Neuromuscular evaluations and functional asymmetry analyses remain central to optimizing conditioning and mitigating injury risk across various populations. An evaluation of inter-limb differences in balance, jumping, and isokinetic strength among elite adolescent basketball players demonstrated that while large strength asymmetries (>20%) exist, they do not significantly differ between sexes, reframing conventional assumptions regarding female injury risk (Lyu et al., 2025). Investigating isokinetic knee strength and agility performance in elite Wushu Changquan athletes established foundational parameters for neuromuscular coordination and lower-limb balance in martial arts science (Zhiyong et al., 2026). From a clinical perspective, a novel cross-line laser balance tool was validated against gold-standard force plates, demonstrating high agreement and proving to be a cost-effective solution for objective balance assessment in individuals with chronic ankle instability (Swails et al., 2025).Comprehensive monitoring of physical performance and physiological responses is crucial for effective load management and intervention programming. Evaluating loadvelocity relationships and sport-specific skill performance in female softball players demonstrated that while mechanical metrics decline post-exercise, integrated biochemical and perceptual markers remain essential for capturing subtle fatigue responses (Zhang et al., 2025). In field testing, a re-evaluation of the 30-15 Intermittent Fitness Test in collegiate soccer players confirmed its high test-retest reliability, while demonstrating that population-specific prediction equations significantly reduce error when estimating maximal oxygen consumption VO2max compared to generalized models (Cheng et al., 2025). Furthermore, a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials demonstrated that plyometric jump training yields significant improvements in jumping, agility, and kicking power in female soccer players, with particularly pronounced effects observed in professional athletes (Hernandez-Martinez et al., 2025). Addressing team sports load management, a comprehensive review synthesized internal and external load in rugby, emphasizing the critical need for multi-sensor algorithms and individualized monitoring frameworks to manage fatigue and reduce injury risk (Lv et al., 2025).Modern advancements in optical sensors and non-invasive technologies are expanding the scope and accessibility of movement analysis. A mini-review evaluated commercial RGB/depth cameras and AI-based pose estimation frameworks, highlighting the rapid evolution toward affordable, non-invasive 2D-to-3D markerless motion analysis for both clinical and sporting environments (Edriss et al., 2025). Additionally, high-sampling-rate thermal imaging combined with chest temperature entropy analysis was introduced as an innovative, non-invasive method to monitor physiological load and excess post-exercise oxygen consumption (EPOC) during incremental cycling (Cui et al., 2025).The collective body of evidence compiled in this Research Topic underscores a profound paradigm shift in human movement assessment, bridging the historical gap between laboratory-based biomechanics and real-world ecological applications. By integrating advanced wearable sensors, machine learning analytics, markerless pose estimation, and sport-specific field protocols, these 14 contributions demonstrate how objective, highresolution monitoring enhances athletic performance, optimizes injury mitigation, and refines clinical rehabilitation across diverse populations worldwide. Beyond their specific findings, the global impact of these studies lies in the democratization and personalization of movement science. Moving away from isolated, one-size-fits-all evaluations, this volume establishes actionable, evidence-based frameworks that adapt to age, sex, athletic tier and clinical status, ranging from customized equipment scaling in youth sports to multi-modal training load management in elite competition.In the future, the trajectory of human movement monitoring might be defined by the seamless convergence of multi-sensor fusion, real-time automated biofeedback and predictive artificial intelligence. As these non-invasive technologies mature, they promise to deliver unprecedented insights into human function, fostering a more precise and globally accessible era of movement analysis in sports. We express our sincere gratitude to all contributing authors, expert reviewers and the editorial team whose dedication made this volume a meaningful contribution to the scientific community.

title: Integrating law, technology, and design: teaching data protection and privacy law in a digital age
abstract: The data protection lawyer of the future will be a key intermediary of innovation—or ‘transaction engineer’—who facilitates and coordinates new forms of business and other social relationships in rapidly evolving multi-disciplinary settings. The effective performance of this function requires legal professionals to develop a different mindset, along with new skills and capacities, specifically a better understanding of the underlying technologies and the value and techniques of legal design, as well as a knowledge of relevant data protection law. Transferable principles for teaching data protection law and privacy law in a digital age are identified. The article proposes a task-oriented, gamified, and sandbox approach to data protection education that delivers a more relevant student experience that cultivates meaningful capacities and skills that are more closely aligned with the needs and values of a digital age. Data protection law and questions of privacy, more generally, are amongst the most disrupted and disruptive sectors of the legal industry today. Algorithm and data-driven companies are driving market development across multiple sectors of the economy.1 Moreover, the exponential growth of these technologies is creating innovative business models and offering new products and services for customers and clients. The health care and financial service sectors are good examples of such data-driven disruption.2 Technological changes make it possible to gather, integrate, and analyse vast amounts of data in unprecedented ways. Recent events such as the Snowden revelations of mass surveillance by intelligence services and government agencies,3 the Facebook–Cambridge Analytica scandal which concerned the obtaining of the personal data of millions of Facebook users without their consent,4 and court decisions such as the Schrems II case,5 which invalidated the European Union (EU)–US Privacy Shield framework of data transfers,6 have raised awareness and concerns about the protection of personal data among legal professionals, the business sector, and the public, more generally. Regulators have responded to such concerns with far-reaching regulatory interventions, such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)7 in Europe and the California Consumer Protection Act (CCPA)8 in the USA. The recent Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic has exacerbated the effects of the digital transformation.9 For example, the pandemic has pushed us further into digital spaces, and changes in behaviour are likely to have lasting effects when the economy returns to normal.10 The pandemic has also increased the uptake of technology-based solutions, tools, and services, accelerating and amplifying the global transition towards a digital economy.11 Given the centrality of data and data protection to our collective future, it is vital that data protection becomes a central pillar of legal education, and it is for this reason that we have set out to identify principles that might drive the development of a new style of data protection education at a graduate level, which integrates an in-depth understanding of law, cutting-edge technologies, and legal design. This will provide students with an opportunity to build upon basic knowledge they acquired as undergraduates and help them to understand—from both an interdisciplinary and technical perspective—how data protection law can interact with innovative products (software and hardware) and services in real-world settings. Moreover, it seems clear that future data protection regulation will be increasingly embedded in the architectural design of the technology itself,12 following the ‘privacy by design and by default’ approach.13 As such, data protection lawyers will operate in multi-disciplinary teams, comprising coders and designers. This new operating environment means that students must acquire a new way of thinking and data protection lawyers of the future will become innovation intermediaries or ‘transaction engineers’.14 As such, the next generation of data protection lawyers will play a vital role mediating between various actors, organizations, and communities, coordinating, and reinforcing a dialogue between diverse professions and businesses. The data protection lawyer of the future needs to be able to understand not only the technical and legal issues involved, but also the necessary human–machine interactions and the interfaces between the various stakeholders and complex systems. As such, transaction engineers will be the linchpin that facilitate business innovation and user creativity across multiple sectors of the economy. This article, therefore, aims to identify and describe some fundamental principles for the advancement of data protection education in this new context, exploring new teaching methodologies and student learning outcomes. Section ‘The disruption of education in a digital age’ briefly outlines the broader context of the disruption of education in a digital age. Section ‘The lawyer of the future as transaction engineer’ suggests that lawyers have been at their most effective when operating as transaction engineers that create opportunities for new forms of business and other social relationships and suggest that this provides a model for the data protection lawyer of the future. Section ‘Principles for integrating law, technology, and design in the legal education of tomorrow’ identifies core principles that can form the basis for designing a programme based on our experience as lawyers and educators. Section ‘Conclusion’ concludes. Over the last half-century, digital technologies have transformed the world. The emergence of computer-based devices and communication infrastructures have triggered multiple economic, social, and cultural effects. The term, ‘digital transformation’, is often used to refer to this shift from analogue, electronic, and mechanical machines to networked, digital devices, and the ongoing social effects associated with the proliferation of these new technologies.15 This process of digitization began in earnest with the launch of the Intel microprocessor in California in the early 1970s and has been driven by an ongoing series of technological innovations, most significantly cheaper and smaller digital hardware (first PCs and, more recently, smartphones); global communication networks and mass connectivity (the Internet); and cloud-based data storage and algorithm-driven processing. With ever-shorter innovation cycles, it seems obvious that these new digital technologies will continue to transform every aspect of our lives. Constant technological disruption is now the new normal and old-world ideas, practices, and organizations are becoming less relevant, even if they are still, obviously, influential. title: Green Intelligence in Finance: Artificial Intelligence-Driven ESG Analytics and Sustainable Investment Performance
abstract: This study examined the role of artificial intelligence (AI)-driven Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) analytics in enhancing sustainable investment performance. While traditional ESG ratings had been widely used in responsible investment strategies, they often suffered from data inconsistency, subjectivity and limited coverage of unstructured sustainability information. AI-based ESG systems were increasingly applied to extract deeper sustainability signals from corporate disclosures, reports and external data sources. Using portfolio-level analysis, this study compared the financial outcomes of portfolios constructed using AI-driven ESG indicators with those based on conventional ESG ratings. The results showed that AI-enhanced high-ESG portfolios achieved higher mean returns and superior Sharpe ratios than both AI-based low-ESG portfolios and traditionally rated ESG portfolios. In addition, AI-driven high-ESG portfolios demonstrated lower downside-risk exposure and smaller maximum drawdowns during market stress, indicating stronger resilience. Regression analysis further revealed that AI-derived ESG scores were more strongly associated with excess returns than traditional ESG metrics. These findings suggested that AI improved the informational efficiency of ESG assessment by capturing more accurate, forward-looking sustainability risks and opportunities. The study concluded that AI-driven ESG analytics strengthened the financial relevance of sustainability integration and supported better-informed investment decision-making. The results carried important implications for investors, regulators and corporations seeking to align AI deployment with high-integrity sustainable finance practices, while also highlighting the need for ethical and transparent AI governance in financial markets. title: The new Editorial Team of JHEP Reports: From successful inception towards an established reputation
abstract: The launch of JHEP Reports has been a clear success. JHEP Reports – the official open access journal of EASL – was created in 2018 and devoted to publishing papers on clinical and translational/basic research in hepatology. In 2022, it received its first impact factor, an astonishing 9.9. Over ∼800 manuscripts were received in 2022, which increased to ∼1,300 in 2023, built upon the quality of its articles and the allure of its impact factor. These remarkable results, achieved in such a short timeframe, can be attributed to: a) great vision and objectives; b) outstanding leadership by the first Editor-in-Chief, Jessica Zucman-Rossi, MD, PhD, her Editorial Team and the EASL Editorial Office; c) the capacity to attract well-cited articles and state-of-the-art reviews, even before its first impact factor was announced; and d) seamless integration and cooperation from the EASL Governing Board and the Editorial Team of Journal of Hepatology. Following this exceptional start, we now have a very lofty goal – and a huge opportunity – to further enhance the visibility and dissemination of liver science in our journal by publishing innovative studies, early clinical trials addressing unique challenges, and modern concepts in clinical and translational research that reflect both emerging and prominent themes. To tackle this task, we have assembled a highly talented, gender-balanced, age-sensitive Editorial Team (Fig. 1), encompassing expertise in the main areas of liver disease research and clinical practice. These domains of excellence include all facets of hepatology, from pathogenesis of hepatic diseases to advances in clinical, basic and translational research in liver tumors, viral hepatitis, liver transplantation and rare diseases, MASLD and alcoholic-related liver diseases, as well as cirrhosis and its complications. We will also address special topics such as statistics, precision medicine, artificial intelligence, and machine learning. In addition, we have appointed a completely new Editorial Board (Fig. 1), which includes both well-established members with a prestigious track record of publications and research achievements, and highly motivated emerging researchers who represent the next generation of hepatology experts. This strategic composition ensures a dynamic and inclusive approach to advancing the journal’s standing and impact in the coming years. Our journal has emerged amid fierce competition among liver-oriented journals. Building upon our success among these publications, we intend to gain further traction and expand our visibility by seeking insights at the frontier of knowledge. Our team aims to capture novel ideas or technologies, attract early clinical trials and promote novel concepts not yet suitable for higher-end journals, particularly for those studies involving human specimens or with a compelling clinical path. In this spirit, we will be launching a unique series of articles tackling the management of liver diseases (including consensus documents and position papers), as well as the design of clinical trials. Furthermore, we will provide education in pioneering technologies for clinicians in topics such as gene editing, nanomedicine, digital health, spatial omics, artificial intelligence, organoids, and circulating biomarkers. To do so, we have already invited a roster of outstanding reviews authored by key opinion leaders. Similarly, JHEP Reports will be instrumental in providing a platform for the dissemination of high-quality research from EASL Young Investigators, including facets of career development and leadership. Finally, we will intensify our efforts to promote JHEP Reports beyond Europe, particularly in America and Asia, and advocate for the perspective of the patient. Teamwork will be critical for our success. Our Editorial Team will work closely with the EASL Editorial Office and continue to rely upon the invaluable support of the EASL Governing Board. With ∼1,500 submissions expected in 2024, we anticipate publishing ∼200 source items per year, including original articles, reviews, short communications and eventually EASL Consensus documents. Ultimately, our overarching goal is to serve the global hepatology community by providing an exciting platform to disseminate research, while attracting new readers and investigators who will move the field forward.

title: Study Group on Cardiogenic Shock and Cardiac Arrest—a global network to improve the quality of care
abstract: Following some years of discussion and debate, during the ESC congress in Amsterdam 2023, the new ACVC Task Force (TF) on cardiogenic shock (CS) and cardiac arrest (CA) underwent its inaugural meeting. The main aim of the TF is to enable development of a global network to share high quality research and standardized education in order to improve the quality of care of patients with CS or CA. Due to the clear and pressing unmet need of the patient population, as well as the uniqueness of the potential for interprofessional exchange and collaboration, the TF was rapidly commuted to a Study Group, and is already active, including a number of relevant Sister Societies and experts from across the world. In this issue of the Science pulse the two founders of the Study Group (Susanna Price and Christian Hassager) along with the current Chair and co-Chair (Guido Tavazzi and Steffen Desch) talk about the past, present, and future of the Study Group. 1) Where does the TF come from? And how long ago? Susanna Price and Christian Hassager During our presidencies (Susanna Price and subsequently Christian Hassager), ACVC shifted focus somewhat from treatment of myocardial infarction and STEMI networks to include some of the most critically ill cardiovascular patients, including those with OHCA and CS. This shift gave ACVC a unique platform within the ESC and beyond, enabling the multiprofessional and multidisciplinary expertise available to be realized to the benefit of these patients. We, together with the rest of the Executive board, felt that this was such an important area for ACVC to maintain—on top of the other ACVC topics of interest—that we felt that we needed a TF (and later a Study Group) addressing this very special and challenging patient population. 2) Why did you think there was a need for it? Susanna Price and Christian Hassager These patient populations are largely not well-served, as their care tends to fall between the domains of critical care and cardiology, emergency medicine, and resuscitation science, with a major challenge being to ensure that the expertise of all disciplines is embraced within a spirit of collaboration—both within the ESC, and also with relevant sister societies in Europe—including ESICM, EuSEM, EuroELSO, and ERC. The Study Group provides a formal platform for collaboration, networking, innovation and education, enabling the collective expertise across Europe and beyond to be brought together to achieve the vision of reducing the burden of cardiovascular disease for these most critically ill patients. 3) Which have been the intermediate but fundamental steps that brought to the foundation of it? Susanna Price, Christian Hassager, and Guido Tavazzi The first step was the realization that we, together with our colleagues across the disciplines, were uniquely placed to formally address these areas of cardiovascular medicine. Following the increasing demand from ACVC members for continued focus in these fields, we discussed our potential next steps at several informal meetings and in the corridors, but we especially remember one late afternoon near the coast in Croatia where following on from some particularly successful conference sessions, formers (Susanna and Christian), active (Kurt) presidents and the current research section chair (Guido) finally decided to formally create a TF. We brainstormed the challenge, composed a brief ‘Terms of Reference’, and proposed members. The first formal meeting of this TF was very well-attended at the ESC congress 2023 in Amsterdam, where during this meeting which included extensive discussions with our colleagues from Europe, North America, and Canada sharing potential priorities to develop. After presentation of the proposed strategy of the TF, the then ACVC President, Kurt Huber, declared we should now consider recognition of the collective expertise as a formal Study Group within ACVC. 4) Which are the strengths of the Study Group? Guido Tavazzi and Steffen Desch The major strength of the CS/CA Study Group is represented by the participants. At the meeting during the recent ACVC congress in Athens, most of the key opinion leaders in these fields from across the globe joined either in person or virtually, defining how to enact the vision and strategy that had been agreed. Additionally, the ACVC network is rapidly expanding geographically and, in addition to the ongoing collaboration with North American colleagues, several countries including from South-East Asia are linking to the community allowing, for the first time, to create a truly global network sharing the same objectives. 5) Which are the main perspectives of the study group? Guido Tavazzi, Steffen Desch, Susanna Price, and Christian Hassager A major challenge is the heterogeneity in patient management related both to differences in how care for critically ill cardiovascular patients is delivered between countries, and lack of standardization of care mostly related to limited, or absence of robust evidence. The main aim of the study group is to standardize management and education in the diagnosis, monitoring, and treatment of the CS and CA patients with a specific focus on the critical care management. This will be only possible by strengthening the network of health care professionals taking care of this group of patients to foster high quality research to frame the current management, gaps and continue define and refine our understanding the unmet clinical needs. The first step will be the development of surveys to map the relevant units along with their structure and current management of CS/CA patients. In parallel, following the publication of quality indicators on post-resuscitation care for OHCA arrest, the development of quality metrics regarding the management and outcome of CS is regarded as fundamental. Additionally, comparison of existing datasets from different countries on epidemiology and outcomes will be paramount to determine similarities and differences in patient's features and diagnostic/therapeutic pathways. Subsequently design of registries, observational studies/trials based on the research priorities identified will serve to define the future of management of these patients, maximizing the global reach of the ESC. Additionally, the involvement of professionals, such as experts in different areas of -omics, genetics, basic science, bio-engineers and artificial intelligent/machine learning will be involved to strengthen the cross-talking amongst different specialities and to frame the future pathways of a better understanding of pathophysiology and management. However, achieving these through implementation of the Study Group strategy is now a key priority for its members, which includes most of the key leaders (and future leaders) in CS and OHCA from across the globe. Only through such a shared vision, collaboration and team work, will such improvement in the quality of patient care be achievable. The aims and structure of the Study Group on CS and CA can be found at the following webpage: https://www.escardio.org/Sub-specialty-communities/Association-for-Acute-CardioVascular-Care-(ACVC)/About/Study-groups. title: Meet Key Digital Health thought Leaders: Gerhard Hindricks
abstract: Many thanks, it is indeed a big honour and privilege to have the opportunity to serve the Digital Health Committee of the ESC as the Chair. Especially in the light of the huge achievement that have been made in the field of cardiovascular digital health by the past digital health committee under the leadership of Martin Cowie and Nico Bruining. It is an ambitious opportunity for me to continue and extend the projects and concepts that were so successful in the last couple of years. Major steps such as the establishment of the European Heart Journal—Digital Health and the various very successful formats of the ESC Digital Summit have been achieved by the previous committee. The importance of digital technologies and applications in the field of cardiovascular medicine will continue to increase with accelerating speed. In my opinion, digital health offers a huge opportunity, possibly the best chance ever, to improve global access to cardiovascular care. Moreover, digital technologies will improve diagnostics and treatment in cardiovascular medicine with an unprecedented intensity. This is why I am so enthusiastic about the role of digital health and so happy that I have the opportunity together with the members of the ESC Digital Health Committee to support these developments. Indeed, it is our goal to further establish the ESC as the global flagship in digital health in cardiovascular medicine. Wherever you look in the various specialties of cardiovascular medicine, you see novel digital technologies and applications. Indeed, the field of arrhythmias and electrophysiology traditionally is the frontrunner on this development path. I just want to mention the achievements in the field of telemedicine by monitoring of pacemakers and defibrillators, the application of wearables for diagnostics in atrial fibrillation and, more recently, the application of artificial intelligence (AI) using machine learning (ML) techniques for in-depth diagnostics from the surface ECG. It is amazing and fascinating to see what digital eyes can discover in a standard electrocardiogram hidden to the human eyes of the cardiologist. Information about ejection fraction and, what is even more fascinating, the detection of past episodes of atrial fibrillation from the sinus rhythm ECG is just breath taking. I believe that this is just the beginning of a huge window for opportunities to improve diagnostics and treatment in cardiovascular medicine. The recent discoveries by applying digital technology and AI in cardiac imaging and in many fields for risk prediction of cardiovascular events are also amazing. As I said before, I believe that digital health is the biggest opportunity to improve the quality of cardiovascular care by better prevention, earlier and more precise diagnosis and better treatment of cardiovascular disease. The application of AI is probably the most important innovation in data analytics. I am not a specialist in data science but I follow this field with great interest. I see huge opportunities particularly in the field of advanced risk prediction in various states of cardiovascular disease. However, with all the enthusiasm we should stay humble on the ground of solid science. One crucial element for the opportunities but also for the risks related to ML and AI is the quality of the data for the training and learning process of neural networks. I think that it is advisable to establish transparent standards for data management to reduce the risk of misleading recommendations based on AI. Moreover, we need to carefully and critically review the results of AI-based analytics and decide where confirmation of findings may be necessary by means of traditional scientific statistical models. However, my bottom line is that I am convinced that ML and AI applications will substantially improve cardiovascular medicine. Indeed, the implementation of digital technologies in medicine is a huge challenge. The roadblocks are multiple and some of these barriers are substantial. First, we need to convince the medical community, the physicians and nurses, the technicians and administrators but also the patients that digital applications in medicine offer such a huge opportunity to improve the quality of care. We need both trust and regulations. Transparency and education is important, and open discussion formats that explain and describe the digital elements in health care are needed. Here I see a huge responsibility but also an opportunity for the ESC Digital Health Committee. We have the experts that can substantially contribute to these important discussions. We will only be successful if we succeed in convincing the community of the benefits of digital health. However, it is also important to open up the discussion regarding the unknowns and the associated risks. Moreover, legal aspects and advocacy play a very important role in this implementation process and we should proactively contribute to this important field. At the end, it will also be an element of appropriate financing and investment in digital technologies. It will cost a lot of money to implement ‘true’ digitization in the healthcare sector. However, I am convinced that it is a great investment and there will be substantial payback thru more efficient care at a higher quality. Together with the excellent members of the digital health committee, I will invest time and effort in effective networking with various partners in the field of digital health. Collaboration with technology companies active in digital health, but also with the pharmaceutical and device industry is urgently needed. We will work in several phases to improve the visibility of digital health for the European Society of Cardiology and the ESC associations. We are currently planning the Digital Summit 2023, an exciting event that will share the latest advances in digital science, education, diagnostics and treatments in cardiovascular medicine. In addition, the ESC Digital Health Committee will contribute several projects to the 2023 ESC Congress in Amsterdam to mark the meeting as an important digital health event in cardiovascular medicine. CardioPulse Digital talks to the new chair of the Digital Health Committee of the European Society of Cardiology: Prof. Dr. med. Dr. h.c. Gerhard Hindricks. Gerhard Hindricks is a Professor of Medicine/Cardiology and the Medical Director of the Heart Center Leipzig. He is the Director of the Department of Electrophysiology of the Heart Center and the General Manager of the Leipzig Heart Institute. Gerhard Hindricks has a longstanding involvement in innovations and the development and clinical implementation of new technologies in the field of cardiovascular medicine and beyond. He has fundamental interest in design and implementation of novel process and diagnostic/therapeutic pathways in medicine. Moreover, Gerhard is principal investigator of multiple international, randomized, and potentially guideline-relevant clinical trials. He has served the European Society of Cardiology in several leadership functions including President of European Heart Rhythm Association and is now the new chair of the ESC Digital Health Committee. He was the Chairman of the 2020 Guidelines of the ESC for the management of atrial fibrillation and the Chair of the ESC Task Force “Evolution of cardiovascular medicine, training and education”. Overall, he has published almost 800 peer-reviewed articles in the leading cardiology journals of the world and was until recently the Editor-in-Chief of the Europace Journal, one of the top international journals in the field of cardiac arrhythmias.

title: Letter from the editor
abstract: Thank you very much for the enthusiastic reception of the new European Heart Journal - Digital Health journal last December! Presenting you with the first issue was a huge challenge for the authors, reviewers, and entire production team, but it was also a huge honour and great pleasure. All this amid the worst global health crisis in modern history. We can now present you the second issue with many more excellent articles. First, a special word of appreciation to our reviewers who tirelessly perform an excellent job, providing both editors and authors with critical, yet constructive, reviews. High-quality reviews enormously help us achieve the high scientific standard for which we strive. Now, it is very difficult to find the time and energy for this so necessary and voluntary review work. We cannot emphasize enough how we value such contributions! We are also very pleased with the number and quality of submissions we are currently receiving from all continents, demonstrating that we already have global reach and showing us that the journal arrived at the right time. In this second issue, we cover a wide variety of different topics. The vast majority comprising artificial intelligence (AI) and remote monitoring, but we also present such topics as electronic health record systems, social media, education, an introduction to digital health in the clinical workspace and, of course, COVID-19-related research. Regarding remote monitoring, we are very pleased to present you with two consensus documents, one of which is a global initiative: ‘2021 ISHNE/HRS/EHRA/APHRS Collaboration Statement on mHealth in Arrhythmia Management: Digital Medical Devices for Heart Rhythm Professionals’. And another from the ESC Working Group e-Cardiology: ‘Using commercially available wearable heart rate and activity tracking technology in primary and secondary cardiovascular prevention’, which jointly provide an exceptional and complete overview of present remote monitoring capabilities. Besides these two consensus documents, we also have several remote monitoring studies using smartphones. Dr Aalami writes about the ‘Reliability and repeatability of a smartphone-based 6-minute walk test as a patient-centered outcome measure’ with an iPhone and Apple Watch. Doctors Campbell and Maurizi are investigating whether patients can use a smartphone for reporting with heart failure patients and the possibilities of Electrocardiogram (ECG) monitoring of COVID-19 patients, respectively. We all think that AI will play a prominent role in medicine and, above all, can have innumerable advantages when considering prevention. Dr Kwon utilizes AI for early detection of heart failure: ‘Assessment of artificial intelligence for early detection of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction based on electrocardiographic features’, using state-of-the-art image analysis. Prof. Tereshchenko is exploring whether ‘ECG Machine Learning to Detect Cardiovascular Disease in African Americans: The Jackson Heart Study’ can provide early detection of cardiovascular disease in communities where access to health care can be problematic. We are all enthusiastic about adopting and applying Digital Health, yet there remain many challenges too. Dr Van Spall reviewed for us the recent literature on the pros and cons of Digital Health in her article: ‘Barriers to and facilitators of the adoption of digital health technology in cardiovascular care: a systematic scoping review’. A valuable guidance for more dialogues, advancements, education, and utilization. Besides these articles, many other contributions are incorporated within this issue. An important aim of the journal is also to further spark discussions about the described outcomes and conclusions, which is why you will notice a number of editorials in this issue. We would like to share with you further advantages of our journal for authors and readers. We are an entirely digital journal, which has its limitations but also provides new opportunities. We no longer discover unexpected articles by randomly browsing through a printed journal but surf straight to what interests. New digital opportunities to promote your work include ESC Society-wide email campaigns and Social Media, which, to be optimally effective, means that graphics are essential. So if you are thinking about submitting an article, add a graphical abstract, it works miracles! We can ensure maximum visibility for your work throughout our global community. Additionally, we offer you the opportunity to include a video presentation that accompanies your article. A 5-min maximum presentation, as if you were presenting your work at a conference. In the current time, where physical conferences are not possible, this could generate extra exposure and promotion for your work. You may have noticed that we recently started bringing accepted items online as soon as possible. These can be found in the advanced articles section of the journal’s website (https://bit.ly/2Ocldti). You can subscribe to an email alert that you will receive as soon as new articles become available. We are looking forward to further shaping our journal together with you. As you know, we want to become ‘the’ platform to exchange and discuss Digital Health developments and solutions. If you have questions or suggestions about how we can further optimize our services for you, then please contact us! Our start was great: our aim is to do even better.

title: Editorial: Diabetes complications in children and adolescents: from low-resource to technology-advanced countries
abstract: The study by Lazar et al. proposes anion gap normalization time (AGNT) as a more reliable marker for diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) resolution in pediatric patients, challenging traditional reliance on pH and bicarbonate levels. Their findings indicate that AG normalizes significantly earlier than these markers, with a median AGNT of 8 hours, preceding PICU discharge by 15 hours. Notably, severe acidosis (pH < 7.1) and hyperglycemia (>500 mg/dL) were strong predictors of delayed AGNT, reinforcing its potential as a clinically relevant indicator. By adopting AGNT as a criterion for de-escalation of intensive care, clinicians may reduce unnecessary PICU stays, minimize patient burden, and optimize hospital resource utilization. However, the study's retrospective nature and absence of ketone body measurements necessitate further prospective validation before AGNT can be fully integrated into DKA management protocols. This research raises an important question: should anion gap normalization replace conventional DKA resolution markers, paving the way for a more efficient and patient-centered approach? [7] The study by Tinti et al. explores the long-term neurological dysfunction in adolescents with type 1 diabetes, highlighting early subclinical alterations in nerve conduction. Using nerve conduction studies (NCS) and follow-up neuropathy screening questionnaires, the study found that while 11.8% of patients showed signs of somatic dysfunction, a significant 41% had reduced hypoglycemia awareness, suggesting early autonomic impairment. Importantly, an abnormal NCS outcome correlated with a 97-fold increased risk of severe hypoglycemia after six years, emphasizing the potential impact of diabetic autonomic neuropathy (DAN) on metabolic control. Despite the small sample size and lack of comprehensive metabolic data, the findings reinforce the need for early screening for neuropathy in pediatric diabetes, particularly through electrophysiological assessments that may identify risk factors before clinical symptoms appear. This study aligns with growing evidence that early autonomic dysfunction in diabetes can lead to increased glycemic variability and hypoglycemia risk, advocating for a more proactive approach in pediatric neuropathy screening to improve long-term diabetes management. [8] The study by Leutheuser et al. investigates the prediction of nocturnal hypoglycemia in children with type 1 diabetes following daytime physical activity using machine learning models applied to continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) and physiological data. The study, conducted in a structured sports camp setting, assessed logistic regression, random forest, and deep neural networks to forecast hypoglycemia over a 9-hour overnight period. Results showed that random forest models using only glucose data achieved the highest predictive accuracy (F2 score: 64.4%), while incorporating physiological data marginally improved performance. Despite variability in model effectiveness, the findings underscore the clinical importance of early hypoglycemia risk prediction, allowing caregivers to take proactive measures, such as adjusting insulin or carbohydrate intake, to prevent overnight complications. However, the small sample size (13 children, 66 nights) and dataset constraints highlight the need for larger-scale validation studies. This research contributes to the growing field of AI-driven diabetes management, but further refinements, including personalized modeling and real-world validation, are essential before clinical implementation. [9] The study by López-López et al. evaluates the real-world efficacy and safety of the MiniMed 780G advanced hybrid closed-loop (AHCL) system in children under 7 years of age with type 1 diabetes (T1D). Analyzing data from 61 pediatric patients across three endocrinology centers in the Canary Islands, the study found that time in range (TIR) increased significantly (up to 13-15%), while time above range (TAR) decreased without an increase in hypoglycemia risk. These metabolic improvements were sustained for up to 12 months, supporting the long-term benefits of AHCL therapy in young children. Importantly, the study also assessed children requiring low total daily insulin doses (<8 units/day) and found no adverse impact on safety or efficacy, suggesting that AHCL systems may be suitable even for those with minimal insulin needs. Despite the retrospective design and small sample size, the findings reinforce the role of automated insulin delivery in achieving optimal glycemic control in very young children with T1D, advocating for its expanded use and further validation in larger cohorts. [10] These studies highlight the need for adaptable solutions to address disparities in diabetes care across different healthcare systems. Complex technologies may not be feasible in low-resource settings, but simple and effective tools like anion gap normalization time (AGNT) and scalable neuropathy screening methods can significantly improve outcomes. These approaches enable early intervention and better complication management without requiring high-cost infrastructure. Costeffective, evidence-based strategies tailored to resource-limited environments will be key to ensuring equitable access to quality diabetes care. [11] Advancements in machine learning (ML)-based predictions and advanced hybrid closed-loop (AHCL) systems have transformed diabetes management in technologically developed settings. These innovations help optimize glycemic control, reduce fluctuations, and lower the risk of complications, enhancing the overall quality of life for people with type 1 diabetes. [12] However, these technologies' high cost and limited availability create barriers for many individuals, especially in low-and middle-income countries. Bridging this gap requires collaboration among healthcare providers, policymakers, and industry leaders to develop policies that ensure these life-changing innovations become affordable and widely accessible.Equitable diabetes care depends on global cooperation. High-resource institutions should take an active role in capacity-building efforts by investing in training programs, telemedicine support, and knowledge-sharing initiatives for healthcare providers in under-resourced regions. Strengthening local expertise and improving access to essential technologies, such as continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) and AHCL systems, can empower clinicians to provide better care for children with type 1 diabetes. Policymakers must prioritize investment in diabetes-related healthcare policies, ensuring that affordability and accessibility remain at the forefront of decision-making.Future research must also consider socioeconomic, cultural, and regional differences to create scalable and practical solutions. Interventions should be designed to meet the specific needs of diverse populations, accounting for variations in healthcare infrastructure, patient education, and treatment accessibility. Sustainable progress in diabetes management will rely on balancing technological innovation with real-world feasibility, ensuring that all children, regardless of their location or financial background, receive the care they need to thrive.This special issue highlights how innovation and research help manage diabetes complications in children and adolescents. By reducing resource gaps and using technology, the global diabetes community can improve care for all young patients. Achieving this goal requires teamwork, advocacy, and a strong commitment to health equity.

title: JustConservation - global data of site-level biodiversity conservation and its social-ecological outcomes (1970-2019)
abstract: This dataset contains evidence collected from 723 studies published in English-language peer-reviewed journals that describe and explore conservation efforts at a single site in 104 countries (1970-2019). The pool of studies was obtained through a keyword search on Web of Science, which returned 69,246 publications, followed by a screening of titles and abstracts using the open access machine-learning assisted software Colandr (11,100 publications screened; cut-off inclusion rate: 3%) and a data extraction phase (1,054 publications), based on the following criteria for inclusion: (1) the study is about biodiversity conservation; (2) the study describes a deliberate intervention; (3) the study provides empirical evidence; (4) the conservation intervention takes place in a specific site through a specific actor or actors; (5) the study identifies a discernible conservation aim, and; (6) the paper identifies a discernible conservation approach.
