title: Cohort Profile: The Copenhagen Infant Health Nurse Records (CIHNR) cohort
abstract: The Copenhagen Infant Health Nurse Records (CIHNR) cohort includes 92 902 infants born from 1959 to 1967 and resident in Copenhagen municipality, Denmark. The cohort was established to assess the impact of early life circumstances on individuals’ health and socioeconomic outcomes. During repeated home visits starting just days after birth, infant health nurses provided guidance on infant nutrition and wellbeing to the mothers. Using structured preprinted forms, the nurses recorded key information at each visit about the parents, the child’s physical health, infant feeding mode, the home, family structure, child care, motor function development, parent-child relationship, wellbeing and mental and environmental factors. Furthermore, the nurses weighed the infants at 2 weeks and 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9 and 12 months of age. A subset of infants received additional visits until 3 years of age. Via a unique government-issued personal identification number that is available for 88 808 individuals in the cohort, these individuals have been prospectively followed up via linkages with national registers on vital statistics, health and socioeconomic circumstances and other cohort studies. The CIHNR cohort is located at the Center for Clinical Research and Prevention, Bispebjerg and Frederiksberg Hospital, Denmark. The steering group of the CIHNR welcomes collaboration and the interest of national and international colleagues (e-mail: [email protected]). In Denmark after World War I, rates of infant mortality during the first year of life were concerningly high due to high rates of morbidity, poor child care and nutrition and housing conditions.1 Inspired by preventive home visits by nurses in Finland, the UK and the USA, a similar service was initiated in Denmark. From 1929 to 1935, the Danish Health Authority in cooperation with the Rockefeller Foundation from the USA, conducted a pilot study of a two-arm cluster, pragmatic trial examining whether an infant health nurse visit programme reduced infant morbidity and mortality in Copenhagen and two rural districts.1 The service was successful and well received, and enacted into law in 1937.2 Immediately thereafter, the municipality of Copenhagen adopted the programme. A critical element in the success of the service was the parallel development of a formal education in infant health nursing which was launched in 1938.3 The infant health nurse positions could be filled by registered nurses who had additional education in maternity care, specialized paediatric care, epidemic or tuberculosis care or care for patients with mental illness. Importantly, all infant health nurses had to pass a course for infant health nurses at Aarhus University.4–6 The service focused on health promotion with the aim of securing children had a healthy start in life, to set the foundation for a healthy adult life. The programme is still running today, although now with need-based visit frequency and attention. The goal of the initial infant health nurse programme was to educate mothers on how to look after the health of their family. This service was free of charge and provided to all families with healthy infants during their first year of life. If sickness was noticed in the child, the nurses were to advise the parents to seek medical help.5,7 Through regular home visits, the nurses provided advice and guidance on infant nutrition, care, growth and development.5,7,–9 One of the nurse’s key tasks was to provide ‘energetic propaganda’ for breastfeeding and ‘to do all she could to make the mother breastfeed her child’.5,10 Further, the nurses were directed to encourage and advise the mothers on the best practices for sleep, cleanliness and consistency in daily routines.10 The nurses provided guidance about the importance of fresh air, physical movement, prevention of infection, the dwelling’s hygiene and social welfare.10 The health nurses filled in a separate record for each infant, and it was used throughout the duration of the programme. During the years 1960–70, a project on the potential benefits of extending the period of the nurse visits until the infant was 3 years of age was initiated in Copenhagen.1,3 Likely because of this project, infant health records from the municipality of Copenhagen for children born from 1959 to 1967 were preserved for general research purposes by the late Professor Mogens Hauge. Since 2007, data from selected subsets have been digitized (Figure 1). Subsequently, recognizing the potential value of these records for research, in 2014 they were all scanned to images and information enabling personal identification was manually computerized. From 2019-2021, an automated transcription of large amounts of information from all pages of the scanned records was conducted. This forms the database of the Copenhagen Infant Health Nurse Records (CIHNR) that can support studies on the determinants of long-term health and social consequences of infant health and development. Cohort formation (created with BioRender.com) The population-based cohort is based on health records from infants born from 1959 to1967 and resident in Copenhagen, who received infant health nurse visits. The scanned paper records comprising 95 323 documents, names and dates of births for the infant and parents and the infant’s sex, were manually computerized by one secretary. After removing duplicate documents, 94 431 documents remained. Among these, special records were identified indicating that 110 infants died and 1419 moved out of the area. As these documents lacked fields enabling the identification of the child or the parents, they were not included in the database. Therefore, the CIHNR includes 92 902 infants with records containing information that could potentially allow for the identification of individuals. From 3 April 1968 onwards, a government-issued personal identification number has been assigned to all people living in Denmark.11 It consists of 10 digits; the first six indicate the day, month and year of birth and the last digit denotes the sex of the person. Using an extensive and conservative algorithm based on matching on the infant’s and parent’s dates of birth and names, and infant sex, the infant records were linked to the identification number. Through this procedure, identification numbers were identified for 88 808 (95.6%) of the infants (45 394 boys, 43 414 girls). The proportion of infants with identification numbers retrieved ranged from 94.3% to 97.6% across the years of birth. Among 65 710 infants for whom information on name and dates of birth for the child, mother and father was available, identification numbers were identified for 98.3%. The reasons for lacking identification are death or emigration of the child before 3 April 3 1968, unresolved matches or random errors in the data. During the years of this cohort, all families in Copenhagen with infants under 1 year of age were offered free and voluntary visits by an infant health nurse.12 The infant health nurse was required to remind parents that her help was free and elective.5,6 If her help was not desired, the nurse was required to leave the home and could not return unless she was asked to do so or until another child was born.5,6 The coverage of the service was high as it was well received by the mothers.12 Causes of non-participation in the service were described as ‘(i) permanent or temporary moving (including vacations), and adoptions; (ii) placing of the infant in a crèche, orphanage, etc.; (iii) the mother’s feeling that she was experienced enough to do without guidance; and (iv) extended stay in the hospital’.12 Reasons for non-participation were not systematically recorded in the records. The exact number of infants whose mothers were resident in Copenhagen and thus were eligible for the programme is unknown but may be estimated from government statistical yearbooks. According to statistical yearbooks from 1959 to 1967, there were 90 592 infants born live to women resident in Copenhagen at the year of delivery.13 These yearbooks do not report how many women with infants under 1 year of age (and who were potentially eligible for the programme) moved in or out of Copenhagen during these years. As such, precisely calculating the population of infants who were eligible for the programme is not possible. Nonetheless, the yearbooks report that 76 983 infants under supervision from a health nurse during these years were born to women resident in Copenhagen, corresponding to 85% of the 90 592 infants born in Copenhagen at the year of delivery.13 Additionally, 10 491 infants under supervision were born to women not resident in Copenhagen.13 Assuming that 85% of those who moved to Copenhagen were under supervision, an additional 1573 infants not under supervision may have moved to Copenhagen. Therefore, by summing the 90 592 live-born infants, the 10 491 under supervision who were not born in Copenhagen, and the 1573 who were not under supervision and not born in Copenhagen, we estimate that 102 656 infants were eligible for supervision. Compared with this, our cohort covers 90.5% ((92 902/102 656)*100) of infants who were potentially eligible for supervision. The infant health nurses visited the home as soon as possible after the birth, given the focus on the importance of initiating breastfeeding. If the infant was born at home, the first visit was to occur within 2–3 days and at the latest 4–5 days after birth. If the child was born at the hospital, the first visit was to occur as soon as possible after discharge. The infant health nurse was to make an average of 11–13 visits during the first year of life, with more visits occurring during the first 2–3 months of life.5,6 A minimum of eight visits was deemed as a satisfactory completion of the programme. The infant health nurses visited the home at least at 2 weeks and 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, and 12 months of the infant’s age. If deemed necessary, additional visits could be given to first-time mothers, when there were problems with breastfeeding, the infant’s wellbeing, the mother’s understanding or similar.5,6 The proportion of the cohort who received a visit at 1 month of age was 84.4%. This proportion decreased to 77.0% and 71.6% at ages 6 and 12 months, respectively. These numbers were similar in boys and girls (Figure 2). From 1–12 months of age, 63.8% of the children had at least seven visits. Percentage of infants who had a visit at each age by the infant health nurse by age (1 to 12 months) for boys and girls During the 1960s, a project examining the effects of extended infant care throughout the first 3 years of life was conducted in the Copenhagen municipality3 with the aim of examining whether there was a need to reform the nurse visiting programme.1 All children in the CIHNR born on the first 3 days of each month and all twins born from 1 January 1959 until 31 December 1967, corresponding to around 10% of the infants, were included in this programme.1 This extended programme included three visits in the second year of life and two visits in the third year of life. As a result of this project, the nurse home visiting programme was changed to include an extra focus on first-time mothers and families with special needs, with both groups receiving visits also during their child's second year of life. The CIHNR contains information on the parents, the home, pregnancy, birth, infant development, nutrition and health care use (Table 1). Information available in the Copenhagen Infant Health Nurse Recordsa GP, general practitioner. Information is computerized for differing subsets of individuals. Additional information was collected in notes form at all visits whenever there was information to report (as opposed to the schematic registration from the home visits at 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9 and 12 months). The midwives provided the infant health nurse with a birth notification5,6 containing information on the pregnancy, the delivery, the infant’s weight and length at birth, the medical history of the mother and social history of the family.14 This information was transcribed to standardized preprinted health records, which were specifically developed to enable the extraction of data for statistical use.4,15 Detailed guidelines on how to fill in the records were provided to the nurses, and they were obliged to keep orderly records.4,15 During the visits, the nurses weighed the children, advised the mother on feeding, sleeping, bathing and growth and development. Per instructions, at each visit they recorded information on the infant’s weight, illness, feeding mode, parental occupation, hygiene standard of the home, family structure, child care, motor function development, parent-child relationship, wellbeing and general health conditions (Table 1).5,6,12 The nurses weighed the children using a steelyard balance (a ‘Bismer scale’). During the 1960s, two versions of the scales were used; the upper limit was 10 kg on one and 12 kg on the other. At the end of the programme, the nurses were required to submit the records to the medical officer within 14 days of the child’s first birthday.5,6 A select set of variables from the CIHNR has been transcribed from all records, using the automated machine learning methods described in Dahl et al.16,17 The accuracy of transcription for these variables ranged from 92% to >99% for most variables. The median was ≥97% (data not shown). The currently extracted information includes birthweight, birth length, information from the home visits, a final report of the duration of partial breastfeeding, length at 1 year, enrolment in the extended programme and participation in each of the visits in Years 2 and 3. Summary measures for selected variables are presented in Table 2. In the coming years, additional information will be made available using machine learning methods. Basic characteristics for individuals in the cohort (n = 92 902) Weights above 10 kg or 12 kg were censored for some infants due to upper limits of the scales used to weigh them. The categories are pre-specified in the records and filled in per instructions to the nurses about record keeping.16 Not transcribed yet. Via linkages based on the personal information and identification numbers in the CIHNR, information on childhood may be obtained from other data resources. The Copenhagen Perinatal Cohort (CPC) is a prospective pre-birth cohort study that followed 9125 individuals born at the National Hospital from 1959 to 1961 from birth, during infancy and the pre-school years and later in adulthood.18,19 It includes information from the hospital records, from health examinations and from questionnaires.18,20 Matches with the CIHNR were identified for 4387 children (many mother-child dyads admitted to that hospital came from other municipalities). All information from the CINHR was manually computerized for these infants. The Copenhagen School Health Records Register contains information from health examinations that included the measurement of child height and weight by doctors and nurses.21 A match on identification number with this resource was found for 30 677 (34.5%) of the individuals in the CINHR. Additionally, a case-cohort sample based on obesity in childhood is available in which all information from the CINHR was manually computerized.22 These linkages enable studies on the early determinants and consequences of childhood body size and growth. Through the unique identification number, linkages for the infants and their families to Danish national registers and cohort studies providing health and social information later in life are possible. We have performed links with several key registers. Most central is the Danish Civil Registration System,11 which has contained computerized vital statistics since 1968. Information on hospital contacts has been available since 1977 through the Danish National Patient Register,23 and on causes of death from the Danish National Cause of Death Register which has been computerized since 1970.24 Moreover, linkages with registers containing information on educational outcomes, income and labour market attachment have been conducted. These linkages enable evaluation of the impact of social-, pregnancy- and birth-related factors on early and late health and socioeconomic outcomes. Using a subset of the CIHNR data in combination with data from Danish school health records,22 we showed that infant weight and weight gain are strongly associated with obesity in childhood from the first months of life and at every age throughout infancy.25 Moreover, through the linkage with the CPC, we showed that higher weight at all ages from birth to 12 months was associated with higher adult body mass index (BMI) and that weight gain between birth and age 3 months was associated with higher adult BMI.19 Recently, we showed that a pattern of very low-moderate increasing weight during infancy was associated with a higher frequency of adult coronary heart disease, but this association did not persist after adjustment for birthweight.26 The data in the full CIHNR contributed to the development of machine learning methods used in the extraction of data, particularly from historical documents. One such application found that the different types of pages (that vary in number and order between records) could be identified and grouped, thus allowing identification of which children received the extended nurse home visiting. In a manually constructed truth evaluation dataset of 234 treated and 3766 untreated individuals, all individuals were correctly classified, meaning that both the positive predictive value and the sensitivity were 100%.17 Major strengths of this population-based cohort are its large size, the linkage possibilities it offers and the possibilities for long follow-up (>55 years). The large size means that it can support studies of common outcomes with great statistical power as well as of rare outcomes occurring in adult life. Attrition from the cohort has occurred mainly due to emigration and death, and there is minimal loss to follow-up because of the register linkages and the unique Danish identification number. Hence, selection bias is limited. Other strengths lie in the frequency and structured recording of health information throughout infancy. Information on breastfeeding was obtained prospectively, which is unusual in large cohorts, and thus it is not subject to recall bias. The wide range of detailed data on the health and social circumstances of the infant can support investigations of associations of these factors. Combined with the low selection and low information bias, as the information was prospectively and objectively measured with minimal recall, and the relatively high coverage, results from this data resource likely have a high degree of both internal and external validity. A weakness of the database is that the infant health service was not set up as a scientific study. Thus, although the information collected was wide-ranging in terms of impact on child health, it did not include all information we would have collected in a research programme today, for instance maternal smoking, alcohol use, anthropometry and infant length. Moreover, an element of subjectivity in the assessments cannot be ruled out, as validated scales were not used. Nonetheless, the programme has a long history of developing through scientific enquiry, and the records were deliberately created in a way to support data extraction. Other limitations are that it was not possible to identify the identification number for all infants, we do not have information on families who did not accept and/or receive the service and we do not have follow-up until 12 months of age for families that discontinued supervision before that age. The CIHNR cohort is located at the Center for Clinical Research and Prevention [www.frederiksberghospital.dk/cihnr]. title: The impact of artificial intelligence on Sri Lanka libraries: an interview with Premila Gamage
abstract: Sri Lanka boasts a rich tradition of libraries that dates back to the 5th century AD, reflecting its long-standing commitment to knowledge and cultural preservation. The modern library movement in Sri Lanka began with the British occupation in 1815, laying the foundation for the organized library systems seen today. The country now has a well-established public library system complemented by a diverse network of school, research, academic, government and NGO libraries. These institutions collectively play a critical role in promoting education, research and cultural heritage across the nation.The National Library of Sri Lanka provides detailed insights into this ecosystem through its “Statistical Handbook on Libraries in Sri Lanka,” which offers comprehensive data on various types of libraries at district and provincial levels. Sri Lanka had approximately 1,176 libraries operating nationwide, reflecting the breadth of its library network. As the libraries continue to embrace digital tools and explore AI integration, they are positioning themselves as pivotal institutions for fostering knowledge, innovation and community engagement in Sri Lanka.We interviewed Premila Gamage, a distinguished librarian and member of the Editorial Board of Digital Library Perspectives, on digital transformation and AI adoption for library services in Sri Lanka.She is a consultant at Verité Research Institute, an independent think tank providing strategic analysis on economics, politics, law and media in Asia. Her expertise spans a wide range of organizations, including the International Federation of Library Associations and Institutions (IFLA), the Access to Learning Award of the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation, the Commonwealth of Learning’s Skills for Work Programme and the M.S. Swaminathan Research Foundation’s INELI South Asia Programme. She has also contributed to the National Centre for Advanced Studies in Humanities and Social Sciences and the Sri Lanka Library Association.Gamage has played a pivotal role as a mentor in the International Network of Emerging Library Innovators (INELI) Program for South Asia, fostering innovation among emerging library professionals. Her leadership extended to the IFLA Public Library Policies Project, where she spearheaded the national initiative in Sri Lanka, aimed at evaluating policymakers’ perspectives on the role, value and impact of public library services. In addition, her efforts to highlight how libraries in the Asia and Oceania region support the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals have been instrumental in showcasing the transformative power of libraries in addressing community needs.As an Accredited Trainer for IFLA, Premila has conducted workshops across countries such as Lebanon, India, Nepal and ASEAN nations, focusing on leadership, technology adoption and capacity building for librarians.With her extensive contributions both locally and internationally, we spoke with Premila Gamage to gain insights into the state of digital transformation in Sri Lanka, the challenges and opportunities of adopting artificial intelligence (AI) in libraries and the potential of open-source tools and Web-based innovations to advance library services. Her profound understanding of global trends, combined with her expertise in local contexts, positions her as a valuable authority on how libraries can embrace modern technological advancements while effectively addressing the needs of their communities:In Sri Lanka, the extent of digital transformation varies significantly across different types of libraries. Most academic and research libraries have implemented basic automation, focusing primarily on cataloging and circulation services. These libraries also maintain Online Public Access Catalogs (OPACs) and, in many cases, institutional repositories. However, the content within these repositories is not always fully accessible. For instance, while repositories may host thesis and dissertation collections, the full texts are often not available for open access.Public and school libraries, on the other hand, lag significantly behind in digital transformation. A substantial number of these libraries have yet to automate even basic services like cataloging and circulation. The National Library of Sri Lanka has made notable strides by maintaining both an OPAC and a repository. Compared to other institutions, the National Library’s repository is relatively open, offering greater accessibility to its digital content. However, overall progress in the broader library ecosystem remains uneven, with many institutions still in the early stages of digital adoption:The adaptation of libraries in Sri Lanka to digital technologies has been gradual and limited, with most efforts concentrated on traditional services. The automation of cataloging and circulation services is widespread among academic and research libraries. Some have incorporated technology into Inter-Library Loan (ILL) and document delivery services, facilitating access to digital or scanned copies of requested materials. However, these advancements are not universally applied, and many libraries, particularly public and school libraries, still operate without even basic automation. The primary use of technology in libraries remains confined to traditional services like cataloging and document delivery, with limited exploration of emerging technologies that could significantly enhance information services.Only a handful of university libraries have taken steps to introduce students to more advanced technologies, such as AI tools for conducting literature reviews. Despite these initiatives, the overall pace of adaptation has been slow. This slow progress underscores the need for a more strategic approach to digital transformation across all types of libraries in Sri Lanka:Barriers to the adoption of advanced technologies like AI in Sri Lankan libraries extend beyond financial limitations, though these remain a significant challenge. Many university libraries already have designated librarians responsible for technology and related services, yet meaningful advancements in implementing AI tools have been limited.Two major factors contribute to this stagnation. The first is a skills mismatch, where library personnel often lack the technical expertise necessary to understand, implement or manage AI-driven tools effectively. This gap in knowledge prevents libraries from fully leveraging technological advancements. The second is the prevalence of negative attitudes among library staff, where resistance to change and skepticism about the value of new technologies act as significant impediments. These attitudes may stem from a lack of exposure to AI’s practical benefits or concerns about job security in an increasingly automated environment.Overcoming these barriers will require a concerted effort to provide targeted training, foster leadership support and highlight successful AI applications in libraries:Digital transformation plays a pivotal role in paving the way for AI adoption in libraries. It forms the backbone of any effort to modernize and aligns library services with the demands of the digital age.Beyond being essential for survival, digital transformation creates the infrastructure and mindset needed to embrace AI. Digitizing collections and automating processes, for instance, establish the groundwork for deploying AI applications like advanced search systems, personalized recommendations or automated cataloging. These transformations not only enhance service quality but also familiarize library staff with the tools and workflows necessary for further innovation. By embedding digital transformation into their strategies, libraries ensure they are well-positioned to adopt AI as a natural and logical extension of their modernization efforts, aligning with global trends and user expectations:One of the most promising areas for immediate AI application in Sri Lankan libraries is cataloging, particularly for local language publications. AI-driven tools, such as natural language processing algorithms, can automate and enhance the cataloging process by efficiently recognizing and organizing content in Sinhala and Tamil. This would significantly reduce the time and effort required for manual cataloging while improving the discoverability of regional and indigenous knowledge resources.AI could also make a substantial difference in information retrieval. Intelligent search systems powered by machine learning can deliver more precise and contextually relevant results, enhancing user experiences. Similarly, user services can benefit from AI-powered chatbots and virtual assistants, which can handle routine queries, guide users in navigating digital collections and provide 24/7 support:Educating stakeholders about the tangible benefits of digital transformation is crucial. I usually start by emphasizing both the short-term advantages, such as improved operational efficiency and user engagement and the long-term gains, including enhanced accessibility, sustainability and alignment with global library standards.As a consultant, I highlight difficulties users face in finding and accessing resources, both internal and external, and demonstrate how these issues hinder libraries productivity and user satisfaction. Real-world examples and case studies help me to illustrate the gap between the current state and a more digitally advanced system.The transition should begin by leveraging the organization’s existing infrastructure to minimize costs. For instance, open-source tools and cloud-based platforms can be integrated into current workflows to achieve significant improvements at a low cost. The focus should be on incremental changes, such as automating repetitive tasks or digitizing high-demand resources, to build confidence and demonstrate value early in the transformation process.By aligning digital transformation goals with the library’s mission and user needs and by showing that such initiatives are feasible and sustainable even with limited resources, I try to guide libraries to embrace and sustain a digitally advanced future.My starting point is that understanding user needs always requires surveys. I aim to illustrate the current challenges in accessing knowledge provided by libraries and external commercial organizations. Through concrete examples, I explain to librarians and administrators the short- and long-term benefits of digital transformation, emphasizing how these can be achieved using the organization’s existing infrastructure, often with minimal cost:The need to address skill mismatches and prepare students and librarians for future challenges is paramount. To achieve this, institutions offering Library and Information Science courses in Sri Lanka should undertake a comprehensive revision of their curricula and evaluation methods. These revisions should emphasize AI literacy, digital tools and practical applications in library services. Building a pool of skilled lecturers and trainers is equally critical, as they will be instrumental in delivering the updated curriculum effectively.For practicing librarians, acquiring relevant skills and introducing AI-driven tools into their workflows is essential. Even small enhancements to existing services, such as personalized recommendation systems or automated literature reviews, can demonstrate immediate value. These implementations should be monitored for tangible results, which can then be leveraged for advocacy efforts.My strategy is to highlight the potential impact of libraries. I share success stories and data-driven results with higher authorities, partners and stakeholders. The impact highlighted by case study evaluations will help me to build a compelling case for the potential of AI in transforming library services.Gradually scaling these initiatives, while reinvesting the benefits of early successes into more complex projects, libraries can overcome the challenges posed by limited infrastructure and budgets. This iterative process builds confidence among librarians and stakeholders, ensuring broader support for AI adoption over time:Introducing AI in a resource-constrained environment requires a strategic, phased approach. Training librarians in fundamental AI concepts and practical skills is a crucial starting point. Workshops and hands-on demonstrations of freely available tools, such as AI-powered tools or document summarizers, can showcase how these technologies enhance day-to-day library tasks.To keep initial implementations manageable, I usually focus on basic services. For example, AI tools can streamline literature searches, automate citation generation or provide basic text analysis for academic researchers. These applications are not only cost-effective but also demonstrate immediate, measurable improvements in service delivery:Sri Lankan libraries, particularly academic and research institutions, appear prepared to experiment with AI, thanks to their familiarity with open-source tools like Koha for library management and DSpace for repositories. These technologies form a solid foundation for integrating AI-driven solutions, such as enhanced search algorithms, recommendation engines and virtual assistants. In addition, academic libraries demonstrate a natural inclination toward innovation, motivated by the need to improve services for students and researchers.However, to fully embrace AI, libraries in Sri Lanka need focused preparation. Training programs are essential to equip librarians with the skills necessary to manage and use AI effectively. This includes understanding data management, machine learning principles and the ethical considerations of AI adoption. Concurrently, improving infrastructure is critical. Libraries must ensure they have the technological resources, including adequate internet bandwidth and computational capabilities, to support AI applications. Collaborative efforts can also play a significant role, where libraries form networks to share tools, expertise and data.Awareness-building among decision-makers and stakeholders is another vital step. As a consultant, I must advocate for the strategic advantages of AI, using pilot projects and case studies to demonstrate its tangible benefits. Partnerships with local and international organizations, as well as participation in the open-source community, can further facilitate AI integration by providing technical support and additional resources:As a consultant, I wish to play a transformative role in this process. By conducting training and capacity-building programs, I hope to enhance librarians’ skills and confidence in using AI tools. My idea is that supporting the implementation of AI tools and providing technical expertise will help ensure a seamless transition.Advocacy programs are also crucial for me in influencing policymakers and stakeholders to prioritize AI adoption in library strategies. Moreover, showcasing successful examples of impact achieved from other international contexts in the Asia and Oceania Area can inspire local adoption while securing resources and funding to sustain these initiatives.Bridging the gap between digital transformation and AI adoption in Sri Lanka involves improving and maintaining the IFLA international framework for experimentation, collaboration and capacity building, ultimately enabling libraries to align with global advancements while meeting the needs of their local communities.

title: S04: Hic sunt dracones! Real-world data-driven knowledge modelling resulting in Semantics and FAIR-LOD based tools and workflows (Standard)
abstract: Florian Thiery, Römisch-Germanisches Zentralmuseum, Department of Scientific IT, Mainz, Germany Brigit Danthine, Universität Innsbruck, Department of Archaeologies, Innsbruck, Austria Mag. Nicole High-Steskal, University for Continuing Education Krems Department for Arts and Cultural Studies Dr. Valeria Vitale, The Alan Turing Institute Dr. Allard W. Mees FSA, Römisch-Germanisches Zentralmuseum, Department of Scientific IT, Mainz, Germany Dr. Karsten Tolle, Frankfurt Big Data Lab, Institute of Computer Science, Goethe-University, Frankfurt am Main, Germany Dr. David G. Wigg-Wolf FSA, Römisch-Germanische Kommission (RGK) des Deutschen Archäologischen Institut (DAI), Frankfurt am Main, Germany, david.wigg-wolf@dainst.de In historical maps, the phrase “Hic sunt dracones” (engl. here be dragons) is used to describe areas which were unknown to the map creator. Today the WWW offers researchers the possibility of sharing their research (data) and enables the community to participate in the scientific discourse and create new knowledge. But much of this shared data is not findable or accessible, thus resulting in modern ‘unknown data dragons’. Often these ‘data dragons’ lack connections to other datasets, i. e. they are not interoperable, and in some cases also lack usability. To overcome these shortcomings, Linked Open Data (LOD) techniques can be used [4]. In 2006 Berners-Lee [2] introduced the concept of LOD, in 2018 Sanderson instigated the “Usable” aspect at EuropeanaTech [5]. Additionally, in 2016 the FAIR principles [1] were introduced: Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Reusable. The Semantic Web offers a variety of vocabularies, ontologies and reference models that can be used for archaeology-related LOD modelling: CIDOC-CRM, SKOS, PROV-O, FOAF, GeoSPARQL, Wikidata, etc. The Linked Data Cloud already provides FAIR and LOUD research data repositories, data hubs and domain-specific ontologies for specific archaeological and humanities domains such as: Nomisma, Kerameikos, Pelagios, OpenContext, Portable Antiquities Scheme, ARIADNE, Linked Open Samian Ware, Linked Open ARS, Linked Open Ogham, and the Ceramic Typologies Ontology. Beyond them, many other networks for graph modelling in the digital humanities, such as the Pelagios Network, Linked Pasts, Graph Technologies / Graphs and Networks in the Humanities offer methods and resources that could be used and further developed for digital archaeological research. The development of ever more repositories poses challenges in handling the complex facets of data quality and completeness. This is especially true for archaeological data, which are based on complex networks of concepts from different domains and linguistic backgrounds. Moreover, it is necessary to include means of assessing uncertainty in the data models to produce and publish transparent FAIR and LOUD data that can also describe specific stratigraphies or the (archaeological) context of objects. To enable non-experts to engage with FAIR and LOUD data, research tools – little minions – were created for different purposes, such as modelling relative chronologies in RDF (e.g. Alligator), modelling and reasoning on vague edges in graph data (e.g. Academic Meta Tool), creating annotated texts and images (e.g. Recogito, Annotorius), and sparql, as well as enhancing Geo-Datasets using the SPARQLing Unicorn QGIS Plugin. In addition, community-driven knowledge bases like Wikidata not only offer data, but also provide a number of tools for using and interacting. The positive feedback on the LOD sessions on data quality, FAIR and LOUD at CAA 2017-2021 encourages the pursuit of the debate. The goal of our online session is to bring together both experts and colleagues interested in learning about FAIR and LOUD data-driven publishing and applications, as well as to collect research application scenarios to jointly promote research domain specific solutions. We would like to discuss application-oriented and data-driven investigations into how to improve technologies for FAIR and LOUD data models as a basis for reproducible and CAREful research and exchange in the Semantic Web, as well as solutions related to one or more of the issues listed below. Issues application of semantic web technologies, such as ontologies (e.g. CIDOC-CRM) or RDF, to the archaeological domain modelling of archaeological artefacts, archaeological context, including the specificity of stratigraphy, uncertainty, and vagueness development of research tools producing or using FAIR and LOUD data identifying sources and dangers of incorrect or ambiguous LOD, e. g. duplicates across different LOD sources keeping track of the provenance of data as a means of solving errors and identifying their source setting up research-question based methodologies and tools in order to label or assess datasets based on their quality dealing with ambiguities resulting from multiple links in the LOD cloud computer vision or machine learning applications built upon controlled, semantic data modelling comprehensible / reproducible workflows and data flows as “Linked Pipes” [3] using RDF for documentation and reproducible research use of Linked Open Data related tools in archaeological research, their implementation and/or enhancement possibilities, challenges, benefits and risks of the Wikimedia Universe in archaeological research implementation of reference models such as CIDOC-CRM in real-world datasets and ways to achieve LOD graphs of facts, beliefs, and/or assertions as a digital archaeological method reasoning with heterogeneous and real world archaeological data in graphs granularity in LOD/graphs/networks graph and RDF representation of specific networks of persons, objects and information relating to research questions interacting with graphs and graph interaction design LOUD techniques as a solution for information and data annotation on objects / artefacts in 2D and 3D (e.g. cuneiform tablets, ogham stones, samian ware, books, texts, …) semantically modelling geospatial data FAIR and LOUD implementation of GeoSPARQL as a geospatial standard in archaeological data things as a concept, such as places (e.g. Pleiades Place/Location), persons (e.g. “potters” as Actors) and events in archaeological LOD overcoming linguistic barriers and increasing accessibility through LOD implementing the CARE-principles through thoughtful LOD application development of educational or Open Educational resources (OERs) to increase use of LOD We encourage presenters to derive the problems addressed from real-world datasets and to formulate proposals for solutions, preferably demonstrating (prototypes of) realised data-driven (web-) applications. Due to the thematic relevance, we target a broad and diverse audience and the challenges described should also be integrated into an archaeological context (excavation, museum, archive, etc.). Only those papers will be taken into consideration which offer the data and tools involved as FAIR data and Open Source tools in Open Science repositories (e.g. Zenodo, OSF, GitHub, GiRetLab). Exceptions to this principle (e.g. dissertation in course) should be explained. This session is organised by the CAA SIG on Semantics and LOUD in Archaeology (SIG Data-Dragon). The core aim of this SIG is to use the SIG format to raise awareness for Linked Data in archaeology by creating a friendly and open platform to discuss and further develop semantics, and LOUD and FAIR data in archaeology. Linked Pasts VII, Ghent, Belgium. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.5781275. [4] Hyland, B., Atemezing, G., Pendleton, M., Srivastava, B. (2013). Linked Data Glossary, W3C Working Group Note 27 June 2013. URL: https://www.w3.org/TR/ld-glossary/. [5] Sanderson, R. (2018). Shout it Out: LOUD by Rob Sanderson, EuropeanaTech Conference 2018. title: Weibull Tail Coefficient Estimation via Linear Combinations
abstract: A todos os participantes, palestrantes e convidados, É com enorme satisfação que a Sociedade Portuguesa de Estatística (SPE), em colaboração com a Universidade do Algarve (UAlg), acolhe o XXVII Congresso da Sociedade Portuguesa de Estatística, que de 22 a 25 de outubro de 2025, no Complexo Pedagógico do Campus da Penha, em Faro.Este evento é um encontro aberto a todos os que partilham interesse pela Estatística e pela Ciência de Dados, sejam investigadores, profissionais ou estudantes.Reconhecido como uma das iniciativas mais marcantes da SPE, o congresso tem por missão divulgar, valorizar e impulsionar o estudo e a aplicação da Estatística e das suas áreas afins.O congresso inicia-se com o minicurso "The Hitchhiker's Guide to Responsible Machine Learning", ministrado pelo Professor Przemyslaw Biecek, da Warsaw University of Technology, Polónia.Este minicurso tem como objetivo introduzir os princípios e práticas de aprendizagem automática responsável.O programa científico integra quatro sessões plenárias, conduzidas por investigadores de reconhecido mérito internacional: A primeira, intitulada "Statistics and Artificial Intelligence in Medicine", de Ana Luísa Papoila, irá focar-se no papel crucial da estatística no desenvolvimento de modelos de IA.A segunda será apresentada por Przemyslaw Biecek, com o título "Explanatory Model Analysis".Durante a palestra, serão apresentados os recentes desenvolvimentos em técnicas de visualização e exploração de modelos preditivos.Na terceira, "The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Data Science", de Renato Assunção, será apresentada uma visão geral dos fatores responsáveis pela IA, com foco na contribuição da Estatística.Na quarta,"One Way to Estimate an Out-of-Sample Quantile of an Unknown Distribution Through Extreme Value Theory", de Cláudia Neves, serão abordadas várias definições de (extreme) out-of-sample quantile através da estrutura dos domínios de atração e a generalização da estimativa de um nível de retorno válido para ambos os casos de limite superior finito ou infinito para a distribuição real subjacente aos dados amostrados.O congresso inclui ainda 10 sessões temáticas, organizadas por diferentes instituições e grupos de investigação, que abordam temas atuais e especializados da Estatística e suas aplicações.Na sessão temática organizada pelo Banco de Portugal será abordado o tema da Anonimização e Proteção de Microdados.Na sessão Estatística em Português -Estatística com África será apresentada a cooperação científica e ensino nos PALOP.Na sessão Paving the Way: Making Careers in Statistics Education Research Visible and Viable, serão exploradas questões relacionadas com carreiras na investigação em educação estatística, numa mesa redonda com os oradores online.A sessão Indústria (PT-MATH.IN) foca-se nas aplicações da estatística à indústria.Na sessão organizada pela Comissão Especializada de Educação da SPE, CEE-SPE, as apresentações serão sobre Ensino e Divulgação da Estatística.Numa parceria entre a SPE e a Sociedade Galega para a Promoción da Estatística e da Investigación de Operacións, será realizada online a sessão SPE-Biometria /SGAPEIO, organizada pela secção de Biometria da SPE e em simultâneo com o XVII Congreso Galego de Estatística e Investigación de Operacións.Na sessão organizada pelo Instituto Nacional de Estatística, INE, serão abordadas as Inovações em Estatísticas Oficiais.Numa parceria entre a SPE e a Associação Portuguesa de Classificação e Análise de Dados, será realizada a sessão SPE/CLAD.Numa parceria entre a SPE e a Associação Portuguesa de Investigação Operacional, será realizada a sessão SPE-APDIO sob o tema Otimização e Aplicações em Investigação Operacional.Na sessão SPE/IPQ/CT225 organizada pela Comissão Técnica do Instituto Português de Qualidade -Aplicação de Métodos Estatísticos será abordada a Standardização Nacional e Internacional em Métodos Estatísticos.Estas sessões promovem o intercâmbio de ideias e experiências entre investigadores, profissionais e estudantes, reforçando o papel da Estatística como ciência transversal e indispensável à compreensão e tomada de decisão em contextos multidisciplinares.Para além destas sessões temáticas, contamos com mais 79 sessões orais e 48 pósteres, organizados em várias áreas, nomeadamente, Séries Temporais, Ciência de Dados, Aplicações em Ambiente, Clima Geociências e Agricultura, Estatística Multivariada, Estatística Computacional, Estatística Espacial, Métodos Não paramétricos, Análise de Sobrevivência, Extremos, Bioestatística e Epidemiologia, Aplicações em Econometria, Finanças e Gestão, Probabilidade e Processos Estocásticos e Métodos Bayesianos.Este é o cenário ideal para homenagear pessoas que dedicaram a sua vida a esta nobre área.O Prémio Carreira representa não apenas o reconhecimento de um percurso de excelência, mas também um sincero tributo de gratidão por uma vida dedicada à ciência e ao ensino da Estatística.A Professora Eugénia Graça Martins, com a sua visão pedagógica e capacidade de motivar o pensamento crítico, contribuiu decisivamente para a valorização da Estatística como disciplina fundamental em tantas áreas do saber.O Professor Fernando Rosado, com o seu compromisso com a qualidade científica, elevou o padrão do trabalho estatístico, deixando um legado de rigor e ética.Mantendo viva a valorização do talento e da inovação, há igualmente lugar para distinguir as comunicações mais recentes, com a atribuição do Prémio SPE 2024 e 2025 e também dos mais jovens com a atribuição do Prémio Estatístico Júnior.Reunindo uma variedade de temas que refletem o dinamismo na área da Es-tatística, o programa procura não só estimular novas parcerias e trajetórias profissionais, como também equilibrar o rigor académico com experiências sociais e culturais enriquecedoras."Abraçado pela marina e pela paisagem deslumbrante da Ria Formosa, o AP Eva Senses Hotel" é o local perfeito para a realização do Jantar do Congresso.Uma oportunidade privilegiada para fortalecer relações profissionais, complementada por uma visita guiada ao centro histórico ou um passeio de barco pela Ria Formosa, que acrescentam ao programa uma dimensão cultural e social, promovendo um equilíbrio harmonioso entre ciência e lazer.Um agradecimento sincero aos nossos patrocinadores, voluntários e a todos aqueles que contribuíram com esforço e dedicação para tornar este evento uma realidade.Desejamos a todos um excelente congresso!

title: Assessing the Impact of Artificial Intelligence on the Olympic Games
abstract: The Olympic Games have always been at the forefront of adopting new technologies to enhance various aspects of the competition.1 In recent years, the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into the Olympics has emerged as a transformative force, promising to revolutionize athlete performance, event management, and audience engagement.2 This technological shift is not merely a trend but a significant evolution that reflects broader changes in how sports are practiced, managed, and consumed in the digital age.3 AI technologies offer unprecedented opportunities to optimize various facets of the Olympic Games. From real-time analytics that provide coaches and athletes with invaluable insights to advanced systems that streamline the logistics of organizing such a massive event, AI is poised to redefine the operational landscape of the Olympics.4 The potential benefits are vast, encompassing enhanced performance metrics, improved safety and security measures, and enriched spectator experiences. These advancements align with the Olympic spirit of pushing the boundaries of human potential and innovation.However, the integration of AI into the Olympics also brings forth a set of complex challenges that need to be addressed.5 The rapid pace of AI development has outstripped the ability of existing regulatory frameworks to keep up, leading to a lack of clear guidelines and standards.6 This regulatory gap raises questions about fairness, accountability, and ethical considerations, particularly in the context of performance enhancement and data privacy.7 The deployment of AI technologies must be carefully managed to ensure that they do not undermine the principles of fair competition and respect for individual rights that are central to the Olympic ethos.8The purpose of this research note is to explore and assess the impact of AI on the Olympic Games, encompassing various dimensions such as athlete performance, event management, and audience engagement. As future developments in AI promise to bring about transformative changes in the future of the Games, this research note aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of how AI is currently being utilized in the context of the Olympics, stress the benefits of this integration, and detect potential challenges. To achieve the above aim, three objectives underpinning this note are to (1) identify how AI is currently applied in the Olympics and stress the benefits; (2) detect the challenges of integrating AI into the Olympics; and (3) introduce a set of contextual recommendations for better engagement.By examining the benefits and challenges associated with AI integration, this research note seeks to offer insights into how AI can improve athlete training and performance analysis, streamline event logistics and security, and create more personalized and immersive experiences for spectators. Additionally, the research note will address ethical concerns, such as data privacy and algorithmic fairness, to ensure that the deployment of AI in the Olympics aligns with principles of equity and transparency. Ultimately, this research note contributes to the broader discourse on the role of AI in sports and large-scale events, providing valuable recommendations for stakeholders involved in the planning and execution of the Olympic Games.The 2018 Winter Olympics in South Korea prominently showcased the integration of AI. During the Opening Ceremony, humanoid robots were featured, symbolizing the country's technological progress. A total of eighty-five robots were deployed to perform a range of tasks, including providing information and carrying out cleaning duties, thereby demonstrating innovative applications of AI in managing events and enhancing operational efficiency.9 Likewise, the Tokyo 2020 Summer Olympics were a pivotal moment for the incorporation of AI into the event. When the 2020 Summer Olympic Games took place in Tokyo a year later than planned because of the COVID-19 pandemic, over 11,000 athletes from 200 countries participated in forty-one sports across forty-two venues. In addition to the postponed schedule and absence of spectators due to pandemic restrictions, the Tokyo Olympics stood out from previous games due to the extensive use of AI technologies. These included robots, wearable sensors, machine learning, and the vast amount of data available for analysis and processing to benefit all participants.10AI-powered technologies play a crucial role in boosting athlete performance and enriching the fan experience. Additionally, robots welcome visitors while ensuring social distancing protocols and autonomous vehicles facilitate the transportation of athletes and officials. Notably, AI was used to compose the theme song, and drones delivered impressive visual displays, showcasing AI's creative capabilities. The integration of AI technologies is not only revolutionizing how the Games are conducted but also elevating the overall experience for athletes, organizers, and fans alike. AI is playing an increasingly pivotal role in the Olympic Games, transforming various aspects, from athlete performance and event management to audience engagement. The integration of AI technologies is enhancing the efficiency, accuracy, and overall experience of the Olympics, making it a more dynamic and engaging event for all stakeholders involved.11 On the field, in the stands, or behind the scenes, there are several ways AI makes an impact at the Olympic games.AI technologies are employed to optimize training regimens, refine performance analysis, and minimize injury risks.12 Machine learning algorithms, such as regression models and classification algorithms, analyze large datasets to predict future performance and assess injury risks based on factors like training load and biomechanics. Artificial neural networks (ANNs), including deep learning models and recurrent neural networks (RNNs), optimize training programs and predict injury risks by learning complex patterns from multifactorial data.13 Natural language processing (NLP) techniques, such as sentiment analysis and text mining, interpret athletes’ language in social media posts and medical reports to gauge their mental state and extract relevant injury information.14 Predictive analytics, employing time-series analysis and survival analysis, forecast optimal training loads, recovery times, and rehabilitation plans, ensuring athletes maintain peak performance while minimizing injury risks. This data-driven approach enables coaches and trainers to create personalized training programs to maximize an athlete's strengths and address their weaknesses.15AI-powered video analysis tools dissect an athlete's movements frame by frame, identifying areas for improvement that may not be visible to the naked eye.16 Computer vision and video analysis tools, including motion capture systems and automated video analysis software, allow for detailed examination of athletes’ techniques, enabling coaches to pinpoint areas for improvement and detect movements that may lead to injuries. In sports like gymnastics or diving, AI can evaluate the precision and execution of complex maneuvers, offering detailed feedback to refine techniques.17 Similarly, in track and field events, AI can analyze an athlete's running form and biomechanics, providing insights that lead to more efficient and effective performance.18 In the Tokyo Olympics, AI has enabled physical tests of athletes to detect early signs of fatigue or stress-induced injuries, a predictive tool that sports organizations and Olympic teams could use to keep athletes safe from future injuries.19One of the most impactful applications of AI in the Olympics is enhancing athlete performance. AI-powered wearable devices monitor an athlete's heart rate, oxygen levels, and muscle activity in real time, providing instant feedback and allowing for on-the-fly adjustments to training routines. These wearables track sleep patterns and recovery times, ensuring athletes are in optimal condition for their events.20 Wearable sensors and IoT devices, such as GPS trackers and smart clothing, monitor real-time physiological and biomechanical data and provide insights into performance metrics like heart rate, speed, and muscle activity. These devices also help in identifying early signs of potential injuries by analyzing movement patterns and physical stress.21 As athletes trained for the Tokyo Olympics, their performance data was gathered through sensors, wearables, and cameras. Devices such as sensors embedded in shoes or bike pedals continuously supplied data, aiding athletes and coaches in adjusting to enhance their competitiveness. Artificial intelligence offered valuable information and insights that were previously inaccessible.22Additionally, AI predicts injury risks by analyzing movement and workload patterns, enabling preventive measures. This predictive capability is especially valuable in high-impact sports where injury risks are significant.23 Moreover, AI can assist in mental training by analyzing an athlete's psychological state and providing insights into their mental well-being.24 This enables coaches to address any psychological issues that may be affecting an athlete's performance, ensuring that they are in peak mental condition for competition. These AI-driven tools and methods provide a comprehensive approach to enhancing athletic performance and safeguarding athletes’ health, offering unprecedented insights and precision in sports science. By leveraging these technologies, coaches and athletes can make data-driven decisions that lead to improved outcomes and reduced injury rates, ultimately contributing to the overall success and longevity of athletes’ careers.AI is significantly enhancing the management and organization of the Olympic Games. One of its primary applications in event management lies in logistics and planning. AI algorithms can process vast amounts of data to optimize scheduling, venue selection, and resource allocation.25 AI can determine the best dates and times for events by analyzing historical attendance data, weather patterns, and matching events. This data-driven approach ensures events are planned with maximum efficiency and minimal conflicts, resulting in higher attendance.26 In terms of attendee management, AI-powered systems streamline registration and check-in processes. Facial recognition technology, for instance, allows attendees to check in without physical tickets or identification, reducing wait times and enhancing security by ensuring only registered individuals gain access.27 Additionally, AI chatbots can handle a wide range of customer service inquiries, from answering frequently asked questions to providing real-time updates on event schedules and locations. These chatbots operate 24/7, offering immediate assistance and freeing up human staff to focus on more complex tasks.28Security is another critical area where AI is making significant contributions. AI-driven surveillance systems can monitor large crowds in real time, identifying potential threats through behavior analysis and facial recognition.29 These systems can alert security personnel to suspicious activities, enabling quicker and more effective responses. Moreover, AI can analyze social media and other online platforms for potential security threats, providing an additional layer of protection.30 The integration of AI in event management not only enhances the efficiency and security of the Olympic Games but also ensures a more enjoyable and seamless experience for all attendees.
