title: Innovation in Cardiothoracic Surgery: From Incremental Progress to Transformative Change
abstract: Technological innovation has continuously transformed medicine, often through incremental refinement of established techniques. In contrast, disruptive innovation does not simply improve existing practice; it changes the logic of care delivery by introducing new technologies or workflows that initially may appear inferior by conventional standards, but ultimately reshape who is treated, how treatment is delivered, and which professionals or systems guide decision-making. Cardiothoracic surgery itself emerged through a series of disruptive innovations. Early cardiac operations in the 1950s relied on hypothermia, inflow occlusion, or cross-circulation.1 The clinical introduction of the heart–lung machine by Gibbon2 fundamentally transformed cardiac care, enabling direct intracardiac surgery and redefining the boundaries of treatable disease. Subsequent advances, including coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG), valve repair, or heart and lung transplantation, were similarly disruptive and initially met with professional scepticism. Importantly, many of these innovations were driven by surgeons themselves, highlighting that the specialty has historically been a primary source of disruptive, transformative change rather than merely a recipient of external sustaining innovation. More recent examples of disruptive innovation include, for example, percutaneous coronary interventions (PCIs) or transcatheter valve therapies: initially developed for patients considered inoperable or at prohibitive surgical risk, they subsequently expanded into broader patient populations and altered referral pathways, treatment boundaries, and the relationship between surgical and interventional care. While much of medical progress has historically been driven by clinician-led, iterative improvement, advances in artificial intelligence (AI), data-driven systems, and automation3 are now introducing changes that extend beyond technical improvement and increasingly affect how clinical decisions are made, how care is organized, and how responsibility is distributed. These developments are not isolated innovations but part of converging socio-technical systems that integrate data, algorithms, digital platforms, and increasingly automated workflows. Cardiothoracic surgery is particularly exposed to these dynamics. The specialty relies on high-cost interventions, operates in data-rich environments, and is subject to increasing pressure to improve outcomes while optimizing limited resources. Over the past decades, progress has been driven primarily by sustaining innovations—refinements in surgical technique, perioperative management, and technology—resulting in a higher standard of care. The current wave of innovation, however, increasingly challenges not only how surgeons operate, but when, for whom, and by whom surgical care is delivered. Importantly, innovation in cardiothoracic surgery does not occur solely through disruption. It reflects a continuum ranging from incremental refinements to system-level transformations, often coexisting and interacting within clinical practice. Understanding the nature of disruptive innovation is therefore no longer a theoretical exercise. It has become a strategic necessity for cardiothoracic surgery as a specialty and for the institutions and scientific societies that represent it. This editorial aims to: Illustrate the distinction between sustaining and disruptive innovation in the context of medicine; Explain why cardiothoracic surgery is particularly susceptible to disruption; Describe typical professional and institutional responses to disruptive change; Explore why established leaders often struggle to adapt; Outline the responsibility of scientific societies, including European Association of Cardio-Thoracic Surgery (EACTS). The distinction between sustaining and disruptive innovation was articulated by Christensen,4 who described how market-leading organizations are often displaced not by inferior performance, but by innovations that initially appear unattractive or irrelevant to established players. Although developed in an industrial context, this framework provides a useful lens through which to examine developments in medicine. Sustaining innovations improve existing practices along dimensions already valued by established users and institutions (Figure 1), such as safety, durability, precision, and procedural success. In cardiothoracic surgery, these include refinements in myocardial protection and valve repair techniques, advances in prosthetic valve function and durability, improved cardiopulmonary bypass technology, enhanced imaging for operative planning, and the evolution of less invasive techniques. These innovations strengthen the existing therapeutic model while preserving the central role of the surgeon while enhancing safety and outcomes. Sustaining vs Disruptive Innovation. Conceptual illustration of performance trajectories over time, showing incremental improvement in sustaining technologies across low, medium, and high-quality use as well as most demanding use levels and the eventual performance crossover of a disruptive technology. The figure was generated with the assistance of OpenAI’s DALL·E (via ChatGPT) based on author-defined input and subsequently refined by the authors. By contrast, disruptive innovations introduce a different value proposition. Rather than competing primarily on conventional performance metrics, they often initially underperform according to traditional standards. For example, from a purely technical perspective, interventional valve therapies may not achieve the same anatomical precision and long-term durability as surgical repair or replacement.5 However, they may offer other advantages, including reduced invasiveness, broader accessibility, shorter recovery, lower system burden, and new modes of decision-making (Figure 1). These short-term benefits have contributed to broader acceptance by patients and referring physicians, thereby accelerating their diffusion and reinforcing their disruptive potential. In cardiovascular medicine, such innovations frequently enter practice by addressing patients previously considered unsuitable for surgery and/or by offering different risk-benefit trade-offs. Percutaneous coronary interventions (PCIs) or transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) exemplifies this trajectory: initially reserved for inoperable or high-risk patients, it has progressively expanded into lower-risk populations, reshaping referral patterns and professional boundaries. However, unlike in industrial settings, healthcare innovation is shaped by biological constraints, ethical considerations, and regulatory frameworks, which often moderate or reshape disruptive trajectories. Thus, incremental innovation typically improves the existing model, whereas disruptive innovation may alter the model itself. Although the general principles of disruptive innovation apply across disciplines, cardiothoracic surgery exhibits characteristics that warrant particular attention. Surgical decision-making involves irreversible interventions, high immediate risk, and clear attribution of responsibility. Training pathways are long, credentialing is rigorous, and evidence generation is slow compared with the pace of software-driven innovation. These characteristics, while essential for patient safety, may slow adoption but do not preclude innovation. Rather, they shape the form innovation takes within the specialty. These features justify a cautious approach to adoption, but they also increase susceptibility to disruption originating outside traditional surgical structures. AI-supported patient selection and referral triage systems6 are already influencing which patients reach surgical evaluation. Machine-learning-based risk prediction models increasingly rival conventional scoring systems such as EuroSCORE II or STS scores.7,8 Automated imaging analysis enables detailed characterization of valve pathology, ventricular function, and aortic anatomy with minimal human input.9 As a result, critical decisions in the patient journey increasingly occur upstream of surgical consultation. In this sense, disruption begins well before the operating room, subtly redistributing clinical authority across digital systems, workflows, and institutions. At the same time, many of these technologies function as decision-support tools rather than replacements, reinforcing the importance of clinical interpretation and multidisciplinary integration. Scepticism towards disruptive innovation is understandable and often justified but carries considerable risk. Across disciplines, professional responses to disruptive change are remarkably consistent. Common reactions include concerns that algorithms cannot capture clinical nuance, fears of eroding professional autonomy, and demands for long-term outcome data before engagement. Another common response is the assertion that clinical teams are fully occupied with routine work—which, for obvious reasons, must take priority—leaving no capacity to engage with seemingly abstract or “immature” disruptive ideas (Figure 2). These responses reflect legitimate concerns related to patient safety, accountability, and evidentiary standards. The Challenge and Reward of Process Improvement. Initial resistance to process improvement—often justified by perceived lack of time—can delay simple changes that ultimately lead to substantial gains in efficiency. The figure was generated with the assistance of OpenAI’s DALL·E (via ChatGPT) based on author-defined input and subsequently refined by the authors. Statements such as “this technology cannot replace surgical judgement” (Table 1) reflect legitimate concerns, but they may sometimes obscure a critical point: disruption rarely aims at direct replacement. Instead, it redistributes decision-making authority across systems, workflows, and time points. Another frequent response is the delegation of innovation to industry or future generations, resulting in externally driven development rather than proactive professional stewardship. Typical Reactions of Surgeons and Institutions “Artificial intelligence cannot replace surgical judgement” “This will never replace clinical judgement” “My patients are different” Overreliance on historical excellence Resistance to automated planning tools Expectation of long-term outcome data before engagement Over-demand for RCT-level evidence before adoption Delegation of innovation to “industry” or “the next generation” Abbreviation: RCT = randomized, controlled trial. While understandable, this reactive posture risks relegating surgeons to downstream users of systems that increasingly shape clinical practice. Christensen’s observation that established leaders often struggle with disruptive innovation4 applies particularly well to cardiothoracic surgery. Centres of excellence are optimized for complex open procedures, supported by infrastructure, training programmes, and performance metrics that reward technical mastery and procedural volume. When disruptive alternatives emerge, misalignment often develops between patient preferences, payer incentives, and institutional priorities. It is important to recognize that these challenges do not reflect a lack of innovation capacity, but rather a structural misalignment between established systems and emerging models of care. Resource allocation typically favours established workflows, while emerging technologies may lack clear reimbursement pathways or institutional ownership. Declining volumes in certain open procedures10,11 further intensify this tension. Past excellence, while foundational, can become structural inertia when value systems emphasize complexity over scalability and system-level efficiency. Consequently, the capabilities that once defined leadership in cardiothoracic surgery may inadvertently constrain adaptation. The term disruptive innovation is frequently applied to AI-based technologies in cardiothoracic surgery. However, not all AI-enabled developments represent disruptive innovation, and disruption does not automatically imply clinical benefit. Conceptual clarity is therefore required to distinguish different forms and degrees of innovation. Importantly, not all technologies labelled as “disruptive” result in sustained clinical impact, and many ultimately integrate into existing frameworks rather than replacing them. Three levels can be distinguished: Incremental innovation refers to technologies that improve existing tasks within the current clinical workflow, without fundamentally changing decision-making structures.12 Examples include automated large image segmentation, preoperative planning support,13 risk stratification,12 and assistance with clinical documentation. Workflow-level disruption refers to technologies that reorganize, compress, or partially automate parts of care delivery. Examples include AI-supported referral triage, automated image interpretation prior to specialist review, or digital platforms that shorten the interval between diagnostic assessment and treatment planning. In such cases, the institutional structure may remain largely intact, the operational logic of care changes. Role-level disruption involves a redistribution of professional responsibilities and authority. Emerging examples of role-level disruption include AI systems influencing which patients are referred for surgical evaluation, platform-based outcome monitoring linked to reimbursement or quality oversight, and partial automation of procedural planning or execution. Additional applications may extend to help in guideline development,14 grant evaluation, and peer review of scientific publications and automated assessment of clinical documentation. Such developments do not necessarily replace surgeons, but they may alter where authority resides and how clinical decisions are being made. Distinguishing between these levels is important because each raises different questions of validation, ethics, governance, and regulation. In practice, the evolution of cardiothoracic care is increasingly characterized by hybrid models rather than binary replacement. Surgical, interventional, and digital approaches are progressively integrated into patient-specific pathways. This convergence suggests that the future of the specialty will be defined less by competition between modalities and more by their coordinated application within multidisciplinary systems. Scientific societies such as the EACTS occupy a pivotal position in navigating innovation. Their role is neither to promote indiscriminate adoption nor to resist change reflexively, but to provide structured leadership in evaluation, implementation, and governance. European Association of Cardio-Thoracic Surgery (EACTS) should foster innovation across its full spectrum, from incremental advances to transformative change, and support researchers in translating promising ideas into clinical use. This role includes several concrete functions. First, EACTS can expand and intensify the to help define standards for evaluation by curating evidence, identifying clinically meaningful end-points, and promoting validation frameworks for emerging technologies such as AI-based decision support, robotic platforms, and digital monitoring tools within the Clinical Practice Guidelines Committee (CPG). Second, EACTS can use and expand current platforms that accelerate exchange and responsible adoption, including scientific sessions during the Annual Meeting, innovation summits, focused webinars, training opportunities, and collaborative research initiatives through the EACTS Innovation Committee and Hub. Such formats help expose surgeons early to developing technologies while preserving critical appraisal. Third, EACTS can contribute to professional guidance through guidelines, expert consensus statements and position documents in areas such as robotics, AI, digital surgery, and data governance. In rapidly evolving fields, such guidance may be essential before high-level trial evidence becomes available. Fourth, EACTS can shape future training and accreditation pathways by defining competencies required for the use of new technologies, integrating innovation into surgical education, and supporting the development of reference centres or centres of excellence. Fifth, EACTS can represent the specialty in regulatory and policy discussions. Initial progress in this direction has already been achieved in contributions to discussions surrounding revisions of the medical device regulation (MDR) concerning the use of robotics in cardiac surgery, in collaboration with other professional organizations such as the European Society of Cardiology (ESC).15,16 In this way, scientific societies can help ensure that innovation develops within standards defined by clinical expertise, patient safety, and ethical responsibility, validation of AI tools, and integration of digital technologies into training and certification pathways. Disruptive innovation in cardiothoracic surgery is neither a distant future scenario nor an external force imposed solely by technology developers. It is an ongoing process shaped by decisions made—or deferred—by surgeons, institutions, and scientific societies. While caution is appropriate, disengagement risks relinquishing influence over how surgical care is organized and governed. The central challenge is therefore not whether disruption will occur, but whether cardiothoracic surgeons will actively lead its integration into clinical practice. As algorithms increasingly influence patient selection and clinical pathways, the principal threat to surgical autonomy may lie not in technological advancement but in the absence of strong surgical leadership to guide its integration in clinical practice. Cardiothoracic surgeons, institutions, and scientific societies must therefore move from awareness to active engagement, ensuring that innovation is aligned with patient outcomes, professional standards, and societal trust. Shaping the Future Rather Than Reacting to It. All authors declare that they have no conflict of interest regarding this Editorial. None declared.

title: December 2024 JUOP: On to the New Year With Resolutions and a Focus on Retrospective Study Opportunities
abstract: A funny sign was posted on social media recently—the image of a Dairy Queen sign with the block letter message below “Ruining Your New Year's Resolution Since 1962.” So true. That day in church, the minister brought up New Year’s resolutions, pointing out that their history goes back some 4000 years to the Babylonians in the era of the new year starting in mid-March. Resolutions involved affirming the reigning king and making promises to the gods. The Romans then moved the calendar start back to January in 46 B.C.—the month named for the god Janus, who was a spirit inhabiting doorways and arches. The significance of Janus was the idea of looking backward into the previous year and ahead to the future. Despite the religious beginnings, New Year’s resolutions have migrated to a more secular tradition with more themes of self-improvement. You can read more on this from an article on the History Chanel authored by Sarah Pruitt.1 For JUOP going into the new year, we finished our second full year with 12 new issues published and received 170 new submissions. We added several new experts to our editorial board. Going into our third year, we hope to pursue PubMed Central indexing and to expand our submission rate and publication size further toward 200 articles per year. In our issue editorials, we have highlighted our 6 key methodologies, and in this article, we highlight the final format of a retrospective study. Our board members Henry Woo and Bernardo Rocco led this writing with their colleague Maria Chiara Sighinolfi, MD. RETROSPECTIVE STUDY OPPORTUNITIES: HARNESSING THE POWER OF PAST DATA In the evolving landscape of medical research, retrospective studies remain a cornerstone, offering unique insights derived from previously collected data. By leveraging this approach, researchers can illuminate patterns, evaluate outcomes, and generate hypotheses that drive clinical innovation. Retrospective studies, despite their inherent limitations, present a wealth of opportunities when strategically designed and thoughtfully interpreted. ADVANTAGES OF RETROSPECTIVE STUDIES Retrospective studies use existing data, allowing for swift analyses without the logistical challenges of prospective trials. These studies are particularly advantageous for rare conditions or long-term outcomes, where collecting new data might be infeasible. In addition, they are cost-effective, often requiring fewer resources compared with prospective designs. By focusing on real-world evidence, retrospective studies bridge the gap between controlled experimental settings and everyday clinical practice, thereby enhancing the external validity of findings. One notable example is their application in rare diseases, where prospective trials often face recruitment challenges. Recently, Qian et al2 retrospectively collected data on open retroperitoneal nodal dissection (RPLND) for testicular cancer. The recruitment of patients in the field is generally poor, and the retrospective design allowed for high-volume collection of cases granting the comparison between the primary and postchemo setting, otherwise not feasible. The authors indicate favorable perioperative outcomes within the open surgery setting. While long-term outcome data are necessary to properly select patients for robotic RPLND, open RPLND, when performed by experienced surgeons, continues to enhance its results and remains the standard approach in current practice.2 Another example of rare condition is urachal carcinoma. Kirisawa et al3 addressed the topic from a retrospective revision of the Japan National Cancer Registry. Within a database of 51 patients, the authors found that the involvement of perivesical fat and tumor grade were significant predictors of poor overall survival. Retrospective analyses have uncovered critical insights into disease progression and response to treatments, guiding both clinical decisions and the design of future studies. The collection of retrospective data sets is the very base of multivariate analysis to guide outcome prediction through the development of models. For example, from the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results Program database, Li et al4 developed a prognostic nomogram for older patients with urothelial carcinoma. A model predicting outcomes is valuable for both physician and patients and may guide decision-making and expectations. Similarly, in long-term outcomes research, retrospective designs have proven invaluable in assessing the durability of interventions, such as diagnostic procedures and pharmacological therapies, over extended periods. For example, the usefulness of prostate specific membrane antigen-positron emission tomography (PSMA-PET) was recently addressed over a consecutive retrospective series of 1220 patients.5 From this data set, PSMA-PET provided a 13.2% absolute increase in the detection of nodal lesion and 24% absolute increase in metastatic lesions compared with MRI; however, the impact of stage migration still remains unaddressed. Similarly, retrospective studies may assess the value of screening interventions over time. By using data from the Military Health System Data Repository, the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on the slowdown of prostate cancer screening was definitely defined, finding an overwhelming 73% reduction in PSA assessment in the early pandemic era.6 In urology, retrospective studies have provided pivotal data on the effectiveness of new minimally invasive technologies, allowing for feasibility and safety assessments. For example, the introduction of new robotic systems was reported by Rocco et al7 within a case series including Hugo RAS and Versius. The experience defined the safety of those new platforms for radical prostatectomy and highlighted the issues—that is, malfunctioning—typical of each robotic systems. CHALLENGES AND MITIGATION STRATEGIES Although valuable, retrospective studies are not without challenges. Issues such as incomplete data, selection bias, and confounding variables can compromise their reliability. To mitigate these limitations, researchers must adopt robust statistical techniques, such as propensity score matching (PSM) or multivariate analyses, to adjust for confounding factors. Houjaij et al8 recently reported on the comparison between partial and radical nephrectomy in terms of complications. From a database including 24,830 patients who underwent kidney surgery, a PSM was performed to adjust for confounding variables. In the field, the covariates used for PSM included age, preoperative hematocrit, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, presence of distant metastasis, hypertension, congestive heart failure, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chronic use of steroids, weight loss > 10%, ascites, bleeding disorders, and American Society of Anesthesiologists physical status. With this mitigating strategy, complications seemed most frequent after radical than after partial nephrectomy. In addition, clear documentation of methodologies and transparent reporting of potential biases are essential for ensuring credibility. Innovative approaches are also emerging to address these challenges. The integration of machine learning algorithms, for instance, allows researchers to handle large data sets efficiently, identifying patterns that might otherwise be obscured by traditional methods. Advanced data imputation techniques are helping to fill gaps in incomplete data sets, ensuring more comprehensive analyses. In urology, the use of these technologies has facilitated the analysis of vast biobanking repositories, enabling researchers to extract meaningful insights about biomarkers linked to urological malignancies and treatment responses. APPLICATIONS ACROSS MEDICAL DISCIPLINES The versatility of retrospective studies extends across numerous fields. In oncology, for instance, retrospective analyses have been instrumental in identifying prognostic factors and refining treatment protocols. For example, large-scale retrospective reviews of cancer registries have elucidated the impact of various therapies on survival rates, paving the way for more personalized treatment approaches. Retrospective analysis may retrieve data from small subgroups of patients, that is, those who are misclassified after assessing long-term outcomes of impact of misclassification of neoadjuvant chemotherapy responders was addressed through a retrospective revision of a prospectively maintained database. Similarly, in cardiology, retrospective data have shed light on the long-term safety and efficacy of interventions such as coronary stenting and valve replacement. In urology, retrospective studies have elucidated long-term outcomes of surgical interventions and the comparative effectiveness of various therapies. These studies have also been crucial in evaluating the impact of technological advancements, such as robotic surgery, on patient outcomes. Furthermore, the integration of retrospective data with modern technologies, such as artificial intelligence, has unlocked new dimensions of analysis, enabling pattern recognition and predictive modeling at unprecedented scales. Biobanking initiatives in urology, which store patient-derived biological samples alongside clinical data, represent a powerful synergy with retrospective research. These repositories have catalyzed discoveries in prostate cancer biomarkers, advancing risk stratification and therapeutic personalization. ETHICAL CONSIDERATIONS Given the reliance on preexisting data, retrospective studies pose unique ethical considerations. Ensuring patient confidentiality and adhering to data governance regulations are paramount. Institutional review boards play a critical role in overseeing these studies, balancing the benefits of research against the need to protect individual rights. Transparency in data handling and ensuring informed consent where applicable are vital components of ethical retrospective research. Furthermore, as data-sharing initiatives gain traction, researchers must navigate complex ethical landscapes to ensure that data usage aligns with both regulatory standards and public expectations. This is particularly important in the era of big data, where the aggregation of data sets from multiple sources can significantly amplify both the potential benefits and risks associated with research. Biobanking efforts, in particular, demand rigorous ethical oversight to ensure that samples and associated data are used responsibly and in line with donor consent. THE FUTURE OF RETROSPECTIVE RESEARCH As electronic health records and large-scale databases continue to expand, the potential for retrospective studies grows exponentially. By incorporating advanced analytics and cross-disciplinary collaborations, researchers can maximize the utility of historical data. Retrospective studies are poised to complement prospective trials, providing a comprehensive view of clinical phenomena and accelerating the translation of research into practice. The integration of retrospective data with cutting-edge technologies, such as natural language processing and blockchain, promises to further enhance the scope and reliability of these studies. Natural language processing can extract valuable insights from unstructured data sources, such as clinical notes, while blockchain ensures data integrity and security, fostering greater trust in research outcomes. These innovations highlight the dynamic and evolving nature of retrospective research, ensuring its continued relevance in the scientific community. In urology, the convergence of retrospective analyses and biobanking is likely to yield transformative advances, particularly in the domains of genetic profiling, immunotherapy, and precision medicine. CONCLUSIONS Retrospective studies are a powerful tool in the research arsenal, offering insights that might otherwise remain obscured. While challenges persist, meticulous design and innovative methodologies can unlock their full potential. The medical community must continue to embrace retrospective research as a vital component of evidence generation, ensuring that lessons from the past inform the advancements of the future. The integration of retrospective analyses with prospective research paradigms can create a synergistic model, where the strengths of both approaches are leveraged to provide a more holistic understanding of clinical questions. By valuing and investing in retrospective research, we can build a robust foundation for medical progress. In urology, this approach is particularly compelling because the wealth of data housed in biobanks offers unparalleled opportunities to unravel complex disease mechanisms and refine therapeutic strategies. Ensuring that the knowledge gained from past data continues to shape and improve patient care for generations to come remains a shared responsibility and a vital goal for the global research community. DECEMBER JUOP ARTICLES Given the focus on retrospective studies, we will abbreviate the article issues for this month into key bullet points: Reviews: Henderson et al9 present a comprehensive, narrative review on somatic and germline testing in prostate cancer. This work includes several focus areas such as guidelines statements, patient selection, care delivery, test ordering options, cost and payer coverage, patient education, and more. Clinical trials: Treacy et al10 present an IRB-approved pilot trial of multiphoton microscopy to assess bladder cancer in cold cup biopsies. They found 80% sensitivity for resection depth and suggest this method be further studied toward the goal of avoiding unnecessary second procedures. Health services research: Smith et al11 looked at the topic of preventive pharmacological therapy for kidney stones. They used claims data from the Optum Clinformatics Data Mart database. They found that follow-up urine testing after prevention could improve medication adherence. Retrospective study: Sood et al12 looked at the practice of using pT0 (pathologic no primary tumor) status at radical cystectomy after chemotherapy for bladder cancer. It is a multilayer set of ideas tested, but a key point is the study of biopsy-proven node-positive patients. There was a high degree of discordance between local and nodal response to chemotherapy. They suggest that nodal response may be more valuable because some patients are pT0 from the transurethral resection of bladder tumor efforts. Rare conditions: Schott et al13 describe a case of ureteroduodenal fistula from an impacted stone. The case discusses etiology, presentation, and the key imaging and endoscopic images. PEOPLE, PLACES, AND THINGS Because December is mostly a holiday season, I did not have any academic events to feature. In Houston, we have mostly mild winter weather and a trip to the local zoo can be fun, rather than a summer visit in 100° heat. It got me thinking that there are several different environments to practice animal photography—aquariums, zoos, wildlife parks, and the actual wild. Depending on how you frame a picture, it may be difficult to tell the difference. Figures 1-4 show some highlights of my visits to these 4 different areas. Enjoy and see you next month.Figure 1.: From the aquarium. A, The sea nettle floats with the current and moves with rhythmic contractions. They are food to many species such as sea turtles, fish, and crabs. To humans, they have a powerful sting from their tentacles. B, Sea turtles—great swimmers; a bit slow on land. As swimmers, they can cross oceans and dive up to 3000 feet.Figure 2.: From the wild. A, This bald eagle is from SE Alaska near Baranof Island. B, An SE Alaska humpback whale breaches in Frederick Sound. Scientists say they do this for communication, play, or to show off, but not sure which. This one jumped constantly for 15 minutes in front of us, so will go with show off. C, From Yellowstone National Park—the bison can weigh up to 2000 pounds and run 35 miles per hour. In the winter, they are often found near thermal areas that keep grass available through the long winter season. D, The brown bear of SE Alaska. In September, the salmon start to spawn and the bears eagerly await along the shorelines. They are often called apex predators.Figure 3.: The preserve. A, This lynx resides at Steve Kroschel’s wildlife center in Haines, Alaska. B, The snowy owl—also from Steve Kroschel’s wildlife center in Haines, Alaska. C, The white rhino—from a nature preserve near Cape Town, South Africa.Figure 4.: The zoo. A, The Chilean flamingo—naturally a more white feather but gains its pink from the food it eats, with its upside-down filtering method. B, The radiated tortoise gets its name from the high dome with yellow lines radiating from the center. As a urologist, I want to come up with some good jokes on how this tortoise compares with the surgical tortoise. C, The lions—from their natural looking habitat. Fortunately this argument resolved quickly as they do not have a good way to get away from each other. D, This orangutan from the Houston Zoo has no problem posing for pictures.

title: Call for Papers: The Pathophysiology of COVID-19 and SARS-CoV-2 Infection
abstract: EditorialThe Pathophysiology of COVID-19 and SARS-CoV-2 InfectionCall for Papers: The Pathophysiology of COVID-19 and SARS-CoV-2 InfectionRory E. Morty and John ZiebuhrRory E. MortyDepartment of Lung Development and Remodelling, Max Planck Institute for Heart and Lung Research, Bad Nauheim, GermanyDepartment of Internal Medicine (Pulmonology), University of Giessen and Marburg Lung Center, Justus Liebig University Giessen, member of the German Center for Lung Research, Giessen, Germany and John ZiebuhrInstitute of Medical Virology, Justus Liebig University Giessen, member of the German Center for Infection Research, Giessen, GermanyPublished Online:04 May 2020https://doi.org/10.1152/ajplung.00136.2020This is the final version - click for previous versionMoreFiguresReferencesRelatedInformationSectionsGRANTSDISCLOSURESAUTHOR CONTRIBUTIONSACKNOWLEDGMENTSAUTHOR NOTESPDF (103 KB)Download PDF ToolsExport citationAdd to favoritesGet permissionsTrack citations ShareShare onFacebookXLinkedInWeChat The world now finds itself in the grip of a coronavirus pandemic. This is our third brush with a newly emerging zoonotic coronavirus since the turn of the millennium. The first of these three episodes started as an epidemic of severe respiratory disease of zoonotic origin that emerged in November 2002 in Foshan, Guangdong Province, People's Republic of China (41, 42). During the ensuing epidemic, the disease, subsequently named severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) (38), was diagnosed in 8,422 patients, and caused 774 deaths in 26 countries spanning five continents. The etiological agent of SARS was identified as a novel coronavirus (12, 17, 18), the SARS coronavirus (SARS-CoV), which is a member of the species Severe acute respiratory syndrome-related coronavirus in the genus Betacoronavirus (9, 13). The SARS epidemic ended on 5 July 2003 (37), and since 2005, no human cases of SARS have been reported (11). The current virus classification collects 39 species into the family Coronaviridae, with 10 more coronavirus species expected to be recognized shortly (13). Coronaviruses are enveloped positive-strand RNA viruses that infect vertebrates (19). Coronaviruses have been known since the 1930s, when infectious bronchitis virus was identified (6) as the cause of an earlier outbreak of highly contagious respiratory disease in chickens in 1931 (26). Subsequently, coronaviruses were identified in mice and pigs in the 1940s (20), and then in humans, when in 1965, 1966, and 1967 three groups of investigators isolated or passaged viruses isolated from human adults with common cold (14, 21, 29, 30). Electron microscopy studies revealed the similarity of these agents associated with common cold in humans to the infectious bronchitis virus of chickens (5) and mouse hepatitis virus (4). Based on the crown ("corona")-like appearance of the surface projections of the virions visualized by electron microscopy, this group of viruses was then named coronaviruses (4, 28). The four endemic human coronaviruses (229E, NL63, OC43, HKU1) are generally associated with upper (rarely, also lower) respiratory tract disease (31). Since the SARS epidemic of 2002–2003, coronaviruses have gone on to cause other severe respiratory disease in two separate outbreaks in humans. The first of these emerged in June 2012 in an adult patient in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, who died of progressive respiratory and renal failure 11 days after hospital admission for respiratory symptoms (39). A novel coronavirus was subsequently isolated from that patient (39), and was named Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus (MERS-CoV) (10) by the Coronaviridae Study Group (CSG), a working group of the International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses (ICTV) that bears responsibility for the taxonomy and classification of viruses in the family Coronaviridae (13). MERS-CoV is the prototype of the species Middle East respiratory syndrome-related coronavirus (44). Within three years of the appearance of the first MERS patient (thus, by 31 May 2015), 1,180 cases of MERS and 483 deaths had been reported to the World Health Organization (WHO) (45). By the end of 2019, 2,499 MERS cases and 858 deaths had been reported to the WHO since the start of the epidemic, from a total of 27 countries (23). The MERS epidemic remains ongoing. In December 2019, a number of pneumonia cases of unknown cause emerged in Wuhan, Hubei province, People's Republic of China, which exhibited a clinical presentation indicative of viral pneumonia (15). The causative agent was identified as a novel coronavirus that was provisionally named 2019-nCoV (43), which was subsequently allocated as another member of the species Severe acute respiratory syndrome-related coronavirus (19). Based on its close genetic relationship to SARS-CoV (and a large number of "SARS-like" animal coronaviruses isolated primarily from bats), the novel coronavirus was named SARS-CoV-2 by the CSG-ICTV (13). The disease caused by SARS-CoV-2 in humans was named by the WHO as "coronavirus disease 2019," in short, COVID-19 (34). Within three months of the appearance of the first COVID-19 clinical cases in Wuhan, the epidemic rapidly spread to include 143 countries, leading the WHO to declare the COVID-19 situation as a pandemic on 11 March 2020 (7). By 2 April 2020, 896,450 COVID-19 cases and 45,525 deaths had been reported globally (35). MERS and SARS (22), and now also COVID-19 (36), appear on the list of 12 diseases identified by the WHO as priority diseases that are considered to pose the greatest public health risk, either due to their epidemic potential, or where there is (also) insufficient available countermeasures. While closely related to SARS and MERS, COVID-19 exhibits a number of peculiar epidemiological, clinical, and pathogenesis characteristics that remain poorly understood. While SARS-CoV-2 appears to be more easily transmitted than SARS-CoV or MERS-CoV, the fatality rate of COVID-19 (≈2.3%) is lower than that of SARS (≈9.5%) or MERS (≈34.4%) (25). Furthermore, early data suggest that the elderly and those with underlying health conditions, including diabetes mellitus, chronic lung disease, and cardiovascular disease, are at higher risk (8). Thus, the rapidly developing COVID-19 pandemic has underscored the need for accelerated research at several levels, including public health, behavior and education, as well as basic, clinical, and translational science. To address this, the WHO convened a two-day meeting on 11–12 February 2020, the primary (immediate) goal of which was to "accelerate research that can contribute to containing the spread of this epidemic and facilitate that those affected receive optimal care." A secondary (mid-long term) goal was to "support research priorities in a way that leads to the development of global research platforms, aiding preparedness for the next unforeseen epidemic and encouraging accelerated research, development and equitable access, based on public health needs, to diagnostics, therapeutics and vaccines." As a conclusion of that meeting, the WHO published a report in the form of a global research roadmap (33), which highlighted research priorities to respond to the current COVID-19 pandemic. This roadmap highlighted a number of research areas of interest to contributors to our Journal, including studies on SARS-CoV-2 natural history (host species restriction and transmission, environmental stability of viruses, virus compartments of replication, and the duration of shedding). Additionally, studies on clinical aspects of COVID-19 were also recommended (delineation of clinical characteristics of disease; pathophysiology of severe disease; and identifying patient risk groups as well as biomarkers and surrogate markers of infection). Further recommendations included preclinical studies on the development of appropriate animal models, the development of vaccines, studies on the immune modulation of disease, as well as the development of therapeutics. The American Journal of Physiology–Lung Cellular and Molecular Physiology—together with our American Physiological Society sister journals—has already begun contributing scientific reports and thoughtful discussion to these pressing issues. These contributions include reports on virus-host interactions, such as those mediated by angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (1, 2, 16, 27, 32); as well as consideration of elevated plasmin(ogen) as a risk factor for COVID-19 susceptibility. Additionally, how diabetes modulates the host-viral interactions and host-immune responses in COVID-19 and other coronavirus infections (24), and related renal injury and COVID-19 (40), has received attention, together with the use of artificial intelligence and machine learning to fight COVID-19 (3). However, to accelerate these efforts, the American Journal of Physiology–Lung Cellular and Molecular Physiology together with our sister journal Physiological Reports is issuing a joint Call for Papers on any aspect of COVID-19 pathophysiology as well as SARS-CoV-2-encoded factors affecting disease progression and outcome (https://journals.physiology.org/calls). This Call particularly encourages the submission of manuscripts on the following themes:The development of in vitro, ex vivo, and in vivo (animal) models of SARS-CoV-2 (and other coronavirus) infection(s). These studies may be submitted to our Journal's Innovative Methodology category of manuscripts.The identification of biomarkers that reveal or allow the monitoring of physiological processes at play during SARS-CoV-2 (and other human coronavirus) infections, either in clinical disease, or in experimental disease models.The identification of pathophysiological processes relevant to viral replication, viral infection; either in clinical disease, or in experimental disease models.The identification of pathophysiological pathways and processes relevant to the onset, maintenance, and progression of disease; either in clinical disease, or in experimental disease models.Studies that explore the impact of sex or gender, as well as young or advanced age on COVID-19 pathophysiology; either in clinical disease, or in experimental disease models.Studies specifically addressing coronavirus-host interactions, including the physiology of virus receptors on host cells, and the nature of the immune response of the host to SARS-CoV-2 and other human coronaviruses.Studies on genetic aspects of SARS-CoV-2 and other coronaviruses that relate to modulating the infectivity and other aspects of virus pathogenicity in in vitro, ex vivo, and in vivo (animal) models.Preclinical studies on the targeting of pathophysiological pathways relevant to onset, maintenance, and progression of disease, to reveal potential candidate novel disease management strategies.Preclinical studies exploring the impact of comorbidities that are modeled in experimental systems—including in vitro, ex vivo, and in vivo (animal) models—on the onset, maintenance, and progression of disease. Such comorbidities may include, but are not limited to, obesity, diabetes, combustible and e-cigarette smoking, and preexisting airways and other lung disease, as well as cardiovascular, renal, and hepatic disease.Clinical reports on unusual and interesting clinical observations in patients with COVID-19 that highlight unique or noteworthy physiological aspects of clinical disease. Manuscripts may be submitted as regular Research Articles or Rapid Reports. Additionally, Reviews, Mini-Reviews, or shorter Perspective articles, together with Case Reports and Letters to the Editor will be considered (Case Reports should be submitted directly to Physiological Reports). All manuscripts will receive expedited handling. Furthermore, all published articles addressing COVID-19 and its etiological agent SARS-CoV-2 are immediately made freely accessible by the American Physiological Society to everybody upon online publication. title: Navigating the artificial intelligence frontier on cataloguing and metadata work in libraries: an interview with Getaneh Alemu
abstract: Getaneh Alemu is an experienced Cataloguing and Metadata Librarian with over two decades of experience in higher education and libraries. He specialises in ensuring that metadata is accurate, consistent, usable and standardised. His expertise covers several key metadata standards and tools, including MARC21, MarcEdit, Dublin Core, AACR2, RDA, LCSH, DDC, Alma and Primo. These standards aim to maximise the visibility, discoverability, accessibility and utilisation of library resources.Getaneh has an impressive academic background that includes a PhD in Metadata for Digital Libraries from the University of Portsmouth, earned in 2014. He also holds an MA in Digital Library Learning from Oslo University College, Parma University and Tallinn University, obtained in 2009. Additionally, he earned an MA in Knowledge and Information Management from Ghent University in 2005 and a BA in Library and Information Science from Addis Ababa University in 2001.His research on metadata is well-documented through key publications such as “Metadata Standards and Models” (2024), “The Future of Enriched, Linked, Open and Filtered Metadata” (2022) and “An Emergent Theory of Digital Library Metadata: Enrich then Filter” (2015).Artificial intelligence (AI) is poised to automate repetitive, data-intensive and pattern-recognition tasks, thereby freeing human cataloguers for more complex work. What impact will this have?We interviewed Getaneh Alemu because his current work demonstrates a proactive engagement with AI in cataloguing. He is actively involved in exploring, testing and evaluating various AI tools. This exploration extends to discussions with colleagues to understand AI’s practical applications in metadata creation, enrichment and the enhancement of library catalogues and discovery systems.Q1.How does Artificial Intelligence currently impact your work as a cataloguer?Currently, the impact of AI on my cataloguing work is mainly in the exploratory phase. I am actively exploring, testing and evaluating various tools, including the new AI Metadata Assistant from Ex Libris, as well as Copilot, ChatGPT and Gemini. Additionally, I am engaged in ongoing discussions with colleagues in the library to gain a better understanding of the practical applications of these technologies in metadata creation and enrichment, as well as in improving the library catalogue and discovery.We are entering an exciting phase and we must engage as active participants rather than as complainers or passive observers. It’s important to remember that AI is not an external force intruding upon our lives; rather, it is a human innovation that we must use wisely, ethically and responsibly. AI is no longer a distant concept, relegated to the realm of science fiction; it is a reality. The emergence of large language models like ChatGPT and Copilot has made AI increasingly relevant to our work, transforming it from an abstract idea into a practical tool for organising and managing bibliographic data. This process is ongoing and requires continuous learning, critical reflection and experimentation, but is happening at a fast pace.I stay informed about the latest developments in Artificial Intelligence by reading authoritative sources, including “New Horizons in Artificial Intelligence in Libraries” (Balnaves et al., 2025), as well as peer-reviewed journal articles and professional discussions on platforms like LinkedIn. In my workplace, a dedicated team of information librarians regularly updates us on new AI tools and innovations. In this regard, my university shows significant proactivity and remains at the forefront of technological advancement. The university has provided a concise online training module covering the fundamental principles of artificial intelligence, which I have successfully completed.Currently, the impact of AI on my professional responsibilities is limited but overall positive. Although its use is not yet widespread, I am involved in a small-scale experimental project that explores the use of AI-generated metadata for subject headings. We plan to provide further updates as this project progresses.Q2. What are some examples of successful AI implementations in metadata management and cataloguing?We’re observing some promising developments, although they are still in the experimental stages. I utilise the Copilot and Gemini AI tools to check Dewey Decimal numbers and to suggest appropriate subject headings. Ex Libris has introduced an AI assistant called “Metadata Enrichment using AI,” which aids in the ongoing enhancement of bibliographic records. It’s essential to note that Ex Libris emphasises the need for human cataloguers to validate the outputs generated by AI to ensure accuracy and trustworthiness.I tested the AI Assistant with both new and existing records to evaluate its capability to create MARC 21 bibliographic records from minimal input. The tool can handle basic bibliographic elements (such as title and author) or visual sources (like a book cover or an image of the table of contents) and generates a draft record that is sent to the Metadata Editor (MDE).For this test, I supplied an image sourced from a publisher’s website, providing the main title, author and year but deliberately omitting the subtitle. The AI inferred and correctly populated the title along with the subtitle, inserted the correct MARC21 245 field, auto-assigned some basic (generic) subject headings (in the 650 LCSH field) and generated a summary note (520). It also embedded provenance metadata via a note indicating: “Part of the metadata in this record was created with the help of the AI Metadata Assistant.” However, some essential metadata elements were missing such as physical description (300), classification numbers (082 / 050), standard identifier and richer (granular) subject access. ISBD punctuation (e.g. colons, commas) and subfield spacing in 245 and elsewhere were also inconsistent. While effective for generating core descriptive metadata, the Assistant requires cataloguer input to ensure full bibliographic control, structural accuracy and standards compliance.AI has significant potential to improve metadata and cataloguing. While it offers powerful capabilities, integrating AI with existing standards and tools requires effort. AI can enhance metadata, providing users with more intuitive access to information through linked subject systems. Additionally, it can address historical biases in classification systems and improve data quality by conducting consistency checks and detecting anomalies in bibliographic records.Q3.What are your thoughts on the risks and ethical considerations of using AI in metadata and cataloguing?AI-augmented metadata must adhere to established ethical principles by prioritising user-centred access and non-discrimination, reflecting IFLA’s emphasis on “user convenience.” This requires actively addressing the inherent biases present in both AI algorithms and the socio-cultural biases that are built into historical metadata standards. As noted by Gartner (2016) and Bowker and Star (1999), metadata is never completely neutral; every standard and category reflects a particular viewpoint while silencing others. This can result in historical classification schemes that represent colonial perspectives or lack appropriate terminology for diverse cultural expressions.To combat these entrenched biases, it is essential to continuously and critically examine, diversify and decolonise metadata practices to ensure inclusivity and equitable representation.Thus, transparency and accountability in the metadata decisions made by AI are crucial. It is important to highlight the vital role of human oversight and the need for collaborative efforts among all metadata professionals to ensure ethical and responsible information practices.Q4.To what extent can AI automate cataloguing tasks and what tasks are best suited for automation?AI holds significant potential to automate various cataloguing tasks, thereby increasing efficiency and freeing up human cataloguers for more complex, nuanced work. The tasks best suited for automation generally involve repetitive, data-intensive, or pattern-recognition processes.One key area is data remediation and normalisation. AI can effectively identify and rectify common errors or inconsistencies present in legacy metadata records, particularly useful for older data, such as pre-RDA records created under AACR2, which often contain numerous abbreviations and display inconsistencies that can be automatically corrected. Similarly, AI excels at format conversion, efficiently transforming metadata from one standard to another, for instance, from MARC21 to BIBFRAME, XML, or compatible formats for archival metadata.AI can also significantly enhance record enrichment and cross-linking. It can automatically augment bibliographic records by adding granular details and establishing crucial connections. This involves incorporating URIs from authoritative sources such as Wikidata, LCNAF and VIAF, thereby ensuring accurate and unique identification of entities like authors, editors, agencies and events, which is vital for achieving full Linked Data compliance. Furthermore, given the exponential growth of e-book, database and e-journal collections, AI is invaluable for identifying defunct links by scanning e-resource records to flag broken or outdated URLs, proactively resolving access issues and ensuring consistent full-text access for users.Other highly suitable tasks for automation include bulk updates and imports, allowing for large-scale changes on bibliographic records or efficient ingestion of new records. AI can also assist in comparing bibliographic record sets, automatically finding common or differing records, similar to an Excel VLOOKUP function. For the initial stages of cataloguing, AI can be instrumental in automatic record generation, creating preliminary bibliographic records directly from full-text books and documents, which human cataloguers can then review.Beyond structured data, AI’s capabilities extend to deciphering illegible texts, extracting information from old handwritten archival materials. It can also assist with intellectual analysis by suggesting relevant subject headings based on content analysis. Finally, AI can ensure records adhere to specific presentation standards like ISBD through automated formatting and indentation and provide initial translations of metadata from one language to another, requiring subsequent human review for accuracy and nuance.Q5. How can AI enhance the discoverability and accessibility of library resources?When integrated with existing standards, systems and practices, AI enhances bibliographic records, improving discoverability and accessibility. It strengthens the core functions of metadata as defined by standards like FRBR, IFLA LRM and RDA. These standards are designed to help users find information, identify relevant resources, select appropriate materials, gain access and explore related content (Riva, Le Boeuf and Žumer, 2017). By harnessing enriched, linked, enhanced and open metadata, AI amplifies these capabilities. It achieves this through automating processes such as content indexing, metadata creation, labelling and summarisation, which makes resources more accessible across various disciplines and contexts. AI also improves information retrieval and analysis, allowing users to find and analyse relevant information within large and complex data sources more effectively. This facilitates better access to extensive collections of data through advanced techniques like intelligent grouping and filtering.Ultimately, AI enables large-scale global access through automated classification, organisation and retrieval. It also offers multi-dimensional subject access through innovations like topic modelling and AI assistants, fostering a richer, interconnected and more equitable learning environment for users.Q6.How can libraries ensure data quality and accuracy when using AI for cataloguing?Ensuring data quality and accuracy is crucial. AI models rely on exceptionally large data sources to learn patterns, highlighting the importance of providing high-quality input data. Discussions about algorithmic bias, as well as the need for transparency and explainability in machine learning, are highly relevant; AI requires accurate provenance metadata. Consequently, librarians must verify metadata for accuracy and consistency. To achieve this, specific targets should be set, quality metrics established and human oversight implemented to maintain the accuracy and consistency of AI-generated metadata.Q7. Can technology replace the cataloguer? Why or why not?My answer is no, and here is why. Technology and innovation are not threats to librarianship but rather indispensable allies in its ongoing evolution. As a profession, we stand on the shoulders of visionary librarians such as Panizzi, Ranganathan, Dewey, Cutter, Garfield, Avram, Otlet and many others, each of whom embraced innovation and the tools of their time to reimagine new ways of thinking, working and information organisation. Their work exemplifies the dynamic and adaptive spirit at the heart of librarianship.Today, with the advent of AI, we are charting a new horizon, one marked not by displacement but by transformation. I am unequivocally in favour of AI, not as a replacement for human expertise but as a catalyst for efficiency, enrichment and improved discovery. We, like our predecessors, must embrace adaptation, readily adjusting our approaches with ethical discernment and unwavering professional integrity. In doing so, we perpetuate librarianship’s legacy as a field that is both profoundly humanistic and dynamically responsive to technological advancements.The future of metadata creation is evolving, blending human expertise with the computational efficiency of AI, as discussed in “New Horizons in Artificial Intelligence in Libraries” (Balnaves et al., 2025). This integration fosters richer and more inclusive metadata ecosystems. In this model, metadata creators, users and AI will collaborate closely. The hybrid approach of co-creating metadata is essential, as human judgement is crucial for maintaining trust and accuracy in light of the limitations of AI, such as bias and factual errors. Instead of viewing technology as a replacement for cataloguers, we should embrace a future where human insight and machine capabilities work together to enhance bibliographic metadata.Q8.What skills will be essential for cataloguers in an AI-driven environment?We must continually explore, learn and better understand AI, actively engaging with it rather than remaining on the sidelines. Being proactive and hands-on involves mastering prompt engineering, delving into the logic behind algorithms and fostering a richer, more engaging research and learning environment. Therefore, essential skills for cataloguers in an AI-driven environment will undoubtedly include comprehensive AI literacy, encompassing prompt engineering and a foundational grasp of AI principles. Deep subject analysis and cataloguing skills will remain paramount, enabling cataloguers to strategically cede repetitive tasks to AI. Furthermore, a strong knowledge of the ethical considerations surrounding AI, coupled with developed technical skills in digital and algorithmic literacy and competencies in developing and applying various AI approaches, will be crucial.Q9.What training or resources should be provided to cataloguers to prepare them for AI integration?To effectively prepare librarians and cataloguers for AI integration, training, development and resources are essential. This includes providing opportunities for direct experimentation with AI tools, such as chatbots, to build hands-on understanding of their capabilities and limitations. Access to open-source toolkits with guides and examples for recommender systems should be made available for those keen to explore coding applications. Furthermore, robust educational resources, like online courses covering AI basics and ethical implications, alongside current research reports on AI’s impact on information professions, are vital. Finally, encouraging and supporting proof-of-concept projects will allow cataloguers to develop crucial technical and business skills in a practical, real-world context. I believe we can all come together to teach one another, continuously experiment and improve our processes. We can achieve this through seminars, conferences, magazines, articles and books.Q10.What role does human oversight and intervention play in AI-assisted cataloguing?Human oversight and intervention are crucial, especially in AI-assisted cataloguing. This situation is reminiscent of the outdated belief that paperless offices would render libraries obsolete. Such hype often overlooks the importance of traditional institutions. Just as physical libraries, archives and museums remain vital despite decades of technological advancements, human involvement will continue to be central in the age of AI.In this era, cataloguers play an essential role in subject analysis and metadata creation. They interpret the content, context and purpose of resources, selecting appropriate subject headings while upholding the principles of Equity, Diversity and Inclusion (EDI). While AI can assist with tasks like keyword extraction, the nuanced process of subject analysis demands human judgement, cultural sensitivity and an understanding of complex standards such as Resource Description and Access (RDA) and IFLA’s Library Reference Model (LRM).Cataloguers are adept at distinguishing between different works and editions, often requiring professional judgement and background knowledge. Although AI can enhance efficiency, it lacks the critical thinking and ethical awareness that skilled cataloguers possess.Q11.How might AI change the future of metadata standards and practices?Efforts are being made to transition from outdated data formats such as MARC and AACR2 to modern standards like BIBFRAME and RDA. Similarly, we must envision and adapt our metadata standards and practices to keep pace with advancements in AI.AI’s influence on metadata is significant, as it will both utilise existing metadata and drive the creation of new standards. Metadata will be essential for establishing trust and authenticity in AI-generated content, ensuring provenance and integrity.Our standards will facilitate interoperability, fostering Linked Data environments, while also guiding ethical AI practices by incorporating usage rights and privacy considerations. As cataloguers, we must strategically integrate AI, recognising its potential for efficiency alongside the necessity for human oversight to address current imperfections like inaccurate data. This moment reflects a “paradigm shift” in how we approach metadata in light of AI’s capabilities.

title: Telemedicine and e-Health Solutions for COVID-19: Patients' Perspective
abstract: Telemedicine and e-HealthVol. 26, No. 7 OpinionFree AccessTelemedicine and e-Health Solutions for COVID-19: Patients' PerspectiveNina Pappot, Gry Assam Taarnhøj, and Helle PappotNina PappotFaculty of Health and Rigshospitalet, University of Copenhagen, Copenhagen, Denmark.Search for more papers by this author, Gry Assam TaarnhøjDepartment of Oncology, Rigshospitalet, University of Copenhagen, Copenhagen, Denmark.Search for more papers by this author, and Helle PappotAddress correspondence to: Helle Pappot, MD, DMSc, Department of Oncology 5073, Rigshospitalet, Blegdamsvej 9, 2100 Copenhagen, Denmark E-mail Address: [email protected]Department of Oncology, Rigshospitalet, University of Copenhagen, Copenhagen, Denmark.Institute for Clinical Medicine, Faculty of Health, Copenhagen, Denmark.Search for more papers by this authorPublished Online:8 Jul 2020https://doi.org/10.1089/tmj.2020.0099AboutSectionsPDF/EPUB Permissions & CitationsPermissionsDownload CitationsTrack CitationsAdd to favorites Back To Publication ShareShare onFacebookXLinked InRedditEmail Like Telemedicine and eHealth, we think that "telemedicine and e-health alternatives can aid in controlling international pandemics."1 We comment on the possible psychological and sociological consequences of the pandemic itself and the solution hereof by telemedicine. One of the first publications on the role of telemedicine for COVID-19, published as a commentary in the New England Journal of Medicine and entitled "Virtually Perfect? Telemedicine for COVID-19," sparsely deals with this aspect.2 The authors focus on the important benefits of telemedicine for the health systems with respect to handling COVID-19 but leave out the patients' perspective. Similarly, Ting et al. have high expectations of digital technologies in their comment in Nature Medicine on March 27, 2020, with a focus especially on monitoring, surveillance, and detection and the potential for machine learning and artificial intelligence.3We agree that telemedicine has the potential to solve many issues in this situation, but to our knowledge, its potential has not yet described and taken into consideration from patients' perspective and nor are the possible great benefits of telemedicine well known. As seen from early data from China,4 many individuals will experience isolation during hospitalization or when quarantining at home. Research has described the many adverse effects of isolation in hospitalized patients,5 in particular anxiety and depression.6 Simple e-health tools may give severely ill COVID-19 patients the possibility of having peer-to-peer communication and easily obtaining relevant health information, probably leading to maintained quality of life and better mental health. We and other researchers within the e-health field have demonstrated the importance of e-health in avoiding feeling lonely and improving or maintaining quality of life during other severe illnesses,7 and this impact may also be of importance for patients and relatives dealing with COVID-19.The aim of this viewpoint is to draw attention to the ongoing importance of patient involvement in healthcare on an individual and organizational level when it comes to urgent e-health solutions for COVID-19. In this commentary, we show a group of e-health providers' perception of their tool's functionality according to e-health solutions for COVID-19, and comment on the solutions' possible use in the context of patient involvement.When searching the internet (using Google®) by using search terms such as "e-health solutions for COVID-19 and patient involvement," very sparse information can be found, and at present, it is not possible to perform literature searches due to very limited published results. However, a "hub" of e-health providers has undertaken the task of providing a global overview of the e-health solutions available for COVID-19.8 Solution providers, consultants advising the healthcare system, and healthcare professionals have been prompted on the internet to contribute with solutions for COVID-19. It has been the hub's aim that all the solutions should be made available across institutions, geographies, and countries. With the hub's permission, we present an overview of the assembled solutions, their functionality, and their distribution by country. Each of the solutions included has been validated by a steering group at the hub according to ease of implementation, COVID-19 impact, post-COVID-19 impact, dependency on external bottlenecks, and localization. The authors have reviewed the solutions with respect to their use for patient involvement during COVID-19.Thirty-eight (n = 38) different providers had their solution included in the hub's overview. In Table 1, eight different functionalities of the included solutions are displayed. Most solutions were Danish, as the hub was situated in Denmark, but in total, there were contributions from 12 different countries. Most solutions were on screening and triage (11/38) and remote patient monitoring (9/38). The hub has added a disclaimer that "it is a preliminary, living, non-exhaustive list compiled with high efforts within a short time frame." By reviewing the solutions, the authors have assessed, that with the exception of solutions for one functionality (supply storage), all solutions have the potential to involve patients. This can be either as individual patient involvement using e-health tools to secure better communication between patients and hospital staff, or as organizational patient involvement using patients' viewpoints to obtain e-health solutions, which integrates the healthcare systems needs and patients' needs, ensuring an improved outcome.Table 1. We screened an e-health hub's list of possible functionalities for e-health tools during COVID-19 and found that for all but one (1/8) of the functionalities, patient involvement may be an element to improve the meaningfulness of the tool, to secure compliance and adherence, but most of all to integrate needs.We suggest and encourage healthcare systems that have the necessary technology to implement telemedicine or to go into cooperation with e-health providers, who have already developed accessible technologies, to be able to offer telemedicine to patients and their relatives. It is of importance that official public-health organizations take on this task, and Hernandez-Garcia et al.9 recently described the difference in information concerning the prevention of COVID-19, when found on websites from official public-health organizations versus digital media, in favor of official public-health organizations. This difference may also count for e-health solutions with patient involvement. Apart from all the logistic improvements and technological advantages, the implementation of e-health for COVID-19 will enable isolated individuals to receive timely information and to maintain a sense of social belonging. When this crisis is over, we must also remember to consider the social, organizational, and technological factors impacting both patients' and clinicians' adoption of mobile health tools, as Jacobs et al. has described for m-health in general,10 and patient involvement might be further needed to suggest usable and meaningful solutions. There is no time for hesitation. It is crucial to employ every possible tool to avoid feelings of loneliness, stress, and anxiety, which may even worsen physical symptoms.
