Replication Data for: Trust in AI Accuracy and Perceived Threat: Drivers of AI-Related Learning
abstract: # Replication Materials ## Trust in AI Accuracy and Perceived Threat: Drivers of AI-Related Learning This repository contains the analysis output files for the paper submitted to *Information and Software Technology* (Special Issue: Human Factor in Generative AI). The analysis uses data from the 2025 Stack Overflow Developer Survey (N = 49,191; analytic sample N = 32,611). --- ## Data Availability The raw survey data are publicly available from Stack Overflow: https://survey.stackoverflow.co/2025 The raw data file is **not included** in this repository due to the Stack Overflow survey data license. To reproduce the analytic sample, download the 2025 survey data and apply the variable selection and filtering steps described in Sections 3.1--3.3 of the manuscript. The file `2025_selected_cols_header.csv` documents which columns were retained. --- ## File Descriptions ### Analytic Sample and Variable Documentation **`2025_analysis_ready_variables.csv`** The fully prepared analytic dataset used in all main models. Contains recoded and filtered variables for the routed subsample (N = 32,611) with non-missing values on AIAcc, AIThreat, and all control variables. This is the direct input to the logistic regression models reported in the paper. **`2025_selected_cols_header.csv`** Column names and variable labels for the subset of 2025 survey items retained for analysis. Provides a reference for mapping original Stack Overflow variable names to the constructs used in the paper. **`2025_variable_summary.csv`** Summary of all variables used in the study, including their role (outcome, focal predictor, control), measurement type, and years of availability. Corresponds to Tables 2--4 in the manuscript. **`2025_keyvars_distribution.csv`** Frequency distributions and descriptive statistics for the key variables (AIAcc, AIThreat, LearnCodeAI) across the full 2025 sample and the analytic subsample. Useful for verifying that the subsample is representative of the routed group. **`main_logit_sample_stats.csv`** Descriptive statistics for the analytic sample (N = 32,611). Reproduces Table 5 in the manuscript, including outcome prevalence, predictor means, and control variable distributions. --- ### Main Model Results **`main_logit_results.csv`** Full output from the primary binary logistic regression model predicting AI-related learning (LearnCodeAI). Contains regression coefficients, standard errors, Wald z-statistics, p-values, odds ratios, and 95% confidence intervals for all predictors. Reproduces Table 6 in the manuscript. **`main_logit_table_ready.csv`** Formatted version of the main logit output prepared for table display. Values are rounded to match Table 6 as published. Useful for verifying that rounding and formatting decisions in the manuscript are consistent with the underlying estimates. **`focal_trust_threat.csv`** Extracted results for the two focal predictors only: trust in AI accuracy (AIAcc) and perceived professional threat (AIThreat). Reproduces Table 7 in the manuscript. Odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals are included. **`ai_learning_model_terms.csv`** Model term definitions and dummy-coding structure for all categorical predictors (Age, EdLevel, Employment, MainBranch). Documents reference categories and indicator variable construction as described in Section 3.4.3 of the manuscript. --- ### Interaction and Subgroup Analyses **`age_interaction_results.csv`** Output from the interaction model testing whether age moderates the trust--learning association (Equation 5 in the manuscript). Contains coefficients and confidence intervals for main effects and Trust × Age interaction terms. **`age_interaction_stats.csv`** Model fit statistics for the age interaction model, including likelihood-ratio test results comparing the interaction model to the baseline specification. Supports the conclusion reported in Section 4.3 that interaction terms were not statistically significant. **`interaction_EdLevel.csv`** Output from the exploratory interaction model for education level. Contains Trust × EdLevel interaction terms and the likelihood-ratio test statistic for the interaction block (p = .1598 as reported in Section 4.4). **`interaction_models_summary.csv`** Combined summary of all exploratory subgroup interaction models (age, education, employment, main branch). Reproduces Table 8 in the manuscript, including block-level likelihood-ratio test results for each moderator. **`predicted_probabilities_4panels.csv`** Predicted probabilities of AI-related learning across trust levels, computed separately for each age group. Used to generate Figure 3 (four-panel plot) in the manuscript. Each row corresponds to one trust level and age group combination. --- ### Robustness Checks **`robustness_summary.csv`** Results from all eight robustness specifications listed in Section 3.5.3. For each specification, the file contains the analytic sample size, McFadden's pseudo-R², odds ratios for trust and threat, and corresponding p-values. Reproduces Table 9 in the manuscript. **`replication_2024_trust_threat.csv`** Results from the partial stability check using the 2024 Stack Overflow Developer Survey (N = 14,870). The outcome variable in this file is AIToolCurrentlyUsing, which differs from LearnCodeAI used in the main analysis. Values are not directly comparable across years and should be interpreted as a descriptive consistency check only, as noted in Section 3.5.3 of the manuscript. --- ## Notes on Reproducibility All analyses were conducted in Python. The main model uses complete-case estimation. Sensitivity analyses with multiple imputation (m = 5) for control variables with missingness above 2% are described in Section 3.4.4 and their results are included in `robustness_summary.csv`. For questions about the analysis files, contact the corresponding author.

title: GLI ATTEGGIAMENTI DEI FUTURI INSEGNANTI VERSO L’IA GENERATIVA: OPPORTUNITÀ, RISCHI E BISOGNI FORMATIVI
abstract: Il contributo indaga gli atteggiamenti e le intenzioni d’uso dei trasformatori generativi di testo tra i futuri insegnanti impegnati nel percorso abilitante iniziale, in Friuli Venezia Giulia, nell’anno accademico 2024/2025. In un contesto in cui questa tecnologia innovativa è di fatto disponibile e già utilizzata dagli studenti, con conseguenze notevoli sulle pratiche di scrittura e di valutazione, lo studio indaga quali siano i fattori e le percezioni legati all’adozione da parte dei docenti e quali possano essere le ricadute sul loro processo di formazione iniziale e continua. Lo strumento adottato è un questionario per la raccolta di dati quantitativi e qualitativi, fondato su un adattamento del Technology Acceptance Model e orientato alla stima dell’utilità e della semplicità d’uso percepite della nuova tecnologia, del grado di fiducia rispetto ai rischi e limiti e di alcuni altri fattori. La struttura mista del campione consente un confronto tra gli atteggiamenti dei futuri insegnanti dell’area umanistica e tecnica scientifica, mentre la presenza di qualche domanda aperta offre spazio a osservazioni di carattere qualitativo. I risultati mostrano un orientamento favorevole verso un impiego dei trasformatori generativi a scuola, anche per compiti linguistici complessi e che richiedono una consapevolezza sul piano semantico, come la semplificazione e il riassunto. Coesistono però preoccupazioni rispetto ai limiti e ai potenziali rischi, per la privacy dei dati ma soprattutto verso l’attendibilità delle informazioni generate, ed è anche alla luce di queste perplessità che emerge un bisogno di formazione specifica sul tema. Si conclude sostenendo l’esigenza di percorsi formativi, iniziali o successivi, che promuovano un’alfabetizzazione e consapevolezza critica nei confronti dell’Intelligenza Artificiale, in considerazione anche delle implicazioni e ricadute sulle future coorti di studenti. The attitudes of future teachers towards generative AI: some educational implications This paper investigates attitudes towards, and intentions to use, generative transformers among pre-service teachers enrolled in their initial teacher education program in Friuli Venezia Giulia, in the 2024/2025 academic year. In a context in which this innovative technology is available and already in use by students, with significant consequences for writing practices and assessment, the study examines the factors and perceptions associated with teachers’ adoption and the potential implications for their initial and in-service professional development. The instrument employed is a questionnaire for the collection of both quantitative and qualitative data, based on an adaptation of the Technology Acceptance Model and aimed at revealing the perceived usefulness and the perceived ease of use of the new technology, the level of trust with respect to risks and limitations, and a number of other related factors. The mixed structure of the sample also allows a comparison between the attitudes of pre-service teachers in the humanities and those in the technical scientific field, while the inclusion of a number of open-ended questions provides space for some qualitative observations. The findings show a favourable orientation towards the use of generative transformers in schools, including for complex language-related tasks requiring semantic awareness, such as text simplification and summarisation. However, concerns regarding limitations and potential risks also coexist, in relation to data privacy but above all for the reliability of the generated information. In light of these observations, a consistent need for specific training emerges, and the paper subsequently concludes by arguing for initial and/or in-service training, oriented to fostering a critical literacy and awareness, also in view of the implications and repercussions for future cohorts of students.

title: Fab26 – Reimagine the Future. Fab26 Research Papers Stream
abstract: FAB26 marked the 25th anniversary of the Fab Lab phenomenon, its network and movement. The conference was as much looking back at that legacy as looking forward to the next 25 years. The fifteen papers in this year's research stream stand at that watershed, building on the past and for the future. The papers fall into three clusters, presented across three sessions: Teaching & Learning, Making with Communities, and Sustaining and Scaling. Teaching & Learning: From First Stitch to Education 5.0 — pedagogy, tools, and AI across the learner's journey — opens with a small piece of hardware: Leirado et al. develop sew:bit, an open-source expansion board that makes the BBC micro:bit work for e-textiles much as the LilyPad once did for Arduino. LaPrade proposes The Armature, a community-first framework carrying middle-school makers at a Title I school in Cleveland toward a professional CAD credential. Yalçın reports seven years of a K-12 FabLab in Istanbul in which students become co-authors of peer-reviewed HCI research. Llàcer Caro and Muñoz Zanón ask what critical thinking means once generative AI is ubiquitous, and offer a toolkit built on deliberate friction. Hernández-Montoya and Miranda close the session with an AI-mediated model joining remote, physical, and mobile Fab Labs at a Costa Rican distance university. Making with Communities: From Visiting to Becoming Infrastructure — resilience and sustainability transitions on the ground — moves outward. Liu and Liao use a seven-day Fab City Challenge to read Shenzhen's Nantou Ancient City through fabrication. Espinoza Gómez et al. ask honestly what it would take to evaluate an itinerant digital fabrication programme in rural Peru, having first run one without a baseline. de Castro Lacerda and Tenório Ramalho de Abreu describe a participatory method for textile waste with women upcycling decommissioned bus-driver uniforms in Brasília. Regina et al. explore village-scale green hydrogen in coastal Bali through five co-designed interventions, built on the existing governance of the Balinese banjar. Anaya Hernández asks whether maker networks actually hold the data needed to be activated in a disaster, and finds the answer uneven. Sustaining and Scaling: From One Workshop to the Full Stack — governance, stakeholders, and measurement of fab initiatives — turns to what makes any of this last. Stadlmann and Holzinger treat maker workshops for children as multi-stakeholder services and find that stakeholders do not agree on what those services are for. Doyo draws on ten years of a Japanese university FabLab to argue that openness is a three-layer achievement of place, governance, and participatory mediation. León Lucano proposes Fab Lab venture studios as a university investment framework for Peru. Freundt et al. report a national faculty-development programme reaching 27 public technical institutes. Vivanco closes with the Fab City Full Stack Metrics Framework, an attempt to make local activity measurable without severing it from the systems it sits in. Twenty-nine papers were submitted to this year's stream. The stream's policy is double-blind peer review, with each paper receiving at least two reviews; on that basis fourteen were accepted and one was rerouted as a preprint. Their thirty-one authors work in twenty-two institutions across thirteen countries. Each paper is deposited separately and carries its own DOI, listed in the contents that follow; this volume gathers their abstracts and is the citable record of the stream as a whole. The research papers stream has run since Fab8 in Wellington in 2012, a history set out in Troxler, Fab Lab Research Papers. From Experiment to Expression (10.5281/zenodo.1344101); the most recent volume was Fab25 Czechia – Bridge the Gap (10.5281/zenodo.16789442). The editors thank the reviewers, who each carried six to eight papers: Serena Cangiano, Pablo C. Herrera, Jan Peuckert, Ivan Sanchez Milara, Alessandra Schmidt, Jessica Stanley, Sarina Till, and Liz Whitewolf.

title: The cardiovascular professional of tomorrow: redefining basic research in the age of artificial intelligence
abstract: Cinzia Perrino is a professor of cardiology at Federico II University in Naples, Italy. Her research focuses on cardiac hypertrophy, heart failure, ischaemia–reperfusion injury, and gut–heart interactions. At the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) Spring Summit and Cardiovascular Round Table 2025 in Paris, she described how artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the landscape of biomedical science and what this means for cardiologists of the future (Figure 1). Cinzia Perrino, professor of cardiology at Federico II University in Naples, Italy Can you describe the current landscape and how AI might impact basic science in cardiology? Basic science in cardiology is going through a difficult time: we are witnessing a divide between expertise and the career paths of those working in clinical and basic research. One of the underlying reasons is the lack of interdisciplinary education, and this has been recognised as an area for improvement by the European Society of Cardiology (ESC). Although in theory AI has the potential to bridge this gap, it also carries the risk of widening it in practice. AI can increasingly surpass humans in numerous tasks. As it is evolving rapidly, what we are talking about today may no longer hold true in a year or so. AI has captured much attention in the public media fuelling high expectations from patients, doctors, and governments alike. The 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded to a team that used AI to crack the long-standing problem of protein structure which scientists had been studying for 50 years. Although AI solved the problem in two years, the reality is more nuanced when we consider that AI analysed existing data to generate new information. What does AI have to offer the cardiologist of tomorrow? AI in basic research can unite different entities to achieve precision healthcare, but there are some caveats. Firstly, basic research is changing. In 2017, we highlighted in an ESC Statement the differences between a hypothesis-driven research approach—where we focus on a specific pathway and follow it—and an unbiased big data-based approach. When I first joined a basic science lab as a medical student 29 years ago, we focused on single dots on a single plane, and now I am leading a registry study in Italy getting samples from patients with peripartum cardiomyopathy. We’re doing multiomics integration, and AI algorithms. Science is changing, and we need to keep pace. What are some of the notable innovations AI has introduced? If you look at different stages of basic science, we have applications for every single step: AI can be a tool to generate new scientific hypotheses. We have semi-autonomous self-driving laboratories, and we can replace humans with generative AI digital twins. The most striking innovation from Japan is an ‘AI scientist’ that can do everything. It generates hypotheses, applies for grants, does the research, analyses the data, drafts the paper, and even does peer review. It’s been hypothesised that by 2050 an AI scientist will be able to win a Nobel Prize with a groundbreaking discovery. Our current scientific knowledge represents just a small fraction of what’s discoverable, and although human researchers can expand knowledge to a certain extent, AI has the potential to reach into vast, undefined territories that we can’t even map. Will we be replaced by AI? There was a commentary published in a journal about radiologists, but which also applies to basic scientists saying: ‘AI won’t replace basic science, but it will replace basic scientists who don’t use it.’ We do know that integrating human expertise with AI capabilities can significantly improve scientific outcomes which become faster and more precise, and this is the winning strategy. We cannot ignore AI anymore; it has to be part of our life, but only scientists can frame research questions to ensure that AI explores meaningful biological problems. Because most AI systems use existing data, we need to identify knowledge gaps and generate high quality big data with accuracy, standardisation, and diversity to bridge those gaps. We also need to design experiments that AI cannot fully automate and design. What are some of the things AI cannot do? Although AI excels at pattern recognition, only human scientists can uncover the mechanisms, and in this context it’s useful to think of AI as a medical device. Human scientists need to validate results with real world experiments to avoid false discoveries, ensuring predictability and clinical translation. We also need to consider regulatory approval, preserve ethics and scientific integrity. We need to fine-tune AI because it is only as good as the data and the algorithms it’s trained on. We are in charge of the models, and AI cannot do everything. There are also a lot of biases related to the utilisation of AI: as basic scientists our job is to understand what they are and how to control them. How can we get a grip on this technology? The ESC is already moving towards appropriate training to keep professionals on top of things in an AI-driven landscape. We should start incorporating AI literacy into curricula to understand the capabilities and limitations for teaching. We don’t need to be developers; we can be consumers or translators or whatever we choose. Core curricula are starting to come out now and this is leading to a change in medical schools and education. For example, in Italy, we have 15 medical technology university schools, with Federico II University students starting cardiology education and training this year after an early focus on biomedical engineering. How medical doctors become qualified is going to change, and the new generation MDs with combined expertise in biomedical engineering will have tremendous opportunities. What out the main points about AI to keep in mind? AI in basic science is a powerful tool with the potential to unlock scientific discoveries that were previously out of reach, but we need to keep in mind that it does not replace human curiosity, creativity, and analytical judgment. Human-AI synergy, rather than substitution, is the way to go right now. The success of AI does not just depend on developing the technology, but also on whether professionals accept and adopt it, and patients trust it. All authors declare no disclosure of interest for this contribution.

title: Det eksperimenterende fællesskab møder generativ kunstig intelligens (GAI)
abstract: I mødet mellem det eksperimenterende fællesskab som pædagogik og GAI som teknologi på kandidatuddannelsen IT-Didaktisk Design ser det ud til at GAI kan fungere som en del af undersøgelsesprocesser. Dette paper handler om mødet mellem det eksperimenterende fællesskab som pædagogik og GAI på den onlinebaserede kandidatuddannelse IT-Didaktisk Design på DPU, Aarhus Universitet. Udviklingsprojektet startede i efteråret 2024, er i fortsat udvikling og foregår bl.a. i et samarbejde med Center for Hybrid Intelligence, BSS, Aarhus Universitet. Centeret stiller bl.a. en Generativ AI RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) til rådighed som en del af projektet. Undervisningen på IT-Didaktisk design søger at etablere de studerende som et eksperimenterende fællesskab. I dette fællesskab skal de studerende bl.a. lære at designe ny og relevant brug af teknologier. De skal arbejde sammen om eksperimenter og om at etablere en relevant pædagogisk brug af digitale teknologier i de kontekster, som teknologierne placeres i. De digitale teknologier tænkes i ind i det åbne laboratorium, hvor analogt og digitalt, fysisk og online, lokalt og globalt kombineres i aktuelle, hybride formater. Enhver given teknologi skal bringes i en anvendelse, der er vigtig for de studerende og som udvider og ændrer deres læringsprocesser. Det pædagogiske spørgsmål til en given teknologi er ikke kun, hvad den kan, men hvad den kan bringes til at kunne. Teknologierne bringes også sammen med andre teknologier i en medieøkologi, hvor deltagerne eksperimenterer med og bruger teknologierne til de formål, de anser som de vigtigste. Det ser ud til at Generativ kunstig intelligens i et eksperimenterende fællesskab med det åbne laboratorium og medieøkologi som omdrejningspunkt kan anvendes til at undersøge og reflektere i en proces, hvor GAI ikke giver svaret for de studerende, men i langt højere grad fungerer som en del af spørgsmålet. RAG´en kan indeholde tekster, der er relevante for det enkelte modul og ser ud til ud fra de foreløbige undersøgelser at kunne blive en del af en pædagogisk processer, hvor de studerende både forholder sig til teksterne på modulet og andre tekster udenfor modulet. title: CIAW Teaching Infographics: Inclusive Learning, Critical AI Literacy, and Responsible Knowledge Practices
abstract: This collection contains three Open Educational Resources (OER) developed by the Center for the Innovation in Ancient Worlds (CIAW) within the Universitat Autònoma de Barcelona Teaching Innovation Project “Veus oblidades a l’Antiguitat: docència inclusiva i pensament crític en temps d’intel·ligència artificial” (Modalitat A, GI517492), directed by Carlos Heredia Chimeno and Isaías Arrayás Morales. The resources were produced during the development of a broader teaching innovation project concerned with three interconnected questions: the inclusion of historically marginalised actors in Ancient History teaching, neurodiversity-aware educational design, and the critical use of generative Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education. Version and methodological context These infographics document an intermediate stage in the development of the project rather than its final pedagogical framework. They were produced while the teaching model was still being tested and revised through classroom implementation. Subsequent reflection on the 2025–26 teaching experiences led to important modifications of some assumptions represented in these materials. In particular, the later framework moved away from associating particular organisational pathways with specific diagnostic profiles and instead made different learning pathways available to all students without diagnostic assignment. It also distinguished more clearly between critical AI literacy and compulsory personal use of generative AI, recognising that students may analyse documented AI-generated material without being required to interact personally with a generative system. The infographics are therefore retained as open records of one stage in the project’s development. They remain useful for teaching, discussion, adaptation, and reflection, but their diagnostic associations and some aspects of their treatment of direct AI participation should not be interpreted as representing the project’s subsequently revised framework. This evolution is itself part of the project’s methodological contribution: teaching innovation is treated here as an iterative process in which implementation, student response, critical reflection, and subsequent redesign may alter the assumptions embedded in earlier educational resources. 1. Inclusive Learning Itineraries: Flipped Learning and AI for Neurodivergence This infographic represents an early version of the project’s work on alternative learning pathways. It combines flipped learning, structured support, multimodal activities, flexible assessment, and AI-supported teaching within a framework originally designed with particular neurodivergent profiles in mind. It presents two organisational pathways: a more structured and sequential route and a more open, creative, and multimodal route. Both were intended to preserve equivalent academic expectations while allowing students to organise and demonstrate disciplinary learning in different ways. Subsequent classroom implementation led to a significant revision of this approach. The project retained the principle that equivalent disciplinary competence may be demonstrated through different organisational routes, but abandoned the association of particular pathways with diagnostic categories. The later framework instead makes multiple pathways available to all students, regardless of diagnosis, preference, or educational background. The infographic should therefore be read as documentation of the earlier diagnostic-association phase from which the subsequent model developed. 2. Rethinking Ancient History: Inclusion, AI, and Forgotten Voices This infographic explores how Ancient History teaching can incorporate historically marginalised actors, multiple perspectives, neurodiversity-aware design, and critical engagement with Artificial Intelligence. It encourages students and educators to examine how historical narratives privilege some actors and perspectives while rendering others less visible. Generated material can be used to identify assumptions, omissions, stereotypes, anachronisms, and unsupported reconstructions, particularly where incomplete ancient evidence encourages apparently plausible narratives to exceed what can actually be demonstrated. The resource also reflects an earlier phase in which direct student interaction with generative AI occupied a more central position within the teaching design. Subsequent implementation led the project to distinguish more clearly between using AI personally and developing the ability to analyse AI critically. The revised framework therefore allows students to work either with directly generated material or with documented instructor-provided AI outputs while being assessed through the same historical criteria. Although developed through Ancient History teaching, the underlying practices—critical comparison of narratives, evidence-based verification, examination of perspective, and distinction between disciplinary competence and organisational format—can be adapted to other areas of the Humanities and Social Sciences. 3. Source Verification and Academic Harassment in the Era of AI This infographic addresses source verification, academic integrity, evidence-based evaluation, and responsible scholarly communication in contexts involving Artificial Intelligence. It emphasises the importance of distinguishing between technical error, weak scholarly practice, bibliographical inaccuracy, and deliberate academic misconduct. Assertions concerning knowledge, authorship, technological use, or research integrity should be supported by evidence proportionate to the seriousness of the claim. The resource also draws attention to the limitations of relying upon assumptions about writing style, productivity, automated AI-detection results, or personal and academic disagreement when evaluating possible inappropriate AI use. It promotes transparent scholarly practice, source verification, documented reasoning, and fair institutional procedures. Within the subsequent development of the wider project, these concerns were more narrowly reformulated around the principle of responsible scholarly judgement: errors, methodological weaknesses, and deliberate misconduct should not be treated as equivalent categories, and conclusions should remain proportionate to the available evidence. Intended uses and transferability These resources may be used in university teaching, curriculum development, staff training, doctoral programmes, seminars, workshops, and discussions concerning teaching innovation, Artificial Intelligence, neurodiversity, historical methodology, source verification, and academic integrity. They may support: curriculum and activity design; discussion of neurodiversity-aware teaching; critical AI-literacy activities; source-verification exercises; multimodal and flexible approaches to assessment; academic-integrity and research-ethics training; interdisciplinary discussion of responsible AI use; reflection on how teaching models evolve through implementation. The resources should be adapted to the disciplinary objectives, evidence base, student population, and institutional context in which they are used. Their broader transferable principle is not the reproduction of a fixed activity, technological tool, or learner typology, but the identification of the disciplinary operation that an activity is intended to teach. Later work arising from the project develops this distinction further by separating disciplinary requirements that should remain common from organisational features that may legitimately vary. Relationship with subsequent publications These OER form part of a broader sequence of outputs produced by the project. They should be read together with subsequent academic publications where the classroom implementations are analysed in greater methodological detail and where several aspects of the original model are revised. In particular, later work develops a framework based on: common disciplinary standards combined with different organisational pathways; pathways available without diagnostic assignment; bounded rather than unlimited choice; critical AI literacy without compulsory personal AI adoption; evidence-bounded historical reconstruction; explicit distinction between evidence, inference, plausibility, and fabrication; assessment based on historical operations rather than surface format. The existence of differences between these earlier OER and the later framework is therefore intentional to preserve the documentary history of the project rather than retrospectively rewriting earlier outputs. Production The infographics were created using Canva Pro and NotebookLM through project-funded licences supporting the production of educational and teaching-innovation materials. This Zenodo deposit contains the three infographic materials only. Theoretical discussion, classroom implementation evidence, methodological revisions, and the subsequently developed teaching framework are presented in the associated academic publications. Recommended citation Center for the Innovation in Ancient Worlds, & Heredia Chimeno, C. (2026). CIAW Teaching Infographics: Inclusive Learning, Critical AI Literacy, and Responsible Knowledge Practices [Open Educational Resources]. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21763472 These materials are preserved as Open Educational Resources documenting the development of the project and may support consultation, teaching, adaptation, critical discussion, and further educational innovation. Appropriate acknowledgement of the original authorship, project context, and related publications should be maintained when the resources are reused or adapted.

title: Letters to the editor: questionable publishing practices in the ChatGPT era
abstract: In line with the Journal’s conflict of interest policy, this paper was handled by Jeroen Hendriks. Letters to the editor in scientific journals express readers’ views, opinions, or concerns related to published work, serving two main purposes: post-publication peer review and sharing experiences with fellow readers.1 Both purposes are important as they contribute to maintaining the high standards of journals.1 Over the past few decades, these letters have been instrumental in stimulating scientific debates. Interestingly, since the mid-1970s, the number of letters to the editor has steadily grown (Central Illustration). In the last decade, PubMed indexed approximately 50 000 letters annually, with peaks up to 64 000 in 2020 and 2021, which can be attributed to the ‘covidization’ of publications.2,3 While this rise in letters to the editor could be seen as a positive contribution to intellectual and scientific discussions, it also raises questions about potential underlying dynamics. The grey bar in 2023 represents the extrapolation of the currently published Letters to the editor towards the entire year. One possible explanation for this growth in letters to the editor is the pressure on medical students to achieve a publication with a PubMed ID. Indeed, academic or advanced training programmes often require applicants to have authored a PubMed indexed publication.4 A quantitative analysis of letters to the editor in 15 medical education journals revealed that about half of the letters were authored by medical students.4 Moreover, there was a temporal increase in letters published by students; and five schools were responsible for 60% of the letters written by medical students.4 It is evident that these letters primarily aim to enhance the CVs of individual students and improve their academic opportunities, rather than advancing science. Therefore, academic and training foundation programmes should re-evaluate the use of a mere PubMed ID as an evaluation criterion. Another driver to submit letters to the editor for some authors is their aspiration to achieve numerous publications within a brief timeframe. For instance, we are aware of an author who had their first publication indexed in Web of Science in July 2022. Since then, 79 articles have been recorded in Web of Science, all of which are letters to the editor or correspondence (data cut: 27 July 2023). An associated author has 2926 papers indexed in Web of Science, 80% of which are registered as letters. Even the papers registered as ‘article’ in Web of Science are likely to be correspondence since they generally consist of two to three pages long (data on file). The plethora of letters published by such ‘prolific non-research authors’5 is unlikely to contribute to the development of science but rather serves the personal ambitions of the authors. It can even dangerously dilute the gain in scientific knowledge as it may distract readers from the ‘real’ science. If non-scientists consider letters to the editor published in a scientific journal as equally valid as robust research reports, there is an obvious risk that opinion and politics could overwhelm science.6 A new player in the field is ChatGPT, an artificial intelligence (AI) language model belonging to the family of natural language processing.7 ChatGPT is very powerful in interpreting and generating text, and some of the most common use cases include chatbots, automated writing, and content creation. Although texts generated by ChatGPT closely resemble those written by humans, it is possible to detect whether they are human-generated or AI-generated.8 Parameters such as perplexity and burstiness serve as indicators to distinguish between human- and AI-generated texts. Though not flawless, these indicators can help in the differentiation process. We recently came across a letter to the editor that appeared to be off-topic. When using an AI detector to check the document (https://gptzero.me/), we found that 60% of the letter was likely written by an AI language model, as indicated by the low perplexity and burstiness scores. Further investigation of the senior author’s publications in PubMed revealed that their very first paper was published on 18 May 2023. Since then (data cut: 27 July 2023), 11 letters to the editor have been published, all with relatively low perplexity and burstiness scores, suggesting AI involvement (data on file). Interestingly, 9 out of the 11 letters were published in the same journal. Although the case described here is anecdotal, it raises the possibility that some authors might be inclined to become ‘letter to the editor generating factories’, catalysed by AI language models. While generative AI certainly has its place in healthcare and science,9 this practice should be added to the list of questionable research practices.10 Dealing with such letters will demand significant time and efforts from editors and original authors in crafting responses, without substantially adding to the scientific discourse. Therefore, the publishing industry needs to develop policies, and editorial offices should be equipped with state-of-the-art AI detectors to identify the fraudulent use of AI in the academic writing process.9 There is no funding for this work. Conflict of interest: None declared. No original data have been used in this editorial.

title: La lettre de motivation assistée par IA : un outil d'inclusion rédactionnelle ou d'exclusion des apprentissages ? Étude expérimentale en Master LEA
abstract: La lettre de motivation assistée par IA : un outil d'inclusion rédactionnelle ou d'exclusion des apprentissages ? Étude expérimentale en Master LEABenjamin Holt11Université de Lille, France.RésuméCette étude examine l’impact de l’assistance par intelligence artificielle générative sur la performance en expression écrite et sur les perceptions d’étudiants de Master en anglais de spécialité. Dans le cadre d’un cours de langue professionnelle en Master LEA à l’Université de Lille, deux groupes équivalents (20 à 25 étudiants chacun) ont réalisé la même tâche en conditions contrôlées : la rédaction d’une lettre de motivation en anglais. Le groupe expérimental pouvait utiliser ChatGPT de manière non guidée, tandis que le groupe témoin disposait uniquement de Microsoft Word. Aucun accès à Internet n’était autorisé, à l'exception de l'accès à ChatGPT pour le groupe expérimental.Un questionnaire pré- et post-test, administré en français, a mesuré les attitudes envers l’IA, la confiance linguistique, les stratégies d’écriture et certaines variables socioprofessionnelles. Les productions écrites ont été évaluées à l’aide d’une grille commune portant sur la structure du texte, la cohérence, la richesse lexicale, la correction grammaticale et la pertinence argumentative. L’analyse a également pris en compte l’adéquation entre la lettre et l’offre d’emploi proposée, notamment la capacité des étudiants à mobiliser les informations issues de la description du poste et des articles de presse fournis sur l’entreprise afin de personnaliser leur argumentation. Un post-activité a évalué la connaissance des principes structuraux de la lettre de motivation.L’analyse comparative vise à déterminer si l’assistance par IA améliore la qualité linguistique objective, modifie le sentiment d’efficacité personnelle et influence l’engagement des apprenants dans le processus de rédaction. Une éventuelle dissociation entre amélioration du produit écrit et compréhension des principes rédactionnels constituerait un indicateur d’exclusion développementale : performance accrue sans consolidation des compétences sous-jacentes.Cette recherche s’inscrit dans une perspective sociocognitive de l’écriture et de l’apprentissage médié par les outils numériques. Dans le prolongement du modèle processuel de l’écriture de Flower & Hayes (1981), l’IA peut intervenir à différents stades de la production écrite (planification, mise en texte, révision) et suppose des compétences spécifiques en littératie numérique et en IA (Ng et al., 2021). Du point de vue socioculturel, il convient de distinguer performance assistée et transformation développementale au sein de la zone proximale de développement (Xi & Lantolf, 2021). L’IA peut fonctionner comme outil de médiation, mais elle peut également favoriser une externalisation excessive des processus rédactionnels (cognitive offloading) susceptible de réduire l’engagement stratégique (Risko & Gilbert, 2016). L’analyse mobilise également la notion de sentiment d’efficacité personnelle (Bandura, 2001) afin d’examiner si l’amélioration éventuelle des performances s’accompagne d’un développement métacognitif ou d’une dissociation entre performance observable et appropriation procédurale. Enfin, la réflexion s’inscrit dans un questionnement plus large sur l’agentivité des enseignants et des apprenants à l’ère de l’IA générative (Godwin-Jones, 2024).Références bibliographiquesBandura, A. title: Stop perfecting the feedback, start supporting the uptake: rethinking AI in writing instruction
abstract: This article discusses the use of text-generating AI applications for providing feedback on students' texts and to help them revise their writing. While feedback through applications based on generative AI (for example, ChatGPT or specific tools such as Writing Coach, Writeable, and others) is often evaluated in terms of quality, even in comparison to feedback from human teachers (Mah et al., 2025;Seßler et al., 2025;Steiss et al., 2024), it is often overlooked that the most important thing is for learners to use and process the feedback to revise their texts (e.g. Lipnevich & Smith, 2022). However, when considering learning situations in elementary and secondary schools, it appears that if text revision takes place at all, it is rarely in a form where previously provided feedback guides the revision (Jansen et al., 2025;Rong et al., 2025). AI appears to have little or no impact on this initial situation, which is what this article aims to discuss. To this end, it is divided into three parts: The first step is to present the potential of genAI for providing feedback on learner texts and to highlight the problem that many learners in elementary and secondary schools do not meaningfully engage with AI-generated feedback for revision. In a second step, we will discuss how this may be due not only to the way AI works, but also to the unfavourable integration of feedback into teaching and learning processes. To provide an alternative, the third step will outline a teaching model that aims to achieve effective integration.Feedback is widely recognized as one of the most powerful tools for supporting learner development in writing (Hattie & Timperley, 2007;MacArthur, 2016;Wisniewski et al., 2020). This holds true for learning to write in the context of L1 acquisition as well as in the context of L2-writing (Hyland, 2016;Hyland & Hyland, 2019). However, for feedback to be effective, it should consist of an internal structure of feed up (Where am I going?), feed back (How am I going?), and feed forward (Where to next?), and be relevant to the learners and given in a timely manner (Brandmo & Gamlem, 2025;Gibbs & Simpson, 2004).Yet, providing feedback that is both timely and targeted remains a significant challenge, especially when teachers are faced with lengthy student texts and larger heterogeneous learning groups (Applebee & Langer, 2011). The public availability of AI could transform this area and take some of the burden of providing feedback off the shoulders of teachers (e.g. Kolade et al., 2024;Nikolopoulou, 2025). Chatbots such as ChatGPT, LeChat, and Gemini, as well as specialized tools like Flint, Writeable, or the Khan Academy's Writing Coach, now deliver instant feedback that numerous studies have shown to resemble human feedback in terms of how it is rated and assessed by researchers (Almegren et al., 2025;Steiss et al., 2024;Usher, 2025). GenAI thus seems to offer teachers a means of transforming feedback from a timeconsuming burden into a more manageable and scalable practice. However, AI-based feedback on texts has conceptual limitations from a writing education perspective. Firstly, the systems are hardly capable of providing feedback on the writing process: Although some AI applications (e.g., Khan Academy's Writing Coach) are able to provide feedback on ideas and drafts, this feedback can only be provided after these texts or text fragments have been entered into the input mask (and submitted) and not during the writing process itself. In other words, the systems are unable to provide feedback on a paragraph, sentence, or word that has just been started while writing. This is particularly problematic given that formative feedback during the writing process has been shown to be crucial for learner development (Graham et al., 2011(Graham et al., , 2015)). Mekheimer (2025) also notes that providing extensive feedback "all at once" at the end of the writing process is suboptimal based on cognitive load theory. Secondly, despite offering high levels of personalisation, AIbased feedback applications may lack depth, logical coherence, and relevance with regard to the learner's text (Elmotri et al., 2025;Venter et al., 2025). It is not uncommon for such applications to focus on the structure of the text, particularly the introduction (e.g. Writing Coach), even when the actual underlying issue in the learner's text is a lack of reader orientation throughout. Individualisation therefore often means measuring all learners in a personalised way while always using "the same yardstick". Thirdly, it is important to remember that AI-based feedback systems (and AI systems in general) only consider the text entered and offer direct solutions on how to improve this specific text. They do not provide any feedback on how writing in general could be improved. This contradicts the goals of learning to write, which also include, for example, identifying problem areas in one's own text and finding alternatives (by oneself) before implementing them (Bereiter & Scardamalia, 1987;Hayes & Flower, 1986). However, if AI applications take over the task of identifying problem areas and searching for alternatives, revising becomes a mindless process of working through AI suggestions, especially for inexperienced writers, which can have a long-term impact on their revision skills and motivation (Helm & Hesse, in press;Jantzen, 2003).While these constraints are important, we would like to turn our attention to what is probably an even more pressing issue: the uptake of AI-generated feedback by learners when revising their writing. Modern feedback research has long pointed out that, in addition to the source of the feedback and the feedback message, the cognitive, behavioural, and affective processing of feedback are also relevant factors -as illustrated, for example, in the Student-Feedback Interaction Model (Lipnevich & Smith, 2022). According to the authors of this model "feedback that is most conducive to improvement is feedback that is somehow processed" (Lipnevich & Smith, 2022, p. 2).Regarding AI-based feedback applications, there is evidence that this processing by students does not take place in a sufficient manner. Both quantitative (Jansen et al., 2025;Yu & Xie, 2025) and qualitative (Rong et al., 2025) analyses of AI feedback usage in text revision revealed that the majority of primary and secondary school students do not make use of it in their revisions. In the context of L1-writing, Jansen et al. (2025) conducted a quantitative study to examine the extent to which elementary and middle school students make changes to their texts after receiving feedback from the German FelloFish platform before submitting them as 'revised versions'. The results showed that 6,889 of the total 14,236 learners surveyed (48%) made no changes at all in response to the AI feedback, while another proportion of learners made only minor changes (Jansen et al., 2025, p. 833). In a detailed examination of the revision process using AI (the Chinese platform Unipus AIGC) among three students in an EFL class, Rong et al. (2025) observed that the highest-performing student in particular was able to efficiently incorporate the AI feedback into their own text, while the weakest learner hardly took the genAI feedback into account. Yu and Xie (2025) compare the uptake of feedback during revision between AI feedback and teacher feedback in high school and show that AI feedback in particular leads to high uptake (86%) in the area of surface-level feedback (e.g., grammar), but only to low uptake (32%) at the meaning level. This suggests that the mere existence of AI feedback does not automatically result in its usage. Notably, similar patterns were already observed in earlier AWE systems such as Criterion (Schroeder et al., 2008), indicating that this problem is not unique to AI but rather endemic to automated feedback in general. Mekheimer (2025) looks at how AI-based feedback applications that target surface features of texts, such as grammar and sentence structure, are used by EFL writers at university. He examines the influence of AI feedback on quality, as well as its frequency of usage. The results show that advanced writers at the university frequently use feedback when revising their work. However, this requires "critical engagement" (Mekheimer, 2025) on the part of the writers, who must weigh up which aspects of the feedback are actually useful for revising their work. This suggests that these complex mental processes are often beyond primary and secondary school writers, preventing them from using the feedback in the first place.Clearly, the mere availability of rapid, personalised feedback through genAI is not a panacea.The assumed benefit of reducing the burden on teachers of providing feedback (e.g. Steiss et al., 2024;Wrede et al., 2023) is immediately negated if learners do not engage with the feedback. When attempting to identify why learners do not take up AI-generated feedback during revision, it would be reasonable to consider potential differences between human and AI feedback. Mah et al. (2025), for example, observe that AI and human teachers may focus on different aspects of a text, providing feedback at disparate levels of text (e.g., primarily at the sentence level in the case of AI). We, however, suspect that neither the (differences in the) quality nor the (technical) functionality of AI-generated feedback alone is responsible for its lack of use by learners, but rather an unfavourable embedding of AI-generated feedback in teaching and the learning processes. The reason for this assumption is that the lack of use of human feedback for text revision, if not properly embedded in teaching, has been recognised for a long time, even before the advent of AI (MacDonald, 1991;Sinclair & Cleland, 2007).We suspect that teachers often present (genAI) feedback as isolated input rather than as a starting point for communication between learners or between learners and teachers.Feedback can be defined as a "dynamic interaction between teacher and student aimed at facilitating learning" (Brandmo & Gamlem, 2025, p. 2). Therefore, the prerequisite for the effectiveness of any type of feedback is that it is embedded in a context that actually allows for dynamic interaction. It would be a mistake to assume that the interactivity of AI feedback by itself (since AI already responds interactively) is sufficient for learning. The task of teachers is (probably now more than ever) to create spaces for dynamic interactions about feedback. Although feedback as such might already be generated by generative AI, teachers should now focus on creating opportunities for discussion about it, i.e. integrating it into social interaction.We suggest approaching AI feedback not as an endpoint but as a catalyst for communication in the classroom. Multi-stage settings can encourage learners to interact with feedback at different levels (Fig. 1). After producing a first draft (phase 1), which generative AI can assist with if necessary, for example by generating ideas, learners receive feedback from the AI in phase 2. In the first crucial revision phase (phase 3), students should revise their texts individually, using AI feedback as a low-stakes starting point. Gero et al. (2023) demonstrate that one of the potentials of AI-based feedback systems is that learners can seek feedback on things that are (still) too personal, so that AI can act as an anonymous support actor (Gero et al., 2023). This seemingly private interaction and work phase helps them address obvious issues in their texts while lowering the threshold for sharing their work later on. Next (phase 4), peer collaboration-whether in pairs or small groups-can create opportunities to discuss both the feedback and its application. This allows the aspect to be fulfilled that feedback is, by definition, a dialogical process and a co-construction in which those receiving feedback never should be reduced to the role of recipients (Brandmo & Gamlem, 2025;Busse et al., 2022).Finally, bringing these discussions back to the whole class (phase 5) enables collective reflection on the quality, appropriateness, and limitations of AI-generated comments. In such a model, the teacher takes on a new role: not as the ultimate judge of text quality, but as a facilitator who helps learners interpret feedback, identify mismatches, and refine their revisions accordingly. This leads to a shift in the teaching dynamic: the teacher is no longer responsible for providing feedback themselves, but they still maintain authority in that they can disagree with or question the AI feedback. After these stages, students should again revise their texts to integrate insights gained from the process.It should be noted that not every writing assignment lends itself to such a multi-stage approach; especially when the texts to be written have clearly defined (and traditional) structures (e.g. argumentative essays), the pattern-oriented approach of AI can provide valuable support in the feedback process. Secondly, the age of the learners must be taken into account. Understanding AI-based feedback alone (Phase 2) places considerable demands on reading skills. In the context of primary school, teacher mediation would certainly be necessary.The position we have outlined in this article has clear implications for AI-oriented research.We propose that, when it comes to research in writing, equal consideration must be given both to the quality of AI feedback and to how AI feedback is embedded in writing instruction.Rather than merely assessing differences in the quality and quantity of human and AI feedback, or the quality of AI feedback across models, tasks or prompts, empirical studies should also be designed to identify characteristics of learning settings in which feedback on a written text leads to productive revision. Studies should also be designed to identify characteristics of learning settings in which feedback on a written text, whether AI-based or not, leads to productive revision (uptake). Examining and identifying the prerequisites for feedback uptake and the goals that teachers and learners associate with it, as well as the extent to which these influence uptake, are key to providing teachers with specific guidance on designing effective learning scenarios. So too will investigating the extent to which a tailormade educational setting can increase uptake. These questions remain relevant even without AI-based feedback. However, they become even more pertinent when AI facilitates feedback, potentially reintroducing it into everyday teaching. Against this backdrop, we should also take advantage of the current focus on AI feedback to address important research questions independent of it (Jensen et al., 2024), particularly those concerning the conditions for effective writing feedback.

title: OpenAI’s Sora: it’s time to update the dissemination methods of medical findings
abstract: The fervor surrounding the utilization of the large language model, ChatGPT, remains unabated1-2. On 16 February 2024, OpenAI introduced Sora, a text-to-video model heralding a significant advancement in artificial intelligence (AI) technology. Unlike its predecessors, Sora possesses the capability to fabricate sleek, high-resolution videos spanning a duration of 60 s, crafted solely from prompt words. Its repertoire includes an array of vibrant hues and intricate camera maneuvers, symbolizing a paradigm shift in generative AI from textual and pictorial realms to the domain of video production3. In comparison to existing video generation models like DALL-E, GENMO, and PIKA, Sora has attained unprecedented milestones in duration, video quality, and adherence to physical laws. While the prevailing standard for video generation stands at a mere ‘3-4s,’ Sora could produce videos up to 1 min in length, all while meticulously adhering to user prompts and maintaining exceptional video quality. Furthermore, Sora boasts profound linguistic comprehension, enabling it to construct emotionally resonant characters and intricate scenarios, and possesses the capacity to decipher and engage with real-world contexts. Many scholars view Sora as a watershed moment in artificial intelligence’s capacity to interpret and visualize temporal narratives, underscoring its profound implications4-5. Leveraging Sora’s considerable potential in video generation, it is imperative to explore its prospective applications in the medical domain. Firstly, within the realm of surgical planning, whereas ChatGPT is confined to text-based blueprints, Sora empowers the generation of comprehensive surgical videos, offering visual insights into procedural intricacies. These visual aids not only facilitate preoperative planning and risk assessment but also mitigate surgical hazards, thereby enhancing patient safety. In medical pedagogy and training, Sora’s ability to generate high-fidelity instructional videos could be invaluable. Different from ChatGPT’s personalized interaction and instant feedback, Sora can effectively convey complex medical information with its vivid visual and multi-sensory experience and is suitable for large-scale medical education and promotion6. These videos could elucidate intricate medical procedures and case studies, serving as vital educational resources for aspiring medical professionals. Additionally, medical case analysis videos foster a deeper understanding of diagnostic methodologies and treatment protocols, thereby refining clinical acumen. In addition, Virtual Reality (VR) is a technology that uses computer systems to create immersive virtual environments, allowing users to experience a simulated world through multiple senses such as sight and sound. The application of VR technology in the field of surgery offers significant advantages7. Firstly, through VR, surgeons could access essential patient data, such as ultrasound, mammography, CT, and MRI scans, in real time during surgical procedures. This information, traditionally limited to 2D flat screens, could now be projected directly into the operating room. This eliminates the need for surgeons to frequently check a separate screen, allowing them to focus entirely on the patient. Additionally, VR headsets enable surgeons to instantly access all necessary digital files, images, and data, thereby enhancing the precision and efficiency of surgeries. Taking spine surgery as an example, the portability and image projection capabilities of VR greatly benefit spine surgeons. During procedures, VR technology simplifies the insertion of pedicle screws and eliminates the need for surgeons to divert their gaze to other devices. Real-time surgical guidance through 3D visualization and augmented reality significantly improves the accuracy and efficiency of spine surgeries. High-fidelity surgical videos generated by text-to-video tools, combined with VR technology, allow medical students to practice surgeries in a virtual environment, reducing the reliance on actual human and animal experiments. In the realm of public health education, videos emerge as potent tools for disseminating medical knowledge. Their visual and auditory appeal renders complex medical concepts more accessible, facilitating enhanced comprehension and retention. Moreover, their versatility enables widespread dissemination across various online platforms (such as YouTube and TikTok), transcending geographic and demographic barriers and reaching diverse audiences, including medical practitioners, patients, and the general populace. For example, in the early stages of the COVID-19 pandemic, the World Health Organization (WHO) produced a series of short videos about protective measures against the coronavirus. These videos were rapidly disseminated through social media platforms, enhancing public awareness and knowledge of protective measures8. More importantly, AI also could play a crucial role in drug discovery and development, as well as clinical trials9-11. By combining natural language processing and computer vision technologies, OpenAI’s Sora could support various aspects of drug research. First, drug development generates vast amounts of complex data, such as genomic and protein structure data. Sora is able to transform this complex data into intuitive videos, aiding researchers in better understanding and analyzing the information12-13. Additionally, this technology could create virtual laboratories to simulate drug synthesis, screening, and testing processes, reducing the risks and costs associated with actual operations. Furthermore, dynamically displaying molecular interactions helps researchers better understand the relationships between drugs and their targets. Finally, the ultimate goal of drug development is public use. Through engaging videos, Sora could translate complex scientific discoveries into easily understandable content, explaining the progress and significance of drug research to the public and investors. Lastly, traditional academic discourse predominantly relies on written mediums such as papers and reports. While text effectively communicates intricate academic concepts, its efficacy is marred by reader fatigue. In contrast, video content, with its audio-visual presentation, offers a more engaging and dynamic medium for conveying abstract notions and research findings. Particularly in elucidating complex experimental procedures or research methodologies, videos offer unparalleled clarity, fostering deeper understanding and mastery. As such, the incorporation of video content into academic communication is poised to assume greater prominence. Notably, an increasing number of scholarly journals advocate for the creation of video abstracts for dissemination on public platforms, indicative of the burgeoning role of video content in scholarly discourse. The advent of Sora portends a transformative trajectory for medical video production, promising to catalyze advancements in academic communication and knowledge dissemination.
