title: Cohort Profile Update: The ‘Seguimiento Universidad de Navarra’ (SUN) study after 24 years of follow-up
abstract: The SUN project is an open-enrolment cohort in Spain that includes 23 321 university graduates, 61.5% of whom are women. It started in December 1999 to investigate the association between the Mediterranean dietary pattern and other lifestyle-related factors and chronic diseases. Follow-up questionnaires are sent every 2 years. The retention rate is 90.6%. This paper updates the earlier profile. Several new areas of research have been developed within the SUN project: mortality, wellbeing, validations and confirmations of different diseases, SARS-CoV-2, and the development of new scores to assess different aspects of health and lifestyle (oxidative balance, macronutrient quality index, definitions of healthy lifestyles, the Paleo-Diet, sustainable diet, dietary obesity prevention index, and diabetes prevention and dietary-based diabetes-risk scores). The database is available to external researchers following the project purposes. Access to the SUN project data can be requested to the SUN Steering Committee at [email protected]. More information is provided at www.proyectosun.es. The SUN project is a Spanish prospective cohort study primarily aimed to investigate the effects of the Mediterranean dietary pattern (MDP) on chronic diseases [1]. The first participants were recruited in December 1999 (n = 79). The cohort is permanently open. The invitations have been sent in waves. The initial mass mailing was done on a large scale to all alumni of the University of Navarra and collaborations with professional associations all across the country. Subsequently, invitations were extended to other professional groups such as regional associations of physicians, nurses, pharmacists, dentists, and engineers. Currently, we are focused on participants’ follow-up. However, invitations are sent to the new University of Navarra graduates each year (∼1600 per year) to increase the number of participants. Therefore, the recruitment has not been homogeneous, with a median of 277 (interquartile range: 687) new participants per year answering the baseline questionnaire (Q0) (Figure 1). The overall response rate is 10%. Annual number of baseline questionnaires received in the SUN cohort (1999–2023). This bar graph illustrates the number of baseline questionnaires submitted by participants each year within the SUN cohort. The data demonstrate temporal trends in cohort recruitment over a 24-year period. The first participants, recruited between December 1999 and December 2000 (n = 4631), have been followed for 24 years. The global retention rate is 90.6%. The Q0 gathers information on socio-demographic characteristics, diet and other lifestyle-related factors, chronic diseases, and treatments. A new questionnaire is sent every 2 years (named ‘Q2’, ‘Q4’, ‘Q6’, until ‘Q24’, depending on the number of years since the participant entered the cohort). A short questionnaire (‘Q_brief’) is sent to participants who do not respond after five mailings. Since the first SUN cohort profile publication (in 2006), nine new questionnaires have been sent. Since April 2004, participants have been able to respond online. In 2018, Carlos et al. [2] reviewed 21 studies from the SUN project that focused on the association between the MDP and several incident chronic diseases, concluding that high Mediterranean diet adherence was associated with a lower incidence of all-cause mortality, cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, weight gain, metabolic syndrome, depression, cognitive decline, and nephrolithiasis, and with a lower heart rate and mitigation of the effects of obesity on cardiovascular disease (CVD) and type 2 diabetes, and our results suggested that the Mediterranean diet may improve fertility. Since the 2018 review, several sub-studies and new validations have been carried out. This paper provides an update of the collected data (Table 1) and new research areas (Supplementary Table S1). The average age of participants has increased, contributing to a higher incidence of age-related diseases, including cognitive decline and neurodegenerative diseases. The number of deceased participants has also increased from 384 deaths in 2018 to 885 in 2024. This allows us to assess risk factors associated with all-cause mortality and cause-specific mortality more accurately. Several specific areas of research have been developed within the SUN project. Participants who were older than 55 years were invited in two recruitment waves (in 2008 and 2014) to a sub-study on cognitive function. In this sub-study, in addition to assessing cognitive impairment by telephone testing (initially, after 2 years and after 6 years), participants were asked to submit saliva samples (a single sample at the beginning of the sub-study) to obtain genomic DNA. Until June 2024, 1918 subjects had answered at least the initial cognitive function-related telephone interview and, among them, 1827 sent saliva samples. A commercial kit for the sample collection (Oragene DNA OG-500 saliva extraction kit from DNA Genotek) was sent by ordinary mail to the participants who agreed to donate saliva samples. The kit included an all-in-one system for the collection, stabilization, and transportation of the saliva. Real-time polymerase chain reaction (PCR) was performed to analyse the following genetic variants: APOE4, CLU, CR1, FTO, PICALM, CETP, TREM2, and FADS1. Mortality was assessed by using a computerized record linkage to the Spanish National Statistics Institute (https://www.ine.es/en/). Dates and causes of death were recorded and encoded by using the 10th Revision of the International Classification of Diseases (ICD-10) from 1999 to 2022. Between March and June 2017, women who reported one or more pregnancies during the follow-up period were invited to complete an online supplementary questionnaire regarding their pregnancy history and their offspring’s health [3]. The final sample consisted of 1485 women. By June 2018, 2371 physicians younger than 65 years (the retirement age in Spain) had replied to the baseline questionnaire and had provided an e-mail account. Among them, 890 replied to an online questionnaire that focused on their clinical practices related to the counselling provided to their patients and their prescription practices. Doctors’ own personal practices and knowledge of healthy lifestyles may help to provide their patients with counselling on cancer screening and on other behaviours more frequently [4]. From April to December 2020, 9677 participants of the SUN cohort answered a brief online questionnaire on COVID-19, including COVID-19 diagnosis and the corresponding date [5, 6]. In February 2023, a second COVID-19 online questionnaire was sent that included questions about SARS-CoV-2 infection and reinfection, symptoms, persistence, contacts, and other possible associated factors and preventive measures including COVID-19 vaccination and its related adverse effects. Up to June 2024, 4230 participants had answered this questionnaire. The validated Spanish version of Ryff’s questionnaire, which is used to evaluate psychological wellbeing [7], has been included in Q18 to evaluate lifestyles associated with better wellbeing. Health is evaluated from a holistic perspective, including purpose in life, social relationships, solidarity, resilience, and autonomy. The association between these aspects and empowerment, as well as the prevention of chronic diseases, has been analysed. Additionally, the Secure Flourishing Index developed at Harvard University [8] has been included in Q24 to assess the maximum state of optimal and complete wellbeing and its association with depression and other non-communicable diseases prevention. Since 2018, the self-reported diagnoses of metabolic syndrome components [9, 10], depression [11], and gastric and duodenal ulcer have been validated [12]. Additionally, the Spanish version of the modified Telephone Interview for Cognitive Status (STICS-m) [13] has been validated. Validations of other diagnoses including anxiety, psoriasis, and asthma are currently in progress. As of June 2024, 23 321 Spanish university graduates had answered the baseline questionnaire, of whom 23 135 had accumulated enough time in the cohort to complete the first follow-up questionnaire. Out of the latter group, 20 971 (91%) have responded to at least one of the follow-up questionnaires. Q24 has been sent to 3356 participants. The median follow-up of the cohort is 14.2 years. Overall, >122 million data are available from a roster of 304 640 person-years. Globally, there are 14 351 females (61.5%) and 8970 males (38.5%). The age at baseline ranges from 20 to 91 years, with a mean age of 34.8 (SD: 10.8) years for women and 42.2 (SD: 13.4) for men. The mean age of the participants in October 2024 was 57.1 years (SD: 12.7)—54.2 (SD: 11.6) for women and 62.0 (SD: 13.3) for men. Around half of the participants (55.5%) were health professionals. Up to June 2024, 1178 participants had decided to cancel their participation for a variety of reasons. We have lost contact with 500 participants due to addresses changes and unavailable phone numbers or e-mail addresses. As of June 2024, 885 participants had died. The cause of death was registered for 879 participants (99%). The main cause of death was cancer (49%), followed by CVD (20%), neurological diseases (7%), respiratory diseases (6%), and external causes (5% unintentional and 2% suicides).
